knowledge_statements.statement_title: The Class C_L^{k,p}(Q)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantitative differentiability class defined on an arbitrary subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, let k,p\in\mathbb{N} with p\le k, and let L\ge 0. The class C_L^{k,p}(Q) consists of all functions f:Q\to\mathbb{R} such that f\in C^k(Q) and \|\nabla^p f(x)-\nabla^p f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\| for all x,y\in Q.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The class C_L^{k,p}(Q) contains exactly the k-times continuously differentiable functions on Q whose p-th derivative is Lipschitz continuous on Q with constant L.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n
k,p\in\mathbb{N},\quad p\le k
L\ge 0
f:Q\to\mathbb{R}

children.title: Nonsmooth Regularity
children.top_down_role: Lipschitz plus related nonsmooth classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz convex objectives normalized through either function variation or bounded subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space. A proper convex function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is \(G\)-Lipschitz on \(C\) if \[|f(x)-f(y)|\le G\|x-y\|\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in C.\] If \(C\) is open, this is equivalent to \(\|g\|_*\le G\) for every \(x\in C\) and every \(g\in\partial f(x)\). On a nonopen constrained domain, bounded subgradients remain a sufficient normalization, while the converse may require a relative or extended-valued subdifferential convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth regularity is commonly normalized by a Lipschitz constant, equivalently by uniformly bounded convex subgradients on an open domain.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and finite-dimensional.
\(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is proper, finite-valued, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(G\)-Lipschitz on \(C\); on open \(C\), this is equivalent to \(\sup_{g\in\partial f(x)}\|g\|_*\le G\).

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of f at x.

children.title: Strong Convexity
children.top_down_role: Strongly convex regimes with condition-sensitive complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued strong convexity relative to a chosen norm, stated through the convex-combination inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space, and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. For \(\mu>0\), the function is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on \(C\) with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\) if, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)\le (1-t)f(x)+t f(y)-\frac{\mu}{2}t(1-t)\|x-y\|^2.\] At every \(x\in C\) with \(f(x)<+\infty\) where a convex subgradient \(g\in\partial f(x)\) exists, this condition yields \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for all }y\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity strengthens the convex-combination inequality by a quadratic distance term. At points admitting a convex subgradient, every such affine model has the corresponding quadratic growth margin.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and finite-dimensional.
\(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\).

children.title: Uniform Convexity
children.top_down_role: Higher-order growth regimes between standard convexity classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type uniform convexity, normalized to recover strong convexity when \(p=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. For \(p\ge2\) and \(\sigma>0\), the function is uniformly convex of power type \(p\) with modulus \(\sigma\) if, for every \(x,y\in C\) with \(f(x)<+\infty\) and every \(g\in\partial f(x)\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{p}\|y-x\|^p.\] Under this normalization, \(p=2\) is ordinary strong convexity with modulus \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-type uniform convexity strengthens each subgradient model by a p-th-power distance term; the quadratic case is strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and finite-dimensional.
\(f\) is proper and convex on \(C\).
\(p\ge2\) and \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is uniformly convex of power type \(p\) with modulus \(\sigma\).

notation.meaning: Power in the uniform-convexity growth term.
Uniform-convexity modulus under the stated normalization.

Because uniform-convexity constants and factors vary across references, a source with a precise definition or theorem locator supporting the σ/p normalization is required.

children.title: Weakly Convex Geometry
children.top_down_role: Weakly convex classes used for stationarity lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Convex Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean weak convexity expressed by convexification with a quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. For \(\rho\ge0\), the function is \(\rho\)-weakly convex on \(C\) if \[x\longmapsto f(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|_2^2\] is convex on \(C\). Equivalently, whenever the limiting subdifferential is used and the subgradient inequality is valid, \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle-\frac{\rho}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2\] for admissible \(x,y\in C\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\). The case \(\rho=0\) reduces to convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly convex function becomes convex after adding a quadratic; its subgradient model may violate convexity by at most a controlled quadratic amount.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is convex.
\(f\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f+(\rho/2)\|\cdot\|_2^2\) is convex on \(C\).

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential in the equivalent inequality.

review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports weak convexity and its subdifferential convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Quadratic convexification is a standard Euclidean definition and fits this leaf. The additional limiting-subdifferential equivalence is qualified only by the circular phrase 'whenever ... the subgradient inequality is valid'; its exact hypotheses and admissible points depend on the chosen subdifferential and domain convention. A source directly supporting both weak convexity and the stated subgradient characterization is required.

children.title: Nonconvex Curvature
children.top_down_role: General nonconvex regimes lacking global convex structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided Euclidean curvature class for twice-differentiable nonconvex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. Given finite constants \(m\le M\), the function has curvature in \([m,M]\) on \(C\) if \[mI\preceq\nabla^2 f(x)\preceq MI\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Equivalently, for all \(x,y\in C\), \[\frac{m}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2\le f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\le\frac{M}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2.\] The class permits nonconvexity when \(m<0\); the quantity \(-m\) bounds negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex curvature class bounds every Hessian eigenvalue between m and M; negative m permits controlled nonconvexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is open and convex.
\(-\infty<m\le M<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(mI\preceq\nabla^2 f(x)\preceq MI\) throughout \(C\), with nonconvexity allowed when \(m<0\).
review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports the chosen two-sided nonconvex curvature class

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-sided Hessian class and Taylor-remainder equivalence are mathematically coherent under the stated open convex C² assumptions, and definition is an appropriate content kind. No source is supplied for this particular two-sided normalization or its use as the terminal nonconvex-curvature class.

children.title: Bounded-Domain Geometry
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound regimes parameterized by domain size.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Domain Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diameter normalization for constrained first-order complexity statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty feasible subset of a finite-dimensional normed space. The domain has bounded geometry with diameter parameter \(D<+\infty\) when \[\operatorname{diam}_{\|\cdot\|}(C):=\sup\{\|x-y\|:x,y\in C\}\le D.\] Consequently, for every initialization \(x_0\in C\) and every optimizer \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), one has \(\|x_0-x_\star\|\le D\). The parameter \(D\) depends on the selected norm and should therefore be paired with regularity constants measured in the associated dual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-domain geometry fixes a finite feasible-set diameter, which uniformly bounds the distance from any feasible initialization to any optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty feasible subset of a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(D<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diam}_{\|\cdot\|}(C)\le D\), hence \(\|x_0-x_\star\|\le D\) for feasible \(x_0,x_\star\).

notation.meaning: A minimizer over the feasible set.

children.title: Distance-Controlled Initialization
children.top_down_role: Complexity comparisons controlled by initial solution distance.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Controlled Initialization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initial-distance normalization relative to the solution set rather than the entire feasible domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) in a finite-dimensional normed space, and suppose the solution set \(X_\star:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is nonempty. An initial point \(x_0\in C\) is distance-controlled with radius \(R\) when \[\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|}(x_0,X_\star):=\inf_{x_\star\in X_\star}\|x_0-x_\star\|\le R.\] If the infimum is attained, this is equivalent to the existence of \(x_\star\in X_\star\) satisfying \(\|x_0-x_\star\|\le R\). This normalization does not require \(C\) itself to be bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance-controlled initialization bounds the starting point’s distance to the solution set, even when the feasible domain is unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) lies in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(X_\star\ne\varnothing\).
\(x_0\in C\) and \(R\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|}(x_0,X_\star)\le R\).

notation.meaning: Distance induced by the selected norm.

children.title: Level-Set Geometry
children.top_down_role: Regimes controlled through initial or reachable level sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry normalized on the initial sublevel set that descent methods are expected to retain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap C\), and define the initial sublevel set \[L_0:=\{x\in C:f(x)\le f(x_0)\}.\] A level-set radius bound relative to the nonempty solution set \(X_\star\) is \[R_{L_0}:=\sup_{x\in L_0}\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|}(x,X_\star)<+\infty.\] Any monotone method satisfying \(f(x_k)\le f(x_0)\) for every iterate remains in \(L_0\) and therefore obeys \(\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|}(x_k,X_\star)\le R_{L_0}\), even if the full feasible set is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level-set geometry bounds distances only on the initial sublevel set; every monotone iterate then inherits that bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap C\).
\(X_\star:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)\le f(x_0)\) implies \(\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|}(x_k,X_\star)\le R_{L_0}\).

notation.meaning: Sublevel set determined by the initial objective value.
Maximum distance from the initial sublevel set to the solution set.

children.title: Norm-Dependent Geometry
children.top_down_role: Domain plus initialization measures tied to a selected norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Dependent Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistent primal-dual normalization of distances, gradients, and first-order complexity parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on a finite-dimensional vector space and its dual norm \(\|s\|_*:=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\langle s,x\rangle\). Geometry-dependent complexity parameters must use this pair consistently: domain or initialization size is measured by \(R:=\|x_0-x_\star\|\) or a diameter in \(\|\cdot\|\), while subgradient size is measured by \(G:=\sup\|g\|_*\). The pairing inequality \[\langle g,x-y\rangle\le\|g\|_*\|x-y\|\] makes products such as \(GR\) invariant under reciprocal rescaling of the primal and dual norms, permitting meaningful comparison of normalized bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complexity constants must use a consistent primal norm for distances and its dual norm for gradients; their paired products are scaling-consistent.
assumptions_latex: The ambient vector space is finite-dimensional.
\(\|\cdot\|_*\) is dual to \(\|\cdot\|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle g,x-y\rangle\le\|g\|_*\|x-y\|\), so primal-distance and dual-gradient parameters form consistent complexity scales.

notation.meaning: Dual regularity bound and primal distance bound.

children.title: Structured Objective Classes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for composite, finite-sum, coordinate, saddle, network, and subspace structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Objective Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical structural representations used to stratify first-order oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A structured objective class is specified by restricting \(f\) to one or more canonical representations: composite form \(f(x)=h(Ax)+r(x)\); finite-sum form \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\); coordinate-access form with queries to selected components of \(\nabla f(x)\); saddle form \(f(x)=\sup_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)\); network form \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x_i)\) with consensus constraints; or subspace form with iterates restricted to an affine or Krylov subspace. A complexity comparison is class-consistent only when the representation and its permitted specialized oracle are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structured classes distinguish composite, finite-sum, coordinate, saddle, network, and subspace representations together with the oracle access each representation permits.
assumptions_latex: All component functions, operators, feasible sets, and oracle interfaces in the selected representation are specified.
The compared methods receive the same structural access.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected representation and oracle interface define the structured problem class used for complexity comparison.

notation.meaning: Linear operator in a composite representation.
Number of component functions in a finite sum.
Payoff or coupling function in a saddle representation.

children.title: Local First-Order Information
children.top_down_role: Navigation for exact value, gradient, subgradient, directional, and residual information.

knowledge_statements.title: Local First-Order Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise information interface underlying deterministic local first-order oracle models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), a local first-order information interface answers a query \(x\in C\) using data determined at \(x\). Canonical responses are an exact value \(f(x)\); a gradient \(\nabla f(x)\) when differentiable; a selected subgradient \(g\in\partial f(x)\); a directional derivative map \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)\), or its value for a queried direction; and a residual \(F(x)\) whose zero encodes stationarity or feasibility. An oracle model must specify which response components are returned, whether selections are adversarial or fixed, and assign one query cost to that complete response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local first-order oracle returns specified pointwise values, gradients, subgradients, directional derivatives, or residuals, with selection rules and query cost fixed in advance.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in C\) is an admissible query point.
The objective or residual operator has the regularity required by each requested response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declared response tuple and selection convention determine the local first-order information available per query.

notation.meaning: Specified subdifferential at the query point.
Directional derivative at x in direction d.
Local residual whose zero represents a target condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum first-order interface with one indexed component exposed per query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), where every \(f_i\) is proper and admits a subgradient at each query point in its domain. A component first-order oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{comp}}\) that, given \((i,x)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\times\mathbb{R}^d\), returns \((f_i(x),g_i(x))\) with \(g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\). One oracle call reveals information about only the selected component; obtaining analogous information for all components at the same point requires \(n\) component calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component oracle evaluates one selected finite-sum term and one of its subgradients; evaluating every term at a common point costs n component calls.
assumptions_latex: \(\partial f_i(x)\neq\varnothing\) at every permitted query point
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{comp}}(i,x)=(f_i(x),g_i(x)),\quad g_i(x)\in\partial f_i(x)\)
review_flags: Exact value-and-subgradient component-oracle convention lacks a supplied supporting locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the component-access leaf, but no inspectable citation supports the exact value-and-subgradient response bundle. The query domain is also stated as all of R^d although a proper extended-valued component need not be finite or subdifferentiable there; the permitted query domain and the meaning of the subdifferential require authoritative calibration.

abla_j f(x)=\langle
abla f(x),e_jangle\), optionally together with \(f(x)\) when value access is included in the declared model. A query therefore reveals one specified coordinate of the gradient rather than the full vector \(
abla f(x)\); full coordinate enumeration at a fixed point uses \(d\) coordinate queries.

children.title: Proximal Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Structured nonsmooth information supplied through proximal responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean proximal interface for a proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex. A proximal oracle for \(h\) accepts \((x,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times(0,\infty)\) and returns the unique point \(z\) minimizing the strongly convex function \(u\mapsto h(u)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|u-x\|_2^2\). Equivalently, its output satisfies \((x-z)/\lambda\in\partial h(z)\). Each invocation is counted as one proximal-oracle query, independently of the internal work required to compute \(z\), unless that work is separately charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal oracle returns the exact minimizer of a function plus a scaled squared-distance regularizer; its internal computation is abstracted as one query.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb{R}^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex
\(\lambda>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{prox}}(x,\lambda)=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(x)=\arg\min_u\{h(u)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|u-x\|_2^2\}\)

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Minimization Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-minimization interface over a fixed feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty and compact. A linear-minimization oracle for \(C\) accepts a vector \(g\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and returns some \(s(g)\in\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle g,s\rangle\), together with the minimum value if the declared interface includes it. Ties may be resolved arbitrarily but consistently with membership in the displayed argmin set. One invocation counts as one linear-minimization query; projections onto \(C\), membership tests, and the oracle's internal arithmetic are not available unless separately specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-minimization oracle returns a feasible point minimizing a supplied linear objective over the fixed domain, with arbitrary valid tie-breaking.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty and compact
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{LMO}}(g)=s(g)\in\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle g,s\rangle\)
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the linear-minimization-oracle convention.

children.title: Sample Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Fresh random samples or stochastic first-order observations.

knowledge_statements.title: Sample Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased stochastic first-order interface for an expectation objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\phi(x;\xi)]\) on \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). A sample first-order oracle, queried at \(x\in X\), draws a fresh sample \(\xi\) independently of the algorithm's past conditional on \(x\), and returns \(G(x,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The interface is unbiased when \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial F(x)\) and integrable when \(\mathbb{E}\|G(x,\xi)\|_2<\infty\). One query counts one sample draw and its associated stochastic first-order evaluation; reuse of stored samples must be declared separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sample oracle draws fresh randomness and returns an integrable stochastic first-order vector whose conditional expectation is a subgradient of the population objective.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\phi(x;\xi)]\) is well defined on \(X\)
\(\mathbb{E}\|G(x,\xi)\|_2<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial F(x)\)
review_flags: No supplied locator establishes the fresh-sample and unbiasedness convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record coherently specifies one stochastic first-order model, but no source supports the combined fresh-sample, conditional-independence, integrability, and unbiased-subgradient assumptions. These choices materially distinguish stochastic oracle models and require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Distributed Information Access
children.top_down_role: Information partitioned across workers or network nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Information Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous graph-based interface combining local oracle calls with neighbor communication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a communication graph with agent \(v\in V\) holding local data or a local function \(f_v\). Under synchronous distributed information access, each round permits every agent to perform declared local computations and oracle calls, send one message to each neighbor, receive the messages sent along incident edges in that round, and update its state from its prior state, local information, and received messages. Information originating at one agent can affect an agent at graph distance \(r\) only after at least \(r\) communication rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Agents access local information and exchange messages with graph neighbors in synchronous rounds; information needs at least graph-distance-many rounds to propagate.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is the fixed communication graph
Communication is synchronous and restricted to edges in \(E\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)>r\Rightarrow\text{agent }v\text{ cannot depend on information originating at }u\text{ after only }r\text{ rounds}\)

notation.meaning: local objective or data source at agent v

children.title: Oracle Query Cost
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured by calls to the stipulated oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Query Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case count of calls to the declared information oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance class \(\mathcal{F}\), an oracle \(\mathcal{O}\), an algorithm \(A\), an error functional \(\operatorname{err}_F\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). For instance \(F\), let \(T_A(F,\varepsilon)\) be the first query index at which the algorithm's designated output \(x_T\) satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{err}_F(x_T)]\leq\varepsilon\), with \(T_A(F,\varepsilon)=+\infty\) if this never occurs. The oracle-query cost is \(Q_A(\varepsilon;\mathcal{F},\mathcal{O})=\sup_{F\in\mathcal{F}}T_A(F,\varepsilon)\). The oracle response and admissible adaptivity must be fixed before comparing costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-query cost is the worst-case number of declared oracle calls needed for the algorithm's output to meet a specified expected-error tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\)
The oracle model \(\mathcal{O}\), instance class \(\mathcal{F}\), and error functional are fixed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_A(\varepsilon;\mathcal{F},\mathcal{O})=\sup_{F\in\mathcal{F}}T_A(F,\varepsilon)\)
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this expected-error worst-case query convention.
Alternative high-probability and deterministic conventions require explicit calibration.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports this particular worst-case expected-error convention. The definition also needs calibration as to whether T_A is a deterministic first successful query budget or a random stopping time, since those interpretations lead to different formulas and complexity notions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle-Call Complexity at Accuracy Epsilon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines analytical complexity using calls to the stipulated oracle rather than arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a method \(\mathcal M\), problem instance \(P\), and accuracy target \(\epsilon>0\), its analytical complexity is the number \(N_{\mathcal O}(\mathcal M,P,\epsilon)\) of calls to the stipulated oracle \(\mathcal O\) required by \(\mathcal M\) to solve \(P\) to accuracy \(\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The analytical complexity of a method on a problem at accuracy epsilon is the number of stipulated oracle calls needed to attain that accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \epsilon>0
\mathcal M\text{ is a method for problem instance }P
\mathcal O\text{ is the stipulated oracle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{\mathrm{analytical}}(\mathcal M,P,\epsilon)=N_{\mathcal O}(\mathcal M,P,\epsilon)

children.title: Component Evaluation Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Component Evaluation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Count of individual finite-sum component evaluations used by an algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\), assign unit cost whenever an algorithm requests the declared information from one indexed component \(f_i\) at one point, such as \(f_i(x)\), a component gradient, or both when jointly returned by the model. If \(B_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is the multiset of component indices evaluated at step \(t\), then the component-evaluation cost through step \(T\) is \(C_{\mathrm{comp}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}|B_t|\). Repeated evaluations and duplicate indices are charged repeatedly; cached reuse is free unless recomputation occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component-evaluation cost sums the number of finite-sum terms queried at every step, counting repeats and all elements of each minibatch.
assumptions_latex: Each requested component response has unit cost under the declared interface
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{comp}}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}|B_t|\)

children.title: Data-Pass Cost
children.top_down_role: Complexity normalized by full traversals of a dataset.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Pass Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dataset-normalized component-access cost, allowing fractional passes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a dataset of \(n\) items, let \(C_{\mathrm{data}}(T)\) denote the total number of item-level evaluations or reads performed through step \(T\), counting repeated accesses. The data-pass cost is the normalized quantity \(P(T)=C_{\mathrm{data}}(T)/n\). Thus one complete sequential scan has cost \(1\), a minibatch of size \(b\) has cost \(b/n\), and \(k\) complete scans have cost \(k\). This convention measures access volume rather than distinct items seen, access order, arithmetic work, or storage traffic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data-pass cost divides total item accesses by dataset size, so a full scan costs one and minibatches contribute fractional passes.
assumptions_latex: The dataset has finite size \(n\geq1\)
Each item-level access is counted once per occurrence
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(T)=C_{\mathrm{data}}(T)/n\)
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the fractional-pass normalization.
The accounting boundary between logical examples and physical reads requires model-specific confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fractional-pass formula is internally consistent and belongs in this definition leaf, but no inspectable citation supports normalization by total item-level accesses or the stated boundary between logical accesses and physical reads.

children.title: Arithmetic Work

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential scalar-operation count under a fixed arithmetic cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a unit-cost arithmetic model specifying the scalar operations that are charged. For an execution represented by a directed acyclic computation graph \(D=(V,E)\), assign each operation vertex \(v\in V\) a nonnegative cost \(w(v)\). The arithmetic work is \(W(D)=\sum_{v\in V}w(v)\); under the flop convention, scalar additions, multiplications, and other declared floating-point operations usually have unit cost. Memory movement, oracle calls, communication, and bit complexity are excluded unless the model explicitly assigns them arithmetic weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arithmetic work is the total weighted count of scalar operations in the computation graph under an explicitly fixed operation-cost convention.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,E)\) is a finite computation directed acyclic graph
The operation weights \(w(v)\geq0\) are fixed before comparison
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W(D)=\sum_{v\in V}w(v)\)

children.title: Parallel Depth
children.top_down_role: Adaptive depth under concurrent query execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Depth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-path execution cost with unlimited processors and unit-time dependency layers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,E)\) be a finite directed acyclic computation graph, and let each operation vertex \(v\) have latency \(\ell(v)>0\). With unlimited processors, operations may execute concurrently only when their predecessors have completed. The parallel depth is the weighted critical-path length \(D_{\parallel}=\max_{p}\sum_{v\in p}\ell(v)\), where the maximum ranges over directed paths \(p\) in the graph. For unit latencies, this is the minimum number of sequential dependency layers required by any schedule respecting \(E\), and it can be smaller than total arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel depth is the latency of the longest dependency path, equivalently the minimum number of sequential layers with unlimited processors under unit latencies.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic computation graph
Every operation latency satisfies \(\ell(v)>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\parallel}=\max_{p\text{ directed path in }D}\sum_{v\in p}\ell(v)\)

children.title: Communication-Round Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Round Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Number of synchronous neighbor-exchange phases before the required output criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a synchronous distributed algorithm on \(G=(V,E)\), one communication round consists of every agent forming messages from information available before the round, transmitting them along incident edges, receiving that round's neighbor messages, and updating its local state. If \(x^{(r)}\) is the designated output after round \(r\), the communication-round cost at tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is \(R_A(\varepsilon)=\inf\{r\geq0:\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{err}(x^{(r)})]\leq\varepsilon\}\). children.title: Deterministic Decision Rules
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds for algorithms without internal randomization.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Decision Rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic first-order oracle model with transcript-measurable iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let a first-order oracle return \(O_f(x)=(f(x),g_f(x))\), where \(g_f(x)\in\partial f(x)\). A deterministic decision rule is a sequence of maps \(\Phi_t\) such that, from a fixed initial state \(s_0\), the query and output satisfy \(x_t=\Phi_t(s_0,O_f(x_1),\ldots,O_f(x_{t-1}))\) and \(\widehat x_T=\Phi_{T+1}(s_0,O_f(x_1),\ldots,O_f(x_T))\). Thus identical oracle transcripts produce identical queries and outputs; no auxiliary random variable enters any \(\Phi_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic first-order method chooses every query and its final output as fixed functions of the preceding oracle transcript and initial state, without internal randomness.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in\mathcal F\) is accessed only through the specified first-order oracle.
The initial state \(s_0\) is fixed independently of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\) and \(\widehat x_T\) are uniquely determined by the observed oracle transcript.

notation.meaning: first-order oracle for the objective f
deterministic decision map at stage t

children.title: Randomized Algorithms

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized first-order oracle model with internal seed independent of the instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be an auxiliary random seed independent of \(f\in\mathcal F\). A randomized first-order algorithm is a sequence of measurable maps \(\Phi_t\) with queries \(x_t=\Phi_t(U,s_0,O_f(x_1),\ldots,O_f(x_{t-1}))\) and output \(\widehat x_T=\Phi_{T+1}(U,s_0,O_f(x_1),\ldots,O_f(x_T))\). Conditional on \(U=u\), these maps define a deterministic decision rule. Performance may therefore be evaluated by expectation or probability over \(U\), while the objective instance remains fixed unless an additional distribution on \(\mathcal F\) is explicitly introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized method uses an instance-independent random seed in addition to the oracle transcript; fixing the seed yields a deterministic decision rule.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is independent of the selected objective \(f\).
All decision maps are measurable with respect to the seed and observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every fixed seed value \(u\), the conditional algorithm is deterministic.

children.title: Distributional Lower-Bound Scope
children.top_down_role: Hard distributions used to extend guarantees across randomized classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Lower-Bound Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional lower bounds over objective instances and their implication for randomized worst-case complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}\) be a class of deterministic algorithms, let \(\mu\) be a probability distribution on instances \(f\in\mathcal F\), and let \(L(A,f)\ge 0\) be a loss after a fixed resource budget. A distributional lower bound establishes \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}}\mathbb E_{f\sim\mu}[L(A,f)]\ge \ell\). Under the hypotheses of an applicable minimax principle, this implies \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{rand}}}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E[L(A,f)]\ge \ell\). The distribution is over instances, whereas the latter expectation is over algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard distribution defeats every deterministic method on average; with an applicable minimax theorem, it yields a worst-case expected lower bound for randomized methods.
assumptions_latex: \(L(A,f)\) is measurable and nonnegative.
The deterministic and randomized algorithm classes satisfy the invoked minimax principle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{rand}}}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E[L(A,f)]\ge \ell\).

notation.meaning: performance loss after the prescribed budget

review_flags: A precise minimax or Yao-principle source and its admissibility hypotheses are not supplied.
The conclusion is conditional because minimax interchange is not automatic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional distributional-to-randomized lower-bound principle fits the leaf and appropriately warns that minimax interchange is not automatic, but no precise minimax or Yao-principle source identifies the required admissibility hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value-oracle lower bound for Lipschitz global optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case deterministic function-value accuracy lower bound over the stated Lipschitz class; no convexity is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(L>0\), and \(\epsilon\in(0,L/2)\). For the class of all \(f:[0,1]^n\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\), any value-oracle method that guarantees \(f(\bar x)-f^*<\epsilon\) for every instance requires at least \(\left\lfloor L/(2\epsilon)\right\rfloor^n\) oracle calls in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any value-oracle method that uniformly obtains objective error strictly below epsilon for every L-Lipschitz function on the n-dimensional unit cube needs at least floor(L/(2 epsilon)) to the nth power oracle calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Span-Restricted Algorithms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-span restriction for first-order methods initialized at a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) and initial point \(x_0\), a first-order method is span-restricted if, for every iteration \(t\ge 1\), its iterate satisfies \[x_t-x_0\in\operatorname{span}\{g_0,g_1,\ldots,g_{t-1}\},\qquad g_i\in\partial f(x_i).\] In the differentiable case one takes \(g_i=\nabla f(x_i)\). The definition restricts each displacement to the linear span of previously revealed first-order directions; scalar coefficients may depend arbitrarily on the observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iterate displacement must lie in the linear span of first-order directions revealed at earlier queries, although the coefficients may depend adaptively on all observations.
assumptions_latex: The method starts from a fixed \(x_0\in\mathbb R^d\).
At query \(x_i\), the oracle returns a selected \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\in x_0+\operatorname{span}\{g_0,\ldots,g_{t-1}\}\) for every \(t\ge1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unrestricted Algorithm Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General adaptive first-order oracle algorithms without span or coordinate-support constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An unrestricted deterministic first-order algorithm over \(\mathbb R^d\) consists of arbitrary decision maps \(\Phi_t\) satisfying \(x_t=\Phi_t(s_0,O_f(x_1),\ldots,O_f(x_{t-1}))\), with no requirement that \(x_t-x_0\) lie in the span of earlier gradients or that its support be previously exposed. A randomized unrestricted algorithm may additionally depend measurably on an instance-independent seed \(U\). Restrictions imposed by the feasible domain, oracle protocol, query budget, measurability, or success criterion remain part of the model and are not removed by the word unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unrestricted algorithms may choose any transcript-dependent query permitted by the domain and oracle protocol, without linear-span or zero-respecting constraints.
assumptions_latex: Queries must lie in the prescribed oracle domain.
Decision maps obey the stated deterministic or randomized information protocol.

children.title: Restriction-Removal Transfers
children.top_down_role: Mechanisms connecting restricted constructions to broader algorithm classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Restriction-Removal Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfer of restricted-algorithm lower bounds to broader classes through resisting-oracle or rotation arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{res}}\subseteq\mathcal A_{\mathrm{all}}\) be restricted and unrestricted algorithm classes. A restriction-removal transfer at budget \(T\) is a construction assigning to every \(A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{all}}\) an instance \(f_A\in\mathcal F\) and a restricted transcript whose first \(T\) oracle interactions have the same loss-relevant information as those of \(A\) on \(f_A\). If every restricted transcript has loss at least \(\ell_T\), then every unrestricted algorithm has a worst-case instance satisfying \(L_T(A,f_A)\ge\ell_T\). Such a conclusion requires the transfer construction; set inclusion alone gives only the opposite lower-bound implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restricted lower bound extends to unrestricted methods only when a resisting-oracle, rotation, or equivalent construction simulates each unrestricted transcript by a hard restricted one.
assumptions_latex: The transfer preserves all oracle responses and quantities used by the loss through budget \(T\).
Each constructed instance \(f_A\) remains in the stated class \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{all}}}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}L_T(A,f)\ge\ell_T\).

notation.meaning: algorithm class satisfying the auxiliary restriction

The record states a conditional transfer schema rather than an unconditional theorem.

children.title: Sequential Adaptivity

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Adaptivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fully sequential oracle interaction with one adaptive query per round.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a sequentially adaptive oracle algorithm, round \(t\) contains one query \(x_t\), chosen after all earlier responses have been observed: \[x_t=\Phi_t(U,s_0,O_f(x_1),\ldots,O_f(x_{t-1})).\] The oracle then returns \(O_f(x_t)\) before \(x_{t+1}\) is selected. The adaptivity depth after \(T\) queries is therefore \(T\), unless some decision maps ignore intervening responses. Sequential query complexity counts oracle calls, while wall-clock or arithmetic complexity requires a separate cost model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequentially adaptive method observes each oracle response before choosing its next query, so T dependent queries can create T rounds of adaptivity.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns the response to round \(t\) before round \(t+1\) begins.
The optional seed \(U\) is independent of the objective instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The query \(x_t\) may depend on every oracle response from rounds \(1\) through \(t-1\).

notation.meaning: oracle response to the round-t query

knowledge_statements.title: Batched Parallel Queries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-adaptive oracle model permitting simultaneous nonadaptive queries within each batch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \(B\)-round batched first-order algorithm chooses in round \(r\) a finite batch \(Q_r=(x_{r,1},\ldots,x_{r,m_r})\) as a measurable function of its seed and responses from earlier rounds only. All responses \((O_f(x_{r,1}),\ldots,O_f(x_{r,m_r}))\) are then returned simultaneously. No query \(x_{r,j}\) may depend on another response from round \(r\). The total query count is \(N=\sum_{r=1}^{B}m_r\), whereas the adaptive-round complexity is \(B\); lower bounds must specify which resource, or which pair \((B,N)\), is constrained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queries within a batch are chosen without seeing one another's responses; only later batches may adapt, so query count and adaptive-round count are distinct resources.
assumptions_latex: Every batch size \(m_r\) is finite.
The oracle returns the complete round-r response vector before round \(r+1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Within-round queries are conditionally nonadaptive, and the algorithm uses \(B\) adaptive rounds and \(N\) oracle calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Local Computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed optimization model separating node-local computation from inter-node communication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a communication graph and suppose node \(i\in V\) initially knows local data defining \(f_i\), with global objective \(F(x)=\sum_{i\in V}f_i(x)\). In each computation phase, node \(i\) may evaluate its local oracle and update local state using only that state, its data, and previously received messages. Information originating at another node can affect node \(i\) only through messages transmitted along edges of \(G\). A complexity statement must separately specify local oracle calls, local arithmetic, communication rounds, and message size whenever those resources are not treated as free.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each node computes from local data and received messages; nonlocal information must travel through the communication graph, and local work is distinct from communication cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) specifies the permitted communication links.
Node \(i\) initially accesses only its local component \(f_i\) and local state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Remote data influence node \(i\) only through edge-constrained messages, so computation and communication are separate resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Communication Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication-constrained distributed model indexed by graph, timing, bandwidth, and counted communication resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network communication scope is specified by a graph \(G=(V,E)\), a timing model, and a message constraint. In a synchronous round, each node may send an admissible message to each neighbor and then update its state from received messages and local information; after \(R\) rounds, information available at node \(i\) can depend only on initial data within graph distance at most \(R\). Communication complexity may count rounds, transmitted messages, bits, or scalars. A lower bound is meaningful only relative to the chosen count, message-size restriction, topology, and synchronization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network lower bounds must fix topology, timing, bandwidth, and the communication unit; after R synchronous neighbor rounds, information travels at most R graph hops.
assumptions_latex: Communication in each synchronous round occurs only across edges of \(G\).
Node updates use local state and messages received by the end of that round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After \(R\) rounds, node \(i\)'s state is independent of initial data at nodes whose graph distance from \(i\) exceeds \(R\).

children.title: Probabilistic Success Criteria
children.top_down_role: Navigation for expected, high-probability, constant-success, and minimax guarantees.

children.title: Expected-Performance Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Complexity claims evaluated through expected error or risk.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Performance Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected optimization-error criterion for randomized first-order algorithms at a fixed resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty feasible set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and define \(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\). Suppose a possibly randomized algorithm outputs \(\widehat x_T\in X\) after resource budget \(T\), and define the nonnegative optimization error \(\Delta_T=f(\widehat x_T)-f^*\). For an accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), an expected-performance guarantee is the condition \[\mathbb E[\Delta_T]\le\varepsilon.\] The expectation is over the algorithm's internal randomness and any oracle noise explicitly included in the model, with \(f\) fixed. For a class \(\mathcal F\) of objectives on \(X\), a uniform guarantee requires \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_T)-f^*]\le\varepsilon.\] This criterion alone does not assert a high-probability bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an objective on a specified feasible set, expected performance requires the mean optimization error after the stated budget to be at most epsilon. Uniform worst-case scope adds a supremum over the objective class, and neither condition alone implies a high-probability guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty and \(f^*>-\infty\).
\(\widehat x_T\in X\) almost surely.
\(\Delta_T\) is measurable and integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_T)-f^*]\le\varepsilon\), or uniformly \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_T)-f^*]\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: algorithm output after resource budget T
infimum of the objective over X

children.title: High-Probability Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Complexity claims carrying an explicit confidence requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform high-probability oracle complexity for randomized first-order algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a problem class, let \(A\) be a randomized algorithm using at most \(T\) oracle calls, and let \(X_T(f)\) be its output on instance \(f\). For an error criterion \(E_f:X\to[0,\infty]\), the bound \(T(\varepsilon,\delta)\) is a uniform high-probability guarantee if, for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), \[\Pr\!\left(E_f(X_{T(\varepsilon,\delta)}(f))\leq\varepsilon\right)\geq 1-\delta.\] Equivalently, \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\Pr(E_f(X_T(f))>\varepsilon)\leq\delta\). The probability includes all algorithmic and oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After the stated number of oracle calls, every instance in the class has error at most the target tolerance with probability at least one minus the failure level.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
The output and error criterion are measurable with respect to the algorithmic and oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\Pr(E_f(X_{T(\varepsilon,\delta)}(f))>\varepsilon)\leq\delta\).

notation.meaning: Problem-instance class over which the guarantee is uniform.
Nonnegative solution-error criterion for instance f.
Number of permitted first-order oracle calls.

children.title: Constant-Success Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds stated for a fixed nonvanishing success probability.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Success Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform randomized oracle complexity at a fixed success probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a problem class and fix a constant \(p_0\in(1/2,1)\) independent of the target accuracy. A randomized algorithm \(A\) has constant-success complexity at most \(T(\varepsilon)\) if its output after at most \(T(\varepsilon)\) oracle calls satisfies, for every \(f\in\mathcal F\), \[\Pr\!\left(E_f(X_{T(\varepsilon)}(f))\leq\varepsilon\right)\geq p_0.\] The probability is over all algorithmic and oracle randomness; no vanishing failure probability is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method reaches the requested accuracy uniformly over the instance class with a fixed probability strictly above one half.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
The success level \(p_0\) is fixed independently of \(\varepsilon\) and the instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\Pr(E_f(X_{T(\varepsilon)}(f))\leq\varepsilon)\geq p_0\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative error criterion for instance f.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard constant-probability success convention in randomized complexity

children.title: Minimax Risk Scope
children.top_down_role: Worst-case risk after optimization over admissible procedures.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Risk Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-instance expected risk optimized over an admissible algorithm class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an instance class \(\mathcal F\), an admissible class \(\mathfrak A_T\) of randomized algorithms using at most \(T\) oracle calls, and a measurable loss \(L_f\), the minimax risk is \[R_T^*(\mathcal F,L):=\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A_T}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E_f\!\left[L_f(X_A(f))\right].\] A minimax lower bound \(R_T^*\geq r_T\) means that every admissible algorithm has some instance whose expected loss is at least \(r_T\). The expectation includes oracle and internal algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimax risk is the smallest worst-instance expected loss attainable by any algorithm obeying the stated oracle budget.
assumptions_latex: \(L_f:X\to[0,\infty]\) is measurable for every \(f\in\mathcal F\).
\(\mathfrak A_T\) specifies the common information and oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T^*(\mathcal F,L)=\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A_T}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb E_f[L_f(X_A(f))]\).

notation.meaning: Algorithms allowed under an oracle budget of T.
Loss used to assess the output on instance f.

children.title: Objective-Gap Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured through objective suboptimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Gap Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive suboptimality for a minimization problem with attained finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be minimized over a nonempty set \(C\subseteq X\), and suppose \(f^*:=\min_{z\in C}f(z)\) is finite. A candidate \(x\in C\) has objective-gap accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) precisely when \[f(x)-f^*\leq\varepsilon.\] For a randomized output \(X_T\), expected and probabilistic criteria apply this same nonnegative gap inside an expectation or probability statement, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible candidate is objective-gap accurate when its objective value exceeds the optimal value by at most the prescribed tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\) and the minimum \(f^*\) is attained and finite.
The reported candidate satisfies \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f^*\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Minimum objective value over the feasible set.

children.title: Solution-Distance Accuracy
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured through distance to a solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Distance Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric distance from a candidate to the full optimal-solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty, and let \(X^*:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}f(z)\) be nonempty. A candidate \(x\in X\) has solution-distance accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) when \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*):=\inf_{x^*\in X^*}d(x,x^*)\leq\varepsilon.\] This criterion measures proximity to the entire solution set and does not require selecting a distinguished minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate is solution-distance accurate when its metric distance to the set of all minimizers is at most the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space.
The optimal-solution set \(X^*\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Set of minimizers of the optimization problem.
Infimum metric distance from x to the solution set.

children.title: Recovery Accuracy

knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric reconstruction error relative to an instance-dependent target object.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathcal F\) determine a target \(\theta(f)\) in a metric space \((\Theta,d_\Theta)\), and let an algorithm return an estimate \(\widehat\theta_T(f)\in\Theta\) after \(T\) oracle calls or observations. The output has recovery accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) on \(f\) when \[d_\Theta\!\left(\widehat\theta_T(f),\theta(f)\right)\leq\varepsilon.\] Uniform, expected, and high-probability recovery criteria are obtained by taking the supremum over \(f\in\mathcal F\), expectation, or probability under the specified information model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery accuracy bounds the metric error between the reconstructed object and the true instance-dependent target.
assumptions_latex: \((\Theta,d_\Theta)\) is a metric space.
The target map \(\theta:\mathcal F\to\Theta\) and estimator output are specified by the recovery model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_\Theta(\widehat\theta_T(f),\theta(f))\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Target object associated with instance f.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Accuracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric violation measured by distance to a nonempty feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be the nonempty feasible set. A candidate \(x\in X\) has feasibility accuracy \(\varepsilon\geq0\) when \[\operatorname{dist}(x,C):=\inf_{z\in C}d(x,z)\leq\varepsilon.\] Thus exact feasibility is the case \(\varepsilon=0\) when \(C\) is closed; for nonclosed \(C\), zero distance certifies membership only in its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate is approximately feasible when its metric distance to the feasible set is at most the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(C\neq\varnothing\).
For equivalence between zero residual and membership, \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,C)\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Infimum metric distance from x to feasibility.

children.title: Smooth Gradient Stationarity
children.top_down_role: First-order stationarity targets for smooth objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Gradient Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity residual for unconstrained differentiable minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. A point \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary in the smooth unconstrained sense when \[\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon.\] At \(\varepsilon=0\), this is the first-order necessary condition \(\nabla f(x)=0\) for a local minimizer. Complexity stated in this criterion counts the resources required to produce a point satisfying the displayed gradient-norm bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth gradient stationarity requires the Euclidean norm of the objective gradient to be no larger than the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb R^n\).
Accuracy is measured in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Gradient of the smooth objective at x.

children.title: Composite Stationarity Mapping
children.top_down_role: Stationarity targets adapted to composite objective structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Stationarity Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proximal-gradient mapping for a smooth-plus-convex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+g\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(f\) is differentiable and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex. For \(\eta>0\), define the composite stationarity mapping by \[G_\eta(x):=\eta^{-1}\!\left(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta g}(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\right).\] A point is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary under this mapping when \(\|G_\eta(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\). Moreover, \(G_\eta(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite stationarity is measured by the proximal-gradient mapping; a zero mapping is equivalent to the composite first-order inclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
\(g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_\eta(x)=\eta^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\eta g}(x-\eta\nabla f(x)))\), and \(\|G_\eta(x)\|_2\leq\varepsilon\) certifies approximate stationarity.

notation.meaning: Proximal operator of the scaled nonsmooth term.

children.title: Constrained Optimality Residuals
children.top_down_role: Residual criteria for constrained optimization problems.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Optimality Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-gradient residual for smooth minimization over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f\) be differentiable. For \(\eta>0\), define \[R_{\eta,C}(x):=\eta^{-1}\left\|x-P_C(x-\eta\nabla f(x))\right\|_2.\] A feasible point \(x\in C\) satisfies the projected optimality-residual criterion at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) when \(R_{\eta,C}(x)\leq\varepsilon\). Exact vanishing is equivalent to the constrained first-order inclusion \(0\in\nabla f(x)+N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constrained stationarity is certified by a small projected-gradient residual; zero residual equals the normal-cone first-order condition.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) is differentiable and \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\eta,C}(x)\leq\varepsilon\), with \(R_{\eta,C}(x)=0\iff 0\in\nabla f(x)+N_C(x)\).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to C at x.

children.title: Saddle Residual Criteria
children.top_down_role: Residual targets for convex-concave or nonconvex saddle formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Residual Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual gap criterion for convex-concave saddle problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be nonempty compact sets and let \(\Phi:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be convex in its first argument and concave in its second. The primal-dual saddle residual at \((x,y)\in X\times Y\) is \[\mathcal G(x,y):=\sup_{v\in Y}\Phi(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}\Phi(u,y).\] The pair is an \(\varepsilon\)-saddle point under the gap criterion when \(\mathcal G(x,y)\leq\varepsilon\). Exact vanishing is equivalent to the saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate pair is approximately saddle-optimal when its worst dual improvement plus worst primal improvement is at most the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty and compact.
\(\Phi\) is finite, convex in its first argument, and concave in its second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{v\in Y}\Phi(x,v)-\inf_{u\in X}\Phi(u,y)\leq\varepsilon\).

children.title: Variational-Inequality Residuals

knowledge_statements.title: Variational-Inequality Residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-gap residual for a variational inequality on a compact convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^n\). For \(x\in C\), define the variational-inequality dual-gap residual by \[g_C(x):=\sup_{z\in C}\langle F(x),x-z\rangle.\] The point \(x\) satisfies the residual criterion at tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\) when \(g_C(x)\leq\varepsilon\). Because \(z=x\) is admissible, \(g_C(x)\geq0\), and \(g_C(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(\langle F(x),z-x\rangle\geq0\) for every \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variational-inequality accuracy is measured by the worst violation of the defining inequality over the feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(F:C\to\mathbb R^n\) is defined at the candidate \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_C(x)=\sup_{z\in C}\langle F(x),x-z\rangle\leq\varepsilon\).

children.title: Primal–Dual Gap Certificates
children.top_down_role: Gap-based evidence coupling primal quality with dual information.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel primal–dual objective-gap certificate under weak duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(F\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(f:E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:F\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper closed convex functions, and let \(A:E\to F\) be linear. Define \(P(x)=f(x)+g(Ax)\), \(p^*=\inf_{u\in E}P(u)\), and \(D(y)=-f^*(-A^*y)-g^*(y)\). For any \(x\in E\) and \(y\in F\) for which \(P(x)\) and \(D(y)\) are finite, weak duality gives \(D(y)\le p^*\le P(x)\). Therefore \(G(x,y)=P(x)-D(y)\ge0\) and \(P(x)-p^*\le G(x,y)\). If strong duality holds, so that \(p^*=\sup_{v\in F}D(v)\), then \(p^*-D(y)\le G(x,y)\) is also a dual-objective error certificate. Consequently, \(G(x,y)\le\varepsilon\) certifies both objective errors to be at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal point and a dual point with finite objectives yield a computable nonnegative gap that bounds primal suboptimality; under strong duality, it also bounds error relative to the optimal dual value.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(f:E\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g:F\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) are proper closed convex functions.
\(A:E\to F\) is linear, and \(P(x)\) and \(D(y)\) are finite.
Strong duality is required for interpreting \(p^*-D(y)\) as error relative to the optimal dual value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(x)-p^*\le G(x,y)\), and under strong duality \(p^*-D(y)\le G(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the linear map A.

children.title: Lower-Model Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certification based on computable lower objective models.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Model Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cutting-plane lower certificate for finite-dimensional convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(Q\subset E\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Suppose that, for each \(i\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\), an oracle point \(x_i\in Q\) and a vector \(g_i\in E\) satisfy \(f(z)\ge f(x_i)+\langle g_i,z-x_i\rangle\) for every \(z\in Q\). Define \(m_k(z)=\max_{0\le i\le k}\{f(x_i)+\langle g_i,z-x_i\rangle\}\), \(\ell_k=\inf_{z\in Q}m_k(z)\), and \(f^*=\inf_{z\in Q}f(z)\). Then \(\ell_k\le f^*\). Whenever \(\ell_k\) is finite and computable, every incumbent \(\bar x_k\in Q\) has the certificate \(0\le f(\bar x_k)-f^*\le f(\bar x_k)-\ell_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum over the feasible set of accumulated affine minorants is a valid lower bound, and its difference from a feasible incumbent value certifies objective suboptimality.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and \(Q\subset E\) is nonempty and convex.
\(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) is convex.
For every \(i\in\{0,\ldots,k\}\), the vector \(g_i\) defines the displayed affine minorant of \(f\) on all of \(Q\).
\(\ell_k\) is finite and computationally available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le f(\bar x_k)-f^*\le f(\bar x_k)-\ell_k\).

notation.meaning: Maximum of the accumulated affine minorants.
Infimum of the lower model over the feasible set.

children.title: Computable Stopping Evidence
children.top_down_role: Observable evidence used to justify termination in complexity comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Computable Stopping Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-interval stopping rule independent of unknown optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization problem with optimal value \(f^*\). At iteration \(k\), suppose the algorithm computes finite scalars \(L_k\) and \(U_k\) satisfying \(L_k\le f^*\le U_k\), with \(U_k=f(x_k)\) for a feasible point \(x_k\). Then \(C_k=U_k-L_k\) is computable and satisfies \(0\le f(x_k)-f^*\le C_k\). Consequently, the stopping test \(C_k\le\varepsilon\) certifies absolute objective accuracy \(f(x_k)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) without access to \(f^*\). A relative test is valid when its displayed positive scaling denominator is itself computable and fixed by the chosen convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computable upper–lower objective interval gives a rigorous stopping test without knowing the optimal value.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k\) is feasible and \(U_k=f(x_k)\).
\(L_k\le f^*\le U_k\).
The requested tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_k\le\varepsilon\) implies \(f(x_k)-f^*\le\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Distance-Controlled Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Euclidean smooth convex oracle class controlled by initial distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constants \(L>0\) and \(R>0\), the unconstrained distance-controlled class \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\) consists of pairs \((f,x_0)\) such that \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable, \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(f\) has a minimizer \(x^*\) satisfying \(\|x_0-x^*\|_2\le R\). First-order complexity in this regime counts value-gradient oracle calls and takes the worst case over this class, with dimension allowed to be sufficiently large relative to the query budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime contains unconstrained smooth convex problems whose starting point lies within a prescribed distance of some minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The ambient space is finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f,x_0)\in\mathcal F_{L,R}\) exactly when the displayed convexity, smoothness, attainment, and distance conditions hold.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-side definition independent of the subsequently selected feasibility oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (E,\|\cdot\|) be finite-dimensional with dual norm \|\cdot\|_*. For L,D>0, the bounded-domain smooth convex objective class consists of pairs (f,Q) such that Q\subset E is nonempty, compact, and convex, \operatorname{diam}_{\|\cdot\|}(Q)\le D, and f is convex and differentiable on a neighborhood of Q with \|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*\le L\|x-y\| for all x,y\in Q. This definition specifies the objective class but not the charged mechanism by which an algorithm generates feasible queries.

Q is nonempty, compact, and convex.
f is differentiable on a neighborhood of Q.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility-Primitive Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating the objective class from constrained-oracle complexity models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bounds on L and \operatorname{diam}(Q) do not alone determine constrained oracle complexity. Projected-gradient, conditional-gradient, and separation-oracle methods respectively use projection onto Q, linear minimization over Q, and separation from Q. A complexity statement transfers between such models only when every charged primitive used in the source model is available or can be simulated in the target model at a stated cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothness and bounded diameter do not determine complexity until the feasibility primitive and its accounting are fixed.

Bounded-Domain Smooth Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-dependent constrained class controlled by feasible-set diameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((E,\|\cdot\|)\) be finite-dimensional, with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\). For \(L,D>0\), the bounded-domain smooth convex class consists of pairs \((f,Q)\) where \(Q\subset E\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, \(\sup_{x,y\in Q}\|x-y\|\le D\), and \(f\) is convex and differentiable on a neighborhood of \(Q\) with \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in Q\). Complexity counts first-order oracle calls together with the prescribed mechanism for producing feasible iterates over \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This constrained regime controls smoothness in a chosen norm and controls scale through the feasible set’s diameter.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(L,D>0\).
\(Q\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem belongs to the regime precisely when its domain diameter is at most \(D\) and its gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the norm pair.

children.title: Deterministic Algorithm Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Convex Zero-Chain Hard Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural quadratic family underlying deterministic smooth-convex first-order hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every k\ge0 and L,R>0, in sufficiently large dimension there exists a convex quadratic q with L-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer x^* satisfying \|x^*\|_2\le R such that q is a first-order zero chain: if x\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_j\}, then \nabla q(x)\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_{j+1}\}. For a universal c>0, every x\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\} satisfies q(x)-q(x^*)\ge cLR^2/(k+1)^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth tridiagonal quadratic reveals at most one new coordinate along the chain and retains an inverse-square gap on the revealed span.
assumptions_latex: k is a nonnegative integer and L,R>0.
The ambient dimension is sufficiently large relative to k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}}q(x)-q^*\ge c\frac{LR^2}{(k+1)^2}.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Zero-Chain Hard Family

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Deterministic Smooth-Convex Black-Box Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General deterministic value-gradient lower bound obtained through resisting-oracle rotation of the zero chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a deterministic algorithm make k adaptive exact value-gradient queries and then output an arbitrary transcript-measurable point. If d\ge 2k+1, there exists a convex function f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R with L-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer x^* satisfying \|x_0-x^*\|_2\le R such that f(x_k)-f^*\ge cLR^2/(k+1)^2 for a universal c>0. Therefore uniform objective accuracy \varepsilon in the nontrivial range requires \Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon}) deterministic oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every deterministic exact first-order method has an inverse-square worst-case error barrier in sufficiently high dimension.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and adaptive.
Each query returns the exact function value and gradient.
The output may be any measurable function of the transcript.
d\ge 2k+1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\rm det}(\varepsilon;L,R)=\Omega\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{LR^2}{\varepsilon}}\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Smooth-Convex Black-Box Lower Bound
Deterministic Algorithm Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case deterministic smooth-convex first-order lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the value-gradient black-box model, let a deterministic algorithm make \(k\) adaptive oracle queries on the unconstrained class \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\). When the dimension is sufficiently large relative to \(k\), there exists a universal constant \(c>0\) and an instance \((f,x_0)\in\mathcal F_{L,R}\) such that its output \(x_k\) satisfies \(f(x_k)-f^*\ge cLR^2/(k+1)^2\). Thus every deterministic method guaranteeing \(f(x_k)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) uniformly over this class requires \(\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) oracle calls in the nontrivial accuracy range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every deterministic first-order method needs order square-root inverse accuracy oracle calls on sufficiently high-dimensional smooth convex problems.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns exact function values and gradients.
The algorithm is deterministic and adaptive.
The dimension may grow with the query budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\rm det}(\varepsilon;L,R)=\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).

children.title: Randomized Algorithm Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Algorithm Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-error randomized smooth-convex first-order lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a randomized value-gradient algorithm \(\mathcal A\), measure performance by \(\sup_{(f,x_0)\in\mathcal F_{L,R}}\mathbb E_{\mathcal A}[f(x_k)-f^*]\). In a sufficiently high-dimensional oracle model, the smooth-convex lower-bound construction yields a universal constant \(c>0\) such that this quantity is at least \(cLR^2/(k+1)^2\) for every \(k\)-query algorithm. Consequently, achieving worst-case expected error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) oracle calls. Any high-probability formulation must separately specify its failure probability and cannot be inferred from the expectation bound alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization does not improve the classical smooth-convex oracle order in worst-case expectation, though high-probability claims require separate analysis.
assumptions_latex: The oracle is exact and the expectation is over internal randomness.
The adversarial instance is fixed before the algorithmic randomness is realized.
The dimension satisfies the hard-distribution construction's requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\rm rand}^{\mathbb E}(\varepsilon;L,R)=\Omega(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).

notation.meaning: Expectation over the algorithm's internal randomness.
