knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expectation Does Not Imply High-Probability Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of an expected-loss transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \Delta>0 and p\in(0,1), let Z equal \Delta/p with probability p and 0 otherwise. Then Z\ge0 and \mathbb EZ=\Delta, while \mathbb P(Z\ge\Delta)=p. Since p may be arbitrarily small, an expected-loss lower bound alone gives no positive universal lower bound on the probability that loss is at least its mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected hardness may be concentrated on an arbitrarily rare event and does not itself imply high-probability hardness.
assumptions_latex: \Delta>0 and 0<p<1.
Z is the displayed nonnegative random loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb EZ=\Delta\quad\text{but}\quad\mathbb P(Z\ge\Delta)=p\to0.

notation.meaning: probability of the rare loss event

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Does Not Imply High-Probability Hardness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected-Loss Distributional Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary Yao-type inequality from deterministic distributional hardness to randomized worst-case expected loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a query budget k, a nonnegative measurable loss \mathcal L, and a probability distribution 
u over admissible instances. Suppose every deterministic k-query decision rule A satisfies \mathbb E_{f\sim
u}[\mathcal L(A,f)]\ge\Delta. If a randomized algorithm \mathcal A uses an instance-independent random seed S and conditioning on S=s yields an admissible deterministic rule A_s, then \mathbb E_{f\sim
u,S}[\mathcal L(A_S,f)]\ge\Delta. Consequently, some fixed instance f in the support class satisfies \mathbb E_S[\mathcal L(A_S,f)]\ge\Delta, and hence \inf_{\mathcal A}\sup_f\mathbb E_S\mathcal L(\mathcal A,f)\ge\Delta.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single hard distribution for every deterministic rule yields a worst-case expected lower bound for randomized algorithms.
assumptions_latex: The hard distribution is fixed independently of the randomized seed.
Conditioning on each seed produces an admissible deterministic k-query rule.
The loss is nonnegative and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{\mathcal A}\sup_f\mathbb E_S[\mathcal L(\mathcal A,f)]\ge\Delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Loss Distributional Transfer
Randomization-Scope Transfers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Yao-type transfer from distributional deterministic hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a query budget \(k\), a loss \(\mathcal L(A,f)\), and a probability distribution \(\nu\) supported on admissible problem instances. If every deterministic \(k\)-query algorithm \(A\) satisfies \(\mathbb E_{f\sim\nu}[\mathcal L(A,f)]\ge\Delta\), then every randomized \(k\)-query algorithm \(\mathcal A\) satisfies \(\sup_f\mathbb E_{\mathcal A}[\mathcal L(\mathcal A,f)]\ge\Delta\). The transfer concerns expected loss and requires the hard distribution to be independent of the algorithm's realized random seed. It does not by itself produce a high-probability lower bound or justify transfer against an adaptive adversary using a different information pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common hard distribution for all deterministic algorithms transfers an expected lower bound to randomized algorithms through a minimax argument.
assumptions_latex: \(\nu\) is fixed independently of the algorithm's random seed.
The deterministic distributional bound holds uniformly over all admissible deterministic \(k\)-query algorithms.
The loss is measurable and its displayed expectations exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\mathcal A}\sup_f\mathbb E_{\mathcal A}[\mathcal L(\mathcal A,f)]\ge\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Performance loss after the query budget.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Huber-Type Sharp Example for Fixed-Step Gradient Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional smooth convex family attaining inverse-linear worst-case order for step 1/L.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix k\ge1 and L,R>0, set a=R/(2k+1), and define h_a(x)=\frac L2x^2 for |x|\le a and h_a(x)=La|x|-\frac L2a^2 for |x|\ge a. Then h_a is convex, continuously differentiable, and has L-Lipschitz derivative, with unique minimizer x^*=0. Starting from x_0=R, the iteration x_{j+1}=x_j-L^{-1}h_a'(x_j) satisfies x_j=R-ja for 0\le j\le k and h_a(x_k)-h_a^*=LR^2/[2(2k+1)].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional Huber-type objective makes fixed-step gradient descent retain an objective gap of order LR squared divided by k.
assumptions_latex: k is a positive integer and L,R>0.
Gradient descent uses step 1/L.
The initial distance to the minimizer is R.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_a(x_k)-h_a^*=\frac{LR^2}{2(2k+1)}=\Omega\!\left(\frac{LR^2}{k}\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Huber-Type Sharp Example for Fixed-Step Gradient Descent
Basic Gradient Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching rate for fixed-step gradient descent on smooth convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(x^*\) minimize \(f\), and assume \(\|x_0-x^*\|_2\le R\). Gradient descent with \(x_{i+1}=x_i-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_i)\) satisfies \(f(x_k)-f^*\le LR^2/(2k)\) for \(k\ge1\). Moreover, worst-case smooth convex instances for this fixed-step method attain error of order \(LR^2/k\). Thus its iteration complexity is \(\Theta(LR^2/\varepsilon)\) within the fixed-step gradient-descent family; this is not an oracle-optimality claim over accelerated methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-step gradient descent has a sharp inverse-iteration worst-case rate, although broader first-order methods can accelerate it.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
A minimizer \(x^*\) exists with \(\|x_0-x^*\|_2\le R\).
The update uses the fixed step \(1/L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)-f^*=\Theta(LR^2/k)\) in worst-case order for the stated fixed-step method.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accelerated Gradient Optimality Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order matching between accelerated gradient and deterministic smooth-convex oracle hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal F_{L,R} be the class of convex functions on Euclidean space with L-Lipschitz gradient and a minimizer x^* satisfying \|x_0-x^*\|_2\le R. Accelerated gradient methods attain f(x_k)-f^*\le C LR^2/(k+1)^2. Conversely, for every deterministic exact value-gradient algorithm using k queries, sufficiently large dimension admits an instance in \mathcal F_{L,R} with f(x_k)-f^*\ge cLR^2/(k+1)^2, where c,C>0 are universal. Hence the deterministic minimax oracle complexity is \Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon}) for 0<\varepsilon\le c_0LR^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated gradient attains the inverse-square smooth-convex oracle barrier and is order-optimal among deterministic exact first-order methods.
assumptions_latex: The objective is convex with L-Lipschitz Euclidean gradient.
A minimizer lies within distance R of the initial point.
The oracle returns exact function values and gradients.
The lower-bound dimension is sufficiently large relative to k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N^*_{\rm det}(\varepsilon;L,R)=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{LR^2}{\varepsilon}}\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Gradient Optimality Correspondence
Accelerated Gradient Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-optimal accelerated rate in the distance-controlled smooth class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \((f,x_0)\in\mathcal F_{L,R}\), an accelerated gradient method produces \(x_k\) satisfying \(f(x_k)-f^*\le CLR^2/(k+1)^2\) for a universal constant \(C>0\). Conversely, for every deterministic exact first-order method using \(k\) oracle calls, sufficiently large dimension permits an instance in \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\) with error at least \(cLR^2/(k+1)^2\), where \(c>0\) is universal. Therefore acceleration matches the deterministic black-box lower bound in order, and the optimal oracle complexity for objective accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is \(\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated gradient methods attain the inverse-square rate and match the deterministic smooth-convex first-order lower bound in order.
assumptions_latex: The function class is \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\).
The oracle returns exact values and gradients.
The lower bound allows dimension sufficiently large relative to \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N^*(\varepsilon;L,R)=\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).

notation.meaning: Universal positive upper- and lower-bound constants.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate comparison under a common smooth class, normalization, oracle, and objective-error criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the Euclidean class of convex functions with L-Lipschitz gradient and \|x_0-x^*\|_2\le R, step-1/L gradient descent has sharp worst-case objective error \Theta(LR^2/k), whereas accelerated gradient has deterministic minimax objective error \Theta(LR^2/(k+1)^2). Consequently, for 0<\varepsilon\le cLR^2, the respective complexities are \Theta(LR^2/\varepsilon) for the fixed-step family and \Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon}) for deterministic accelerated oracle-optimal methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration changes worst-case objective decay from inverse-linear to inverse-square and improves inverse-accuracy dependence to its square root.

Both use exact first-order information and objective-error accuracy.

Basic-to-Accelerated Rate Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative separation between gradient descent and acceleration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the distance-controlled class \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\), fixed-step gradient descent guarantees objective error of order \(LR^2/k\), whereas accelerated gradient methods guarantee order \(LR^2/k^2\). The separation compares worst-case rate guarantees under the same exact first-order oracle and initial-distance normalization; it does not assert that every individual instance exhibits the slower basic rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration changes worst-case error decay from inverse-linear to inverse-square, producing a square-root improvement in accuracy dependence.

Basic gradient descent uses step \(1/L\).
Complexities are compared in the same objective-error convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian bounds for operator-quadratic instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Hessian formula and the additional spectral condition sufficient for smooth strong convexity and the stated condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu>0\), \(Q_f\ge1\), and let \(A\) be a bounded self-adjoint linear operator on \(\mathbb R^\infty\). Define \[f_{\mu,Q_f}(x)=\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}8\langle x,Ax\rangle+\frac\mu2\|x\|^2.\] Then \(f_{\mu,Q_f}\) is twice Fréchet differentiable and, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^\infty\), \[\nabla^2f_{\mu,Q_f}(x)=\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}4A+\mu I.\] If additionally \(0\le A\le4I\), then, for every \(x\), \[\mu I\le\nabla^2f_{\mu,Q_f}(x)\le\mu Q_f I=:LI.\] Consequently, under this additional condition, \(f_{\mu,Q_f}\in\mathcal S^{\infty,1}_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^\infty)\) and its condition number is \(Q_f=L/\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic defined by a bounded self-adjoint operator has the displayed constant Hessian. The smoothness, strong-convexity, and condition-number conclusions additionally require the operator inequality 0 ≤ A ≤ 4I.
assumptions_latex: \mu>0
Q_f\ge1
A:\mathbb R^\infty\to\mathbb R^\infty\text{ is bounded and self-adjoint}
f_{\mu,Q_f}(x)=\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}8\langle x,Ax\rangle+\frac\mu2\|x\|^2
0\le A\le4I\ \text{only for the Hessian bounds and class-membership conclusion}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional lower bound for the next estimate-function minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Notation and baseline hypotheses are inherited from the referenced estimate-sequence proposition; the statement records both the initial lower bound and its consequent form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the setting of Proposition~2.22 and suppose \(\phi_k^*\ge f(x_k)\). Then
\[
\phi_{k+1}^*\ge (1-\alpha_k)f(x_k)+\alpha_k f(x_Q(y_k;L))
+\left(\frac{\alpha_k}{2L}-\frac{\alpha_k^2}{2\gamma_{k+1}}\right)\|g_Q(y_k;L)\|^2
+\frac{\alpha_k(1-\alpha_k)\gamma_k}{\gamma_{k+1}}\langle g_Q(y_k;L),v_k-y_k\rangle.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\phi_{k+1}^*\ge f(x_Q(y_k;L))
+\left(\frac{1}{2L}-\frac{\alpha_k^2}{2\gamma_{k+1}}\right)\|g_Q(y_k;L)\|^2
+(1-\alpha_k)\left\langle g_Q(y_k;L),\frac{\alpha_k\gamma_k}{\gamma_{k+1}}(v_k-y_k)+x_k-y_k\right\rangle.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality System for the Tridiagonal Quadratic Hard Instance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded characterization of minimizers for the quadratic defined using the source-dependent tridiagonal operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu>0\), \(Q_f>1\), and let \(A:\ell_2\to\ell_2\) be the infinite tridiagonal operator specified in Definition 2.18. Define
\[
f_{\mu,Q_f}(x)=\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}{8}\langle x,Ax\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|x\|^2-\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}{4}\langle e_1,x\rangle.
\]
Then \(x^*\in\ell_2\) minimizes \(f_{\mu,Q_f}\) if and only if
\[
\left(\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}4A+\mu I\right)x^*-\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}4e_1=0,
\]
equivalently,
\[
\left(A+\frac4{Q_f-1}I\right)x^*=e_1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the specified tridiagonal quadratic on ℓ₂, a point is a minimizer exactly when its gradient vanishes, equivalently when it solves the stated infinite-dimensional linear system.

Q_f>1

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Hard Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tridiagonal strongly convex quadratics exposing one coordinate per query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\mu<L\), let \(T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be a symmetric positive-semidefinite tridiagonal path matrix with \(\|T\|_2\le4\), and set \(H=\mu I+(L-\mu)T/4\). For \(b=\beta e_1\), define \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Hx\rangle-\langle b,x\rangle\). Then \(\mu I\preceq H\preceq LI\), so \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth. Starting from \(x_0=0\), every zero-respecting first-order method has \(x_k\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}\); choosing \(m>k\) leaves an unrecovered tail of \(x^*=H^{-1}b\), which supplies the lower-bound error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tridiagonal strongly convex quadratic reveals coordinates sequentially, leaving an inaccessible minimizer tail after finitely many zero-respecting queries.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, tridiagonal, and \(\|T\|_2\le4\).
The method is zero-respecting and starts from \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu I\preceq\nabla^2f\preceq LI\) and \(x_k\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the hard-instance leaf, but the statement is not reliable as written without a precise construction. An arbitrary positive-semidefinite tridiagonal matrix with norm at most four need not have nonzero path couplings or produce a nonzero minimizer tail, so the final lower-bound assertion does not follow from the displayed assumptions. A source giving the exact hard matrix, indexing convention, zero-respecting model, and tail estimate is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning of symmetric positive-definite quadratic objectives in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite and let \(f(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\). If \(0<\mu=\lambda_{\min}(Q)\leq\lambda_{\max}(Q)=L\), then \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Its spectral condition number is \(\kappa(Q)=L/\mu\). Equivalently, \(\mu\lVert v\rVert_2^2\leq v^{\mathsf T}Qv\leq L\lVert v\rVert_2^2\) for every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite quadratic, the smallest and largest Hessian eigenvalues are its strong-convexity and smoothness constants; their ratio is the spectral condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succ0\).
The ambient norm is \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(Q)=\lambda_{\max}(Q)/\lambda_{\min}(Q)=L/\mu\).

notation.meaning: Smallest and largest eigenvalues of Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-System Interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between minimizing a positive-definite quadratic and solving its normal linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\) with \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), the unique minimizer \(x_\star\) satisfies \(Qx_\star=b\). At any \(x\), the negative gradient equals the linear-system residual: \(r(x)=b-Qx=-\nabla f(x)\). Moreover, \(f(x)-f(x_\star)=\tfrac12\lVert x-x_\star\rVert_Q^2=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert_{Q^{-1}}^2\). Thus gradient-oracle progress on the quadratic is exactly residual reduction for the associated symmetric positive-definite system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a positive-definite quadratic is equivalent to solving Qx=b; the negative gradient is the residual, and objective error equals half the squared energy error.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succ0\).
\(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star=Q^{-1}b\) and \(f(x)-f(x_\star)=\tfrac12\lVert b-Qx\rVert_{Q^{-1}}^2\).

notation.meaning: Energy norm, the square root of zᵀQz.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Subspace Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-span first-order iterates on a symmetric positive-definite quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\), let \(r_0=b-Qx_0\), and define \(\mathcal K_t(Q,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,Qr_0,\ldots,Q^{t-1}r_0\}\). Any method satisfying \(x_t\in x_0+\operatorname{span}\{\nabla f(x_0),\ldots,\nabla f(x_{t-1})\}\) necessarily has \(x_t\in x_0+\mathcal K_t(Q,r_0)\). Consequently, \(x_t-x_\star=p_{t-1}(Q)r_0-Q^{-1}r_0\) for some polynomial \(p_{t-1}\) of degree at most \(t-1\), reducing worst-case error analysis to polynomial approximation on the spectrum of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-span first-order iterates remain in an affine Krylov subspace, so their quadratic error is governed by low-degree polynomial approximation over the Hessian spectrum.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succ0\).
The method obeys the stated linear-span condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\in x_0+\mathcal K_t(Q,r_0)\).

notation.meaning: A polynomial of degree at most t−1.

knowledge_statements.title: Known-Curvature Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax deterministic first-order complexity when both smoothness and strong-convexity constants are supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f(x_\star)\), and suppose \(L\) and \(\mu\) are known. In the deterministic first-order oracle model, accelerated gradient methods attain \(f(x_N)-f(x_\star)\leq\varepsilon\) using \(N=O\!\left(\sqrt{L/\mu}\,\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\) oracle calls. For dimensions large enough relative to \(N\), the worst-case lower bound has the same order. Hence the minimax oracle complexity is \(\Theta\!\left(\sqrt\kappa\,\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\), up to universal constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With known L and μ, accelerated first-order methods achieve the optimal worst-case order √κ log(Δ₀/ε) for reducing function-value error to ε.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\) and \(\Delta_0>\varepsilon>0\).
The oracle returns exact function values and gradients.
The dimension is sufficient for the matching lower-bound construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\star(\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt\kappa\,\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Curvature Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-complexity comparison when numerical curvature constants are withheld from the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N_{\mathrm{unk}}(\varepsilon;\mu,L)\) denote minimax deterministic first-order complexity over \(\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\) when the algorithm receives no numerical values of \(\mu\) or \(L\). Let \(N_{\mathrm{known}}(\varepsilon;\mu,L)\) be the corresponding complexity when both constants are supplied. Since every unknown-curvature algorithm is admissible in the known-curvature model, but not conversely, \(N_{\mathrm{unk}}(\varepsilon;\mu,L)\geq N_{\mathrm{known}}(\varepsilon;\mu,L)\). Therefore the known-curvature lower bound \(\Omega\!\left(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\) also applies when curvature is unknown; a matching adaptive upper bound requires additional algorithmic and stopping assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Withholding L and μ cannot reduce minimax complexity, so the known-curvature lower bound remains valid; matching adaptive upper bounds depend on the permitted estimation and stopping mechanisms.

The unknown-curvature algorithm is not given numerical values of \(L\) or \(\mu\).
\(\Delta_0>\varepsilon>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Restarted Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic restart of an accelerated convex method under known strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\), and suppose a convex accelerated routine started at \(z\) returns \(A_m(z)\) satisfying \(f(A_m(z))-f(x_\star)\leq 2L\lVert z-x_\star\rVert_2^2/(m+1)^2\). Choose an integer \(m\geq\lceil\sqrt{8L/\mu}\rceil\), set \(z_0=x_0\), and update \(z_{s+1}=A_m(z_s)\). Then \(f(z_{s+1})-f(x_\star)\leq\tfrac12(f(z_s)-f(x_\star))\). Stop after \(S=\lceil\log_2(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\rceil\) epochs and output \(z_S\); the total gradient complexity is \(O\!\left(\sqrt\kappa\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarting an accelerated convex routine every order-√κ iterations yields a one-half gap contraction per epoch and total complexity of order √κ log(Δ₀/ε).
assumptions_latex: The accelerated routine satisfies \(f(A_m(z))-f(x_\star)\leq 2L\lVert z-x_\star\rVert_2^2/(m+1)^2\).
\(f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\) with known \(L\) and \(\mu\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(z_S)-f(x_\star)\leq\varepsilon\) after \(mS=O\!\left(\sqrt\kappa\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\) gradient calls.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Adaptation Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonidentifiability of global strong convexity from finitely many unrestricted first-order observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix distinct query points \(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1}\in\mathbb R^n\) and suppose an algorithm observes only \((f(x_i),\nabla f(x_i))\). Without a prescribed function class or a priori curvature bounds, these finitely many observations cannot certify a positive global strong-convexity modulus: whenever the data admit a smooth strongly convex interpolant, one may alter a smooth interpolant outside neighborhoods of the queried points while preserving all recorded values and gradients, yet destroy global strong convexity. Thus curvature adaptation based solely on a finite transcript requires structural assumptions, additional oracle information, or a performance guarantee that does not claim certification of the global modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite first-order data cannot by itself certify global strong convexity, because unseen regions may be modified without changing queried values or gradients.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many exact values and gradients are observed.
No global function class or curvature bounds are supplied.
The domain contains points outside neighborhoods of the queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transcript \(\{(x_i,f(x_i),\nabla f(x_i))\}_{i=0}^{N-1}\) does not identify any certified global modulus \(\mu>0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unrestricted finite-transcript nonidentifiability claim is plausible, but it is a nontrivial failure theorem and has no citation. A precise interpolation, bump-function, or oracle-indistinguishability source is required to support the quantifier 'whenever' and the stated domain and smoothness conditions.

children.title: Gradient-Method Optimality

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Method Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal constant step size within stationary gradient descent on spectrally bounded quadratics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\) with \(\sigma(Q)\subseteq[\mu,L]\), constant-step gradient descent satisfies \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)\). Its worst-case error contraction over this spectral interval is \(\rho(\alpha)=\max_{\lambda\in[\mu,L]}|1-\alpha\lambda|\). The minimizing step is \(\alpha_\star=2/(L+\mu)\), for which \(\rho_\star=(L-\mu)/(L+\mu)=(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)\). Consequently, reducing the norm error by a factor \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) requires and suffices, within this stationary family, \(\Theta\!\left(\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among constant-step gradient iterations on the spectral interval [μ,L], step 2/(L+μ) minimizes worst-case contraction and gives order κ log(1/ε) complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succ0\) and \(\sigma(Q)\subseteq[\mu,L]\).
The step size is constant across iterations.
Error is measured in any Q-eigenvector-compatible norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{\alpha>0}\max_{\lambda\in[\mu,L]}|1-\alpha\lambda|=(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated-Method Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax optimality of acceleration for smooth strongly convex deterministic first-order optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Over \(\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\), accelerated gradient methods with the supplied parameters \(L\) and \(\mu\) produce iterates satisfying \(f(x_k)-f(x_\star)\leq C\Delta_0\exp(-c k/\sqrt\kappa)\) for universal constants \(C,c>0\). Conversely, in sufficiently large dimension, every deterministic first-order method has a member of this class for which \(f(x_k)-f(x_\star)\geq c'\Delta_0\exp(-C' k/\sqrt\kappa)\), with universal \(c',C'>0\). Hence acceleration is minimax order-optimal, and the oracle complexity for function-gap accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is \(\Theta\!\left(\sqrt\kappa\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated gradient methods match the deterministic first-order lower bound, achieving the minimax order √κ log(Δ₀/ε) for smooth strongly convex objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in\mathcal F_{\mu,L}(\mathbb R^n)\) and \(L,\mu\) are supplied.
The first-order oracle is exact and deterministic.
The dimension is sufficient for the lower-bound construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\star(\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt\kappa\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon)\right)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov-Method Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-gradient optimality over affine Krylov spaces for positive-definite quadratic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\succ0\), \(Qx_\star=b\), and \(r_0=b-Qx_0\). In exact arithmetic, the conjugate-gradient iterate \(x_k\) is the unique minimizer of \(\lVert x-x_\star\rVert_Q\) over \(x_0+\mathcal K_k(Q,r_0)\). Equivalently, it chooses the degree-\(k\) residual polynomial that is optimal for the realized spectral measure. If \(\sigma(Q)\subseteq[\mu,L]\), then \(\lVert x_k-x_\star\rVert_Q\leq2((\sqrt\kappa-1)/(\sqrt\kappa+1))^k\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert_Q\), and convergence occurs in at most the number of distinct eigenvalues of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugate gradient minimizes energy error over each affine Krylov space, has a √κ-dependent Chebyshev bound, and terminates after at most the number of distinct eigenvalues.

Arithmetic is exact.
\(\sigma(Q)\subseteq[\mu,L]\) for the displayed condition-number bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For accuracy ratio \(\eta=\Delta_0/\varepsilon>1\) and condition ratio \(\kappa=L/\mu\), representative iteration counts are \[N_{\mathrm{GD}}=\Theta\!\left(\kappa\log\eta\right),\qquad N_{\mathrm{acc}}=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt\kappa\log\eta\right),\qquad N_{\mathrm{CG}}=O\!\left(\min\{n,\sqrt\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}})\}\right).\] The first rate is optimal only within the stationary constant-step gradient family; the second is minimax optimal over general smooth strongly convex objectives; the third concerns symmetric positive-definite quadratics in exact arithmetic and may improve through spectral clustering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent scales linearly with κ, acceleration with √κ, and conjugate gradient with the smaller of dimension and a √κ logarithmic bound, subject to their respective models.
assumptions_latex: The gradient and accelerated rates use function-gap accuracy on \(\mathcal F_{\mu,L}\).
The conjugate-gradient rate uses relative energy-norm error for an SPD quadratic.
All oracle computations are exact and deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{GD}}:\!N_{\mathrm{acc}}\) exhibits \(\kappa\) versus \(\sqrt\kappa\) conditioning dependence, while \(N_{\mathrm{CG}}\leq n\) in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Nonsmooth Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax deterministic local-oracle bound on a Euclidean ball when dimension may grow with the query budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_2(x_0,R)\subset\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\) contain the convex functions that are \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(\|\cdot\|_2\) on this ball and attain a minimum there. For every deterministic method making at most \(T\) adaptive calls to a local first-order oracle, there are universal constants \(c,c_d>0\) such that, whenever \(d\ge c_dT\), some \(f\in\mathcal F_{L,R}\) satisfies \[f(x_T)-\min_{x\in B_2(x_0,R)}f(x)\ge c\frac{LR}{\sqrt{T+1}}.\] Consequently, guaranteeing error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(T=\Omega((LR/\varepsilon)^2)\), subject to the stated dimension condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In sufficiently high Euclidean dimension, deterministic local first-order methods need order (LR/ε)² oracle calls to minimize an L-Lipschitz convex function on a radius-R ball.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm on \(B_2(x_0,R)\).
The algorithm accesses \(f\) only through an adaptive deterministic local first-order oracle.
The dimension satisfies \(d\ge c_dT\) for a universal constant \(c_d>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_T)-f^*\ge cLR/\sqrt{T+1}\), hence \(T=\Omega((LR/\varepsilon)^2)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Euclidean nonsmooth convex first-order lower bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower bound for span-based subgradient schemes on locally Lipschitz convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let n\in\mathbb{N}, x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n, R>0, M>0, and 0\le k\le n-1. Let \mathcal{P}(x_0,R,M) be the class of convex functions f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} for which there exists a minimizer x^* satisfying \|x^*-x_0\|\le R and such that f is M-Lipschitz on B_2(x^*,R). Then there exists f\in\mathcal{P}(x_0,R,M) such that every optimization scheme producing x_0,\ldots,x_k with \[x_t\in x_0+\operatorname{Lin}\{g(x_0),\ldots,g(x_{t-1})\},\quad t=1,\ldots,k,\] for some g(x_i)\in\partial f(x_i), satisfies \[f(x_k)-f^*\ge\frac{MR}{2(2+\sqrt{k+1})},\qquad f^*:=\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every dimension n and iteration count k at most n−1, there is a convex objective with a minimizer within distance R of the initial point and Lipschitz constant M on the stated ball such that every span-based subgradient scheme has error at least MR divided by 2(2+sqrt(k+1)) at iteration k.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb{N},\quad x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n
R>0,\quad M>0
0\le k\le n-1
\mathcal{P}(x_0,R,M)=\{f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}: f\text{ convex and }\exists x^*\in\arg\min f,\ \|x^*-x_0\|\le R,\ f\text{ is }M\text{-Lipschitz on }B_2(x^*,R)\}
x_t\in x_0+\operatorname{Lin}\{g(x_0),\ldots,g(x_{t-1})\},\quad g(x_i)\in\partial f(x_i)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f\in\mathcal{P}(x_0,R,M)\ \forall\text{ qualifying schemes},\quad f(x_k)-f^*\ge\frac{MR}{2(2+\sqrt{k+1})}.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Dependent Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mirror-descent scaling for Lipschitz convex optimization in a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex, let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and suppose every returned subgradient satisfies \(\|g_t\|_*\le G\). Let \(\psi\) be \(1\)-strongly convex with respect to \(\|\cdot\|\), and assume \(D_\psi(x^*,x_1)\le D^2/2\) for a minimizer \(x^*\). Mirror descent with constant step \(\eta=D/(G\sqrt T)\) and weighted average \(\bar x_T\) obeys \[f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)\le \frac{GD}{\sqrt T}.\] Thus this geometry yields the oracle guarantee \(T=O(G^2D^2/\varepsilon^2)\); the norm and mirror map enter through the dual bound \(G\) and Bregman radius \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth mirror descent reaches ε error in order G²D²/ε² calls, where G is measured in the dual norm and D by the mirror map.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and its oracle subgradients satisfy \(\|g_t\|_*\le G\).
\(\psi\) is \(1\)-strongly convex relative to \(\|\cdot\|\).
A minimizer \(x^*\) satisfies \(D_\psi(x^*,x_1)\le D^2/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_T)-f(x^*)\le GD/\sqrt T\), so \(T=O(G^2D^2/\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: dual norm of the chosen primal norm
Bregman divergence generated by the mirror map

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Subgradients Need Not Be Bounded
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the Lipschitz-to-bounded-subgradient converse on a nonopen relative domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=[0,\infty)\subset\mathbb R\) and let \(f(x)=0\) on \(Q\). Then \(f\) is convex and \(0\)-Lipschitz on \(Q\), but its relative convex subdifferential at the boundary point satisfies \[\partial_Q f(0)=(-\infty,0].\] Thus Lipschitz continuity on a closed convex domain does not bound every relative subgradient at boundary points; an open-domain or appropriately interior formulation is required for the converse used in the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant function on a half-line is Lipschitz, yet its relative subdifferential at the endpoint is unbounded, showing why the converse needs an open-domain qualification.
assumptions_latex: Subgradients are taken relative to Q.
\(f\equiv0\) on Q.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lipschitz continuity on a nonopen convex domain does not imply that every relative subgradient is bounded.

notation.meaning: subdifferential relative to the domain Q at zero

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Subgradients Need Not Be Bounded

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polar and Bidual Representations of the Dual Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent finite-dimensional representations and the standard lp specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional normed space \((E,\|\cdot\|)\) with unit ball \(B\), the dual unit ball is the polar \[B^\circ=\{g\in E^*: \langle g,u\rangle\le1\ \text{for every }u\in B\},\] and \[\|g\|_*=\sigma_B(g)=\max_{u\in B}\langle g,u\rangle.\] Under the canonical identification \(E\cong E^{**}\), \[\|u\|=\max_{\|g\|_*\le1}\langle g,u\rangle.\] In \(\mathbb R^d\), the norm dual to \(\|\cdot\|_p\), \(1\le p\le\infty\), is \(\|\cdot\|_q\), where \(1/p+1/q=1\) with the usual endpoint conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual norm is the support function of the primal unit ball, the primal norm is recovered from the dual unit ball, and lp and lq are paired dual norms.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional.
For the lp specialization, \(1\le p\le\infty\) and \(q\) is the conjugate exponent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|g\|_*=\sigma_B(g)\), \(\|u\|=\max_{\|g\|_*\le1}\langle g,u\rangle\), and \((\ell_p^d)^*=\ell_q^d\).

notation.meaning: polar of the primal unit ball

knowledge_statements.title: Polar and Bidual Representations of the Dual Norm
Dual-Norm Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual norm and its equivalence with bounded subgradients and norm-Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional normed space \((E,\|\cdot\|)\) with dual space \(E^*\), the dual norm is \[\|g\|_*:=\sup_{\|u\|\le1}\langle g,u\rangle,\qquad g\in E^*.\] It satisfies \(\langle g,u\rangle\le\|g\|_*\|u\|\). If \(Q\subset E\) is convex and \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) is convex, then the uniform condition \(\|g\|_*\le L\) for every \(x\in Q\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\) implies \(|f(y)-f(x)|\le L\|y-x\|\) for all \(x,y\in Q\). On an open convex domain, the converse holds for every subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dual norm measures first-order oracle outputs; bounded dual-norm subgradients are precisely the local geometric condition underlying Lipschitz continuity.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(Q\subset E\) is convex.
\(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) is finite and convex.
For the converse, \(Q\) is open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|g\|_*\le L\) implies \(|f(y)-f(x)|\le L\|y-x\|\); on open \(Q\), the converse also holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mirror Map, Bregman Divergence, and Induced Radius
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines only the geometry used to parameterize norm-dependent lower bounds, excluding mirror-update existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex in a finite-dimensional normed space \((E,\|\cdot\|)\), and let \(\psi\) be differentiable at the points considered. If \(\psi\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex on \(Q\), then \[D_\psi(y,x):=\psi(y)-\psi(x)-\langle\nabla\psi(x),y-x\rangle\ge\frac{\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2.\] For a reference point \(x_0\), define \[R_{\psi,Q}^2(x_0):=\sup_{x\in Q}2D_\psi(x,x_0),\] which may equal \(+\infty\). This definition asserts no attainment of a Bregman-proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly convex mirror map generates a directed Bregman divergence and a possibly infinite reference-point radius used in geometry-sensitive complexity bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(\psi\) is differentiable wherever \(D_\psi\) is evaluated.
\(\psi\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex on \(Q\), with \(\sigma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_\psi(y,x)\ge(\sigma/2)\|y-x\|^2,\qquad R_{\psi,Q}^2(x_0)=\sup_{x\in Q}2D_\psi(x,x_0)\in[0,+\infty].

notation.meaning: directed Bregman divergence generated by psi
strong-convexity modulus relative to the selected norm

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror Map, Bregman Divergence, and Induced Radius
Mirror-Map Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strongly convex distance generator and its Bregman geometry for mirror methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a convex subset of a finite-dimensional normed space \((E,\|\cdot\|)\). A differentiable function \(\psi:Q\to\mathbb R\) is a \(\sigma\)-strongly convex mirror map when \[\psi(y)\ge\psi(x)+\langle\nabla\psi(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma}{2}\|y-x\|^2\] for all \(x,y\in Q\). Its Bregman divergence is \[D_\psi(y,x):=\psi(y)-\psi(x)-\langle\nabla\psi(x),y-x\rangle,\] and therefore \(D_\psi(y,x)\ge(\sigma/2)\|y-x\|^2\). The associated mirror step with dual vector \(g\) and step size \(\eta>0\) minimizes \(\eta\langle g,x\rangle+D_\psi(x,x_t)\) over \(x\in Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mirror map generates a Bregman divergence that dominates squared primal distance and defines the proximal update used by mirror descent.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is convex in a finite-dimensional normed space.
\(\psi\) is differentiable on the points at which its Bregman divergence is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_\psi(y,x)\ge(\sigma/2)\|y-x\|^2\), and the mirror step is the stated Bregman-regularized minimization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Mirror-Map Geometry, and the strong-convexity and Bregman formulas are internally consistent. A source is required, and the asserted mirror step also needs a cited convention or conditions ensuring that the displayed minimization has a solution when Q is not assumed closed or compact.

children.title: Geometry-Mismatch Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Rate losses when oracle, domain, or prox geometries are incompatible.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Mismatch Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss incurred when oracle regularity and prox geometry are measured in incompatible norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\|\cdot\|_a\) describe the Lipschitz class and let a method use geometry \(\|\cdot\|_b\). Suppose \(m\|u\|_a\le\|u\|_b\le M\|u\|_a\) for every \(u\). Then the dual norms satisfy \((1/M)\|g\|_{a,*}\le\|g\|_{b,*}\le(1/m)\|g\|_{a,*}\). Hence a bound \(\|g\|_{a,*}\le L\) permits only \(\|g\|_{b,*}\le L/m\), while a radius \(\|x-x^*\|_a\le R\) permits \(\|x-x^*\|_b\le MR\). A generic nonsmooth bound expressed in geometry \(b\) may therefore worsen from \(LR/\sqrt T\) to \((M/m)LR/\sqrt T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing to a mismatched norm can multiply the usual nonsmooth complexity constant by the norm-equivalence distortion M/m.
assumptions_latex: The two norms obey \(m\|u\|_a\le\|u\|_b\le M\|u\|_a\) with \(0<m\le M\).
Oracle subgradients satisfy \(\|g\|_{a,*}\le L\).
The feasible displacement satisfies \(\|x-x^*\|_a\le R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The product of the dual subgradient bound and primal radius in geometry \(b\) can be as large as \((M/m)LR\).

notation.meaning: dual norms associated with the two primal norms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container. The primal and dual norm-equivalence inequalities are correct, and they yield the stated worst-case product distortion. A source is nevertheless required for the nontrivial transfer from those inequalities to the claimed generic nonsmooth-rate boundary and its precise scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Nonsmooth Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-error lower bound for randomized local first-order algorithms in sufficiently high Euclidean dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\) be the class of convex \(L\)-Lipschitz functions on a Euclidean ball of radius \(R\). For every possibly randomized algorithm making at most \(T\) adaptive calls to a local first-order oracle, there is a distribution over instances in \(\mathcal F_{L,R}\) and universal constants \(c,c_d>0\) such that, when \(d\ge c_dT\), \[\mathbb E\bigl[f(x_T)-\min_x f(x)\bigr]\ge c\frac{LR}{\sqrt{T+1}}.\] The expectation is over both the instance distribution and the algorithm's internal randomness. Thus randomization alone does not improve the minimax exponent, and expected error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(T=\Omega((LR/\varepsilon)^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In sufficiently high dimension, randomized local first-order algorithms retain the nonsmooth lower bound Ω(LR/√T) in expected error.
assumptions_latex: The objective is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz on a Euclidean ball of radius \(R\).
The algorithm has only adaptive local first-order oracle access.
The dimension is at least a universal constant times \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[f(x_T)-f^*]\ge cLR/\sqrt{T+1}\), hence \(T=\Omega((LR/\varepsilon)^2)\).

notation.meaning: expectation over hard instances and algorithmic randomness

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Sensitive Oracle Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifier boundary separating high-dimensional resisting-oracle lower bounds from fixed-dimensional behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonsmooth oracle lower bound of the form \(f(x_T)-f^*\ge cLR/\sqrt T\) is dimension-sensitive when its hard instance requires \(d\ge d_0(T)\), typically with \(d_0(T)=\Omega(T)\). Such a statement has quantifier order \[\forall T\;\forall A_T\;\exists d\ge d_0(T)\;\exists f_d:\quad f_d(x_T)-f_d^*\ge cLR/\sqrt T.\] It does not imply the fixed-dimensional assertion obtained by placing \(d\) before \(T\). In fixed finite dimension, localization or cutting-plane procedures may exploit accumulated separating information, so a high-dimensional resisting-oracle construction cannot by itself establish the same asymptotic lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower bound whose hard dimension grows with the query budget does not establish the same rate when dimension is fixed first.
assumptions_latex: The lower-bound construction requires \(d\ge d_0(T)\).
The algorithm receives local first-order oracle responses.
Dimension is treated as a complexity parameter rather than a fixed universal constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The growing-dimension lower bound does not imply \(\forall d\,\forall T\,\exists f_d\) with the same \(T^{-1/2}\) obstruction.

notation.meaning: minimum dimension required by the hard construction
an algorithm using at most T oracle calls
a hard objective in dimension d

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind correctly matches the container, and the distinction between a dimension chosen after the query budget and a fixed dimension is logically sound. The claims about typical linear dimension growth and possible fixed-dimensional escape through localization or cutting planes require specific supporting sources.

children.title: Cutting-Plane Access
children.top_down_role: Regimes permitting global localization through cutting-plane information.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Localization algorithm using objective subgradients as separating cuts for the minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a compact convex localization set \(K_0\subset\mathbb R^d\), choose a query point \(x_t\in K_t\) and request \(f(x_t)\) and \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\). Maintain the best queried point \(\hat x_t\). Convexity gives \(f(y)\ge f(x_t)+\langle g_t,y-x_t\rangle\); therefore, whenever \(f(x_t)>f^*\), every minimizer lies in \(H_t:=\{y:\langle g_t,y-x_t\rangle\le0\}\). Update \[K_{t+1}:=K_t\cap H_t,\qquad \hat x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le i\le t}f(x_i).\] Stop when a prescribed localization-width, volume, or certified objective-gap criterion is met, and output the incumbent \(\hat x_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting-plane method queries a subgradient, retains the halfspace containing every minimizer, shrinks the localization set, and returns the best query.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on a compact convex set \(K_0\).
Each query returns a valid subgradient \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\).
The query-point rule selects \(x_t\in K_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizer in \(K_0\) remains in \(K_{t+1}=K_t\cap H_t\), and the output is the best queried point.

notation.meaning: subgradient halfspace retained after query t
best queried point through iteration t

children.title: Complete-Data Escape Routes
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes when full problem data replaces local oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete-Data Escape Routes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of black-box lower bounds when the objective is supplied by a finite explicit representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lower bound proved for a local first-order oracle applies only when the algorithm's information about \(f\) is restricted to oracle transcripts. If instead the input supplies a complete finite representation \(\mathcal D(f)\)—for example, all affine pieces of a polyhedral objective—an algorithm may inspect and globally process \(\mathcal D(f)\). For \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^\top x+b_i)\) over a represented convex set \(Q\), minimization is equivalent to \[\min_{x,t}\{t:x\in Q,\ a_i^\top x+b_i\le t\ \text{for all }i\}.\] Consequently, a local-oracle query lower bound does not transfer without accounting for representation size and the permitted global computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit access to every affine piece can convert a nonsmooth problem into a finite convex program, escaping lower bounds based solely on local oracle information.
assumptions_latex: The objective has the explicit representation \(f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}(a_i^\top x+b_i)\).
The feasible set \(Q\) is convex and explicitly represented.
The algorithm may read and globally process the complete input data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing \(f\) is equivalent to the displayed epigraph program, so local-oracle query lower bounds do not automatically apply.

notation.meaning: complete finite representation of the objective

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the epigraph reformulation of a finite maximum of affine functions is correct. A source is required for the broader information-model conclusion distinguishing complete-data access from local-oracle query lower bounds.

children.title: Dimension-Free Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of dimension-independent nonsmooth lower-bound claims.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Dimensional Localization Defeats a Uniform Inverse-Square Barrier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-dimensional witness against extrapolating a growing-dimension nonsmooth lower bound uniformly to every dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[-R,R]\to\mathbb R\) be convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz. Beginning with \(I_0=[-R,R]\), query the midpoint \(m_t\) of \(I_{t-1}\) and obtain \(g_t\in\partial f(m_t)\). If \(g_t>0\), retain the left half; if \(g_t<0\), retain the right half; and if \(g_t=0\), return \(m_t\). Each retained interval contains every minimizer consistent with the returned subgradient. After \(T\) nonterminal queries, the midpoint \(\bar x_T\) of \(I_T\) satisfies \[f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le L\,\operatorname{dist}(\bar x_T,X^*)\le \frac{LR}{2^T}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In one dimension, exact subgradient-sign bisection gives geometric objective accuracy, disproving any uniform extrapolation of the high-dimensional inverse-square barrier to every fixed dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(L\)-Lipschitz on \([-R,R]\).
Each query returns an exact subgradient.
The minimizer set \(X^*\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_T)-f^*\le LR2^{-T}\), so \(T\ge\lceil\log_2(LR/\varepsilon)\rceil\) suffices for error at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: retained localization interval after t queries
midpoint of the final localization interval

knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Localization Defeats a Uniform Inverse-Square Barrier
Dimension-Free Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion distinguishing genuinely dimension-free oracle bounds from bounds valid only above a budget-dependent dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle lower bound \(T(\varepsilon,L,R,d)\ge\Phi(\varepsilon,L,R)\) is dimension-free only if its constants and validity range are independent of \(d\) throughout the stated dimension class. A theorem requiring \(d\ge d_0(\varepsilon)\) or \(d\ge d_0(T)\) establishes instead \[\sup_{d\ge d_0(T)}\ \sup_{f\in\mathcal F_d}\bigl(f(x_T)-f^*\bigr)\ge\Delta_T,\] not \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_d}(f(x_T)-f^*)\ge\Delta_T\) for every fixed \(d\). Thus suppressing dimension from the displayed rate is legitimate only after retaining the theorem's dimension condition or proving uniformity over \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A displayed rate is not truly dimension-free if its hard instance requires dimension to grow with accuracy or the oracle budget.
assumptions_latex: The problem classes \(\mathcal F_d\) are indexed by dimension.
The proposed lower bound may impose a dimension threshold \(d_0\).
Oracle complexity counts adaptive information queries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A condition \(d\ge d_0(T)\) prevents the bound from being uniform over every fixed dimension.

notation.meaning: claimed residual lower bound after T queries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, and the main warning about budget-dependent dimension thresholds is correct. The displayed supremum statement omits the algorithm quantifier governing x_T, so its exact lower-bound interpretation is not self-contained; a source is also needed for the proposed dimension-free criterion.

children.title: Uniformly Convex Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for curvature classes extending strong convexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform-Convexity Growth and Distance Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power growth and gap-to-distance conversion at an attained minimizer under the seed normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is \((\mu,p)\)-uniformly convex and \(x^*\) is a minimizer with \(0\in\partial f(x^*)\), then \[f(x)-f(x^*)\ge \frac{\mu}{p}\|x-x^*\|^p.\] Consequently, the minimizer is unique and \[f(x)-f(x^*)\le\varepsilon\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \|x-x^*\|\le\left(\frac{p\varepsilon}{\mu}\right)^{1/p}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power-type uniform convexity gives uniqueness, power growth at the minimizer, and an objective-gap-to-distance certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, convex, and \((\mu,p)\)-uniformly convex under the seed normalization.
A minimizer \(x^*\) is attained and \(0\in\partial f(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)-f(x^*)\ge(\mu/p)\|x-x^*\|^p\), and an \(\varepsilon\)-gap implies \(\|x-x^*\|\le(p\varepsilon/\mu)^{1/p}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Convexity Growth and Distance Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Power-Type Uniform Convexity under the Subgradient Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixes the local modulus convention used for degree-p uniformly convex complexity classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex in a normed space, \(p\ge2\), and \(\mu>0\). A proper convex function \(f\) is \((\mu,p)\)-uniformly convex on \(Q\) under the subgradient normalization if, for all \(x,y\in Q\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{p}\|y-x\|^p.\] At \(p=2\), this is strong convexity with quadratic term \((\mu/2)\|y-x\|^2\). Constants in midpoint or Jensen-gap definitions must be converted before their moduli are identified with this \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local convention uses growth μ‖y−x‖^p/p above every supporting hyperplane; alternative conventions may use a different numerical modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is convex.
\(f\) is proper and convex, with the inequality imposed where \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(y)-f(x)-\langle g,y-x\rangle\ge\frac{\mu}{p}\|y-x\|^p.

notation.meaning: modulus under the displayed subgradient normalization

knowledge_statements.title: Power-Type Uniform Convexity under the Subgradient Normalization
Uniformly Convex Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-type uniform convexity, with strong convexity as the quadratic special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be convex in a normed space \((E,\|\cdot\|)\), let \(p\ge2\), and let \(\mu>0\). A proper convex function \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) is \((\mu,p)\)-uniformly convex on \(Q\) if, for every \(x,y\in Q\) and every \(g\in\partial f(x)\), \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{p}\|y-x\|^p.\] When \(p=2\), this is strong convexity with modulus \(\mu\) under the displayed normalization. For \(p>2\), the condition supplies power-type growth beyond each supporting hyperplane and defines a distinct curvature regime for first-order complexity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform convexity requires function growth of at least μ‖y−x‖^p/p above every supporting hyperplane; p=2 recovers strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is convex in a normed space.
\(f\) is proper and convex with nonempty subdifferential at the points considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(y)-f(x)-\langle g,y-x\rangle\ge(\mu/p)\|y-x\|^p\) for all admissible \(x,y,g\).

notation.meaning: power or degree of uniform convexity
convex subdifferential of f at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Uniformly Convex Regimes, and the displayed power-type definition consistently recovers the stated strong-convexity normalization at p=2. A specific authoritative source is required because uniform-convexity definitions and constants vary by convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Growth from a Minimizer of a Uniformly Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex-analysis result for degree-p uniform convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) be a convex subset of a normed vector space, and let \(d:Q\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Suppose \(p\ge 2\), \(\sigma_p>0\), and
\[
d(y)\ge d(x)+\langle\nabla d(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma_p}{p}\lVert y-x\rVert^p
\quad\text{for all }x,y\in Q.
\]
If \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}d(x)\), then
\[
d(x)\ge d(x^*)+\frac{\sigma_p}{p}\lVert x-x^*\rVert^p
\quad\text{for every }x\in Q.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a differentiable function is uniformly convex of degree p with constant sigma_p on a convex set and attains its minimum at x*, then its value at every x exceeds the minimum by at least (sigma_p/p) times the pth power of the distance from x to x*.
assumptions_latex: Q\text{ is a convex subset of a normed vector space}
d:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is differentiable}
p\ge 2,\quad \sigma_p>0
\forall x,y\in Q:\ d(y)\ge d(x)+\langle\nabla d(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\sigma_p}{p}\lVert y-x\rVert^p
x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in Q}d(x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in Q:\ d(x)\ge d(x^*)+\frac{\sigma_p}{p}\lVert x-x^*\rVert^p

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex, strictly convex, strongly convex, and concave functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional definitions on a nonempty convex domain; strong convexity uses the stated quadratic modulus convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex and let $f:S\to\mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is convex if, for all $x_1,x_2\in S$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $f(\alpha x_1+(1-\alpha)x_2)\leq\alpha f(x_1)+(1-\alpha)f(x_2)$. It is strictly convex if this inequality is strict whenever $x_1\neq x_2$. It is strongly convex with modulus $c>0$ if, for all such $x_1,x_2,\alpha$, $f(\alpha x_1+(1-\alpha)x_2)\leq\alpha f(x_1)+(1-\alpha)f(x_2)-\tfrac12c\alpha(1-\alpha)\|x_1-x_2\|^2$. The corresponding concavity notions hold for $f$ exactly when the respective convexity notions hold for $-f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity bounds a function at every strict convex combination by the same combination of its endpoint values. Strict convexity makes the bound strict for distinct endpoints, and strong convexity strengthens it by a positive quadratic separation term. Concavity and its strict or strong variants are defined by applying the corresponding convexity definition to the negative function.
assumptions_latex: S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty and convex}
f:S\to\mathbb{R}
x_1,x_2\in S
\alpha\in(0,1)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex, strictly convex, or strongly convex according to the stated Jensen inequalities, and }f\text{ is correspondingly concave iff }-f\text{ is correspondingly convex.}

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-plus-Proximable Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composite convex minimization with gradient access to one term and exact proximal access to the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The smooth-plus-proximable regime consists of problems \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^d}F(x):=f(x)+g(x)\), where \(f\) is proper, convex, differentiable, and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, while \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex. An oracle query may return \(f(x)\) and \(\nabla f(x)\), and, for any declared \(\lambda>0\), the exact point \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(v):=\arg\min_{z\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{g(z)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert z-v\rVert^2\right\}.\] Complexity counts these gradient and proximal queries separately or under an explicitly stated joint-query convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective splits into a smooth convex term queried by gradients and a closed convex term accessed through exact proximal evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.
\(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The available primitive information is \(\nabla f\) together with exact evaluations of \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}\).

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of the nonsmooth component.

knowledge_statements.title: Whole-Objective Proximal-Oracle Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle model granting exact proximal points of the entire convex objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper, closed, convex function \(F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), a whole-objective proximal oracle accepts \((v,\lambda)\in\mathbb R^d\times(0,\infty)\) and returns the unique point \[P_F(v,\lambda):=\arg\min_{z\in\mathbb R^d}\left\{F(z)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert z-v\rVert^2\right\}.\] The oracle is exact: the returned point satisfies \(0\in\partial F(P_F(v,\lambda))+\lambda^{-1}(P_F(v,\lambda)-v)\). Oracle complexity counts calls to \(P_F\), and comparisons with first-order models must state whether function values or subgradients are additionally available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A whole-objective proximal oracle exactly minimizes the objective plus a quadratic centered at the query point; each such minimization is one oracle call.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns the unique exact proximal point \(P_F(v,\lambda)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Proximal Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap model for an inexact response to a convex proximal subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and define \(Q_{v,\lambda}(z):=F(z)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\lVert z-v\rVert^2\) for \(\lambda>0\). A point \(\widetilde p\in\operatorname{dom}F\) is an \(\eta\)-approximate proximal response at \((v,\lambda)\) in the objective-gap sense if \[Q_{v,\lambda}(\widetilde p)-\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^d}Q_{v,\lambda}(z)\leq\eta,\qquad \eta\geq0.\] Because \(Q_{v,\lambda}\) is \(1/\lambda\)-strongly convex, this criterion also implies \(\lVert\widetilde p-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(v)\rVert\leq\sqrt{2\lambda\eta}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate proximal response solves the regularized proximal subproblem to a declared objective-gap tolerance, which also bounds its distance from the exact response.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\) and \(\eta\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{v,\lambda}(\widetilde p)-\inf Q_{v,\lambda}\leq\eta\) and \(\lVert\widetilde p-\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda F}(v)\rVert\leq\sqrt{2\lambda\eta}\).

children.title: Inner-Solve Cost
children.top_down_role: Computational expense incurred within each proximal request.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Solve Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost assigned to computing one approximate proximal response by an inner algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an inner algorithm computes an \(\eta\)-approximate minimizer of \(Q_{v,\lambda}\) using a primitive oracle for the proximal subproblem. Its inner-solve cost is \(C_{\mathrm{in}}(v,\lambda,\eta)\), the number of primitive oracle calls required to guarantee the declared approximation criterion. If a uniform bound is needed over an admissible query set \(\mathcal Q\), define \[C_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda,\eta):=\sup_{v:(v,\lambda)\in\mathcal Q}C_{\mathrm{in}}(v,\lambda,\eta).\] Any complexity claim treating an approximate proximal response as one unit-cost call must instead disclose this inner cost or explicitly postulate a unit-cost approximate-proximal oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost of an approximate proximal call is the primitive work needed by its inner solver, uniformly over allowed query points when required.
assumptions_latex: A primitive oracle and an approximation criterion for the proximal subproblem are fixed.
\((v,\lambda)\) belongs to the admissible query set \(\mathcal Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One approximate proximal response costs \(C_{\mathrm{in}}(v,\lambda,\eta)\) primitive calls, or at most \(C_{\mathrm{in}}(\lambda,\eta)\) uniformly.

notation.meaning: Primitive-oracle complexity of an inner solve.

children.title: Nested Oracle Accounting
children.top_down_role: Complexity measures combining outer requests with inner oracle work.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Oracle Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total primitive-query accounting for an outer method containing inexact inner proximal solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an outer method making \(T\) iterations. At iteration \(t\), let it use \(q_t\) direct primitive-oracle calls and request one approximate proximal response with parameters \((v_t,\lambda_t,\eta_t)\), computed at cost \(C_{\mathrm{in}}(v_t,\lambda_t,\eta_t)\). Under this cost convention, the total primitive-query count is \[N_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(q_t+C_{\mathrm{in}}(v_t,\lambda_t,\eta_t)\right).\] If several inner solves occur at one iteration, their costs are summed. Reporting only \(T\) gives an end-to-end primitive-query count only under an explicitly stated unit-cost convention; under any other cost model, \(T\) is an iteration count and the inner costs must be bounded separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: End-to-end primitive-query accounting adds all direct outer calls and every primitive call spent inside proximal subproblem solves; iteration count alone requires a stated cost convention.
assumptions_latex: Each direct and inner oracle invocation has a specified unit of cost.
The outer method performs \(T\) iterations.
One approximate proximal response is requested per iteration in the displayed formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated convention, the end-to-end primitive-query count is \(N_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}(q_t+C_{\mathrm{in}}(v_t,\lambda_t,\eta_t))\).

notation.meaning: Direct outer primitive calls at iteration \(t\).
Primitive-query cost of the inner solve at iteration t.

children.title: Proximal Accuracy-Cost Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between response precision and total complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Accuracy-Cost Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance selection balances accumulated outer error against the work of inner proximal solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an outer convergence guarantee after \(T\) iterations has the form \[\mathcal E_T\leq B_T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t\eta_t,\] where \(B_T\) is the exact-proximal bound, \(w_t\geq0\), and the inner cost \(C_{\mathrm{in}}(v_t,\lambda_t,\eta_t)\) is nonincreasing in \(\eta_t\). To guarantee \(\mathcal E_T\leq\varepsilon\), admissible tolerances must satisfy \(B_T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t\eta_t\leq\varepsilon\). Among such schedules, the end-to-end cost is minimized by solving \[\min_{\eta_t\geq0}\sum_{t=1}^{T}C_{\mathrm{in}}(v_t,\lambda_t,\eta_t)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t\eta_t\leq\varepsilon-B_T.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal tolerances should be only tight enough to fit the outer error budget, chosen to minimize the summed inner-solve cost.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal E_T\leq B_T+\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t\eta_t\) with \(w_t\geq0\).
Inner cost is nonincreasing as the allowed tolerance increases.
\(B_T\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal tolerance schedule minimizes total inner cost subject to \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}w_t\eta_t\leq\varepsilon-B_T\).

notation.meaning: Outer optimization error after T iterations.
Sensitivity weight of the t-th proximal error.
Error bound with exact proximal responses.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the tradeoff container, but the additive error model and weights are method-dependent and have no source. Moreover, calling the displayed optimization end-to-end optimal requires direct outer costs and query parameters to be fixed or independent of the tolerance schedule. A method-specific source is needed before choosing the reliable formulation.
