children.title: Aggregate Convexity
children.top_down_role: Convexity properties of the averaged objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity imposed on the averaged objective rather than necessarily on its components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex set, let \(f_i:C\to\mathbb R\), and define \(F:C\to\mathbb R\) by \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). The finite-sum objective is aggregate convex on \(C\) if, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\le \theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y).\] Aggregate convexity constrains only the average and does not, by itself, imply convexity of any individual \(f_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The average objective satisfies the convexity inequality, even though one or more individual components may be nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and convex.
\(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) is finite-valued on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is convex on }C.\)

children.title: Component-to-Average Transfer
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound consequences linking component structure to aggregate behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-to-Average Transfer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers componentwise convexity and gradient regularity to the arithmetic average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex and let each differentiable \(f_i:C	o\mathbb R\) be convex with \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient. Define \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) and \( ar L=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n L_i\). Then \(F\) is convex and, for all \(x,y\in C\), \[\|
abla F(x)-
abla F(y)\|\le  rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|\le  ar L\|x-y\|.\] Hence componentwise convexity and component Lipschitz constants provide valid aggregate convexity and smoothness guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging convex smooth components preserves convexity, and the average of their gradient-Lipschitz constants is a valid smoothness constant.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is convex.
Each \(f_i\) is convex and differentiable with \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\text{ is convex and has }\bar L=n^{-1}\sum_iL_i\text{-Lipschitz gradient}.\)

notation.meaning: Arithmetic mean of component smoothness constants.

children.title: Aggregate-Only Convexity Regime

children.title: Nonconvex Component Geometry
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum classes permitting nonconvex individual components.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Component Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows negative component curvature while retaining a convex average objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and convex, and let \(f_i:C\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. The decomposition has nonconvex component geometry when there exist \(i\), \(x\in C\), and \(v\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \[v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2 f_i(x)v<0.\] In the aggregate-only convexity regime this is permitted provided \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n f_j\) remains convex, equivalently \(\nabla^2F(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in C\). Thus component curvature may be indefinite although average curvature is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some component has negative curvature in some direction, while the Hessian of the averaged objective remains positive semidefinite everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is open and convex.
Every component is twice continuously differentiable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists i,x,v:\ v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f_i(x)v<0\), while \(\nabla^2F(x)\succeq0\) for all \(x\in C\).

children.title: Convex Aggregate Geometry
children.top_down_role: Convexity retained only by the averaged objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Aggregate Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First- or second-order characterization of convexity for the averaged objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and convex, let each \(f_i:C	o\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and define \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\). The aggregate has convex geometry precisely when \[
abla^2F(x)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
abla^2f_i(x)\succeq0\qquad	ext{for every }x\in C.\] Equivalently, \(F(y)\ge F(x)+\langle
abla F(x),y-xangle\) for all \(x,y\in C\). Neither characterization requires the individual Hessians \(
abla^2f_i(x)\) to be positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The averaged Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere, equivalently the aggregate obeys its supporting-hyperplane inequality; individual component Hessians may remain indefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is open and convex.
Every \(f_i\) is twice continuously differentiable on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is convex on }C\iff n^{-1}\sum_i\nabla^2f_i(x)\succeq0\text{ for all }x\in C.\)

children.title: Cross-Component Cancellation
children.top_down_role: Aggregate convexity produced through compensation among components.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Component Cancellation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quadratic construction exhibiting cancellation of opposing component curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\mu\ge0\), \(\rho>\mu\), and \(x=(x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^2\). Define \[f_1(x)=\frac\mu2\|x\|^2+\frac\rho2(x_1^2-x_2^2),\qquad f_2(x)=\frac\mu2\|x\|^2-\frac\rho2(x_1^2-x_2^2).\] Each component is nonconvex because its Hessian has eigenvalue \(\mu-\rho<0\), but their average satisfies \[F(x)=\frac{f_1(x)+f_2(x)}2=\frac\mu2\|x\|^2.\] Hence the equal and opposite indefinite curvature terms cancel across components, making \(F\) convex, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex when \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonconvex quadratics can have equal and opposite indefinite curvature, so their average is a convex or strongly convex quadratic.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho>\mu\ge0\).
The aggregate is the arithmetic mean of the two displayed components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_1\text{ and }f_2\text{ are nonconvex, while }(f_1+f_2)/2=(\mu/2)\|x\|^2\text{ is convex}.\)
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct quadratic construction verified by its displayed Hessians and average.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Componentwise Nonconvexity Penalty
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound costs attributable to missing componentwise convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Nonconvexity Penalty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies, as an extended-real value, the worst negative curvature hidden by a convex finite-sum average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let each \(f_i\in C^2(C)\). Define the componentwise nonconvexity penalty by \[\rho_{\mathrm{cmp}}=\max_{1\le i\le n}\sup_{x\in C}\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f_i(x))\}\in[0,+\infty].\] Equivalently, \[\rho_{\mathrm{cmp}}=\inf\left\{\rho\ge0: x\mapsto f_i(x)+\frac{\rho}{2}\|x\|^2\text{ is convex on }C\text{ for every }i\right\},\] with the convention \(\inf\varnothing=+infty\). Thus \(\rho_{\mathrm{cmp}}=0\) exactly when all components are convex; it may be positive or infinite even when their average is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The penalty is the possibly infinite worst negative component curvature, equivalently the infimum of common quadratic regularization strengths making every component convex. It is zero exactly when all components are convex and may be positive or infinite for a convex average.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
Each component belongs to \(C^2(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_{\mathrm{cmp}}=0\iff f_i\text{ is convex on }C\text{ for every }i\), and \(\rho_{\mathrm{cmp}}=+infty\) when no finite common quadratic regularization makes all components convex.

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric Hessian.

review_flags: The negative-curvature quantity is standard, but the terminology and its intended finite-sum complexity role require a dedicated source.

children.title: Strongly Convex Finite-Sum Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for condition-sensitive incremental complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Finite-Sum Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition-sensitive finite-sum class with strong convexity imposed on the aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex, let \(f_i:C\to\mathbb R\), and define \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\). The problem belongs to the strongly convex finite-sum regime with parameter \(\mu>0\) when, for all \(x,y\in C\) and every \(g\in\partial F(x)\), \[F(y)\ge F(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle+\frac\mu2\|y-x\|^2.\] If \(F\) is differentiable, one may take \(g=\nabla F(x)\). This aggregate condition does not alone require the individual components to be strongly convex or convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The averaged finite-sum objective satisfies the strong-convexity inequality with parameter μ, without necessarily imposing convexity on each component.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is convex.
\(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\) is proper and subdifferentiable on the points considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is }\mu\text{-strongly convex on }C.\)

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential of F at x.

children.title: Component Smoothness Classes

children.title: Uniform Component Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum classes sharing a common component smoothness bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Component Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A common Euclidean gradient-Lipschitz bound imposed on every finite-sum component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let every \(f_i:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. The finite-sum representation has uniform component smoothness with constant \(L\ge0\) if, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and all \(x,y\in C\), \[\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2.\] The same constant must control every component. Consequently, the average \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) also has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(C\), although its smallest valid smoothness constant may be strictly less than \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the Euclidean norm, one common constant bounds the gradient variation of every component. The same constant also bounds the average gradient, possibly non-sharply.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
Every component \(f_i:C\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
All bounds use the Euclidean norm \(\|\cdot\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\) for every \(i\) and all \(x,y\in C\), and \(\|
abla F(x)-
abla F(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\).

children.title: Average Smoothness
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum classes controlled through aggregate component regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Average Smoothness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-square component-gradient regularity used in finite-sum oracle analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and let each \(f_i:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. The family is average smooth with constant \(L_{\mathrm{av}}\ge0\) if, for every \(x,y\in C\), \[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|^2\le L_{\mathrm{av}}^2\|x-y\|^2.\] By Jensen's inequality, the aggregate \(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\) then has \(L_{\mathrm{av}}\)-Lipschitz gradient. This condition permits individual components to have gradient-Lipschitz constants larger than \(L_{\mathrm{av}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mean squared change of component gradients is bounded by a common quadratic rate, which implies smoothness of the averaged objective.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f_i\) is differentiable on \(C\).
The component gradients and domain use a fixed Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla F(x)-\nabla F(y)\|\le L_{\mathrm{av}}\|x-y\|\text{ for all }x,y\in C.\)
review_flags: Average smoothness has multiple conventions; the mean-square version selected here requires a finite-sum complexity source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mean-square condition and its Jensen consequence are mathematically precise, but “average smoothness” has competing conventions and requires a finite-sum complexity source. Uniform component smoothness is a sufficient stronger condition, not a logical prerequisite for defining mean-square average smoothness.

children.title: Heterogeneous Component Regularity
children.top_down_role: Complexity with unequal smoothness across components.

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Component Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise Lipschitz-gradient regularity with nonuniform constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), for \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), be differentiable. The family has heterogeneous component regularity \((L_1,\ldots,L_n)\) if each \(L_i\ge 0\) and
\[\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|_2\le L_i\|x-y\|_2\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d.\]
The constants may depend on the component and need not be uniformly bounded independently of \(n\). Associated aggregate parameters include \(L_{\max}=\max_i L_i\), \(L_{\mathrm{av}}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n L_i\), and \(L_{\mathrm{rms}}=(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nL_i^2)^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each component has a Lipschitz gradient, but its smoothness constant may differ; maximum, arithmetic-mean, and root-mean-square constants summarize the family.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\)
Each \(f_i\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|_2\le L_i\|x-y\|_2\) for every component and all \(x,y\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the gradient of component i
arithmetic mean of component smoothness constants

children.title: Smoothness-Aggregation Gap
children.top_down_role: Rate distinctions between uniform and average regularity control.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothness-Aggregation Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap between componentwise and aggregate gradient smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), where each differentiable \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) has an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient with \(L_i\ge 0\). Then
\[\|\nabla F(x)-\nabla F(y)\|_2\le L_{\mathrm{av}}\|x-y\|_2,\qquad L_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nL_i,\]
although component-oracle arguments based on uniform smoothness may use \(L_{\max}=\max_iL_i\). When \(L_{\mathrm{av}}>0\), the ratio \(L_{\max}/L_{\mathrm{av}}\) can equal \(n\): for \(d=1\) and any \(L>0\), take \(f_1(x)=nLx^2/2\) and \(f_i(x)=0\) for \(i>1\). Then \(F(x)=Lx^2/2\), while \(L_{\max}=nL\) and \(L_{\mathrm{av}}=L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-sum average can be much smoother than its least-smooth component; when the average smoothness bound is positive, the maximum-to-average smoothness ratio can grow linearly with the number of components.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\)
Each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable with an \(L_i\)-Lipschitz gradient, where \(L_i\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla F)\le L_{\mathrm{av}}\le L_{\max}\), and, when \(L_{\mathrm{av}}>0\), \(L_{\max}/L_{\mathrm{av}}\) may equal \(n\).

children.title: Nonconvex Finite-Sum Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Organizes incremental lower bounds for stationary-point and objective-accuracy targets in nonconvex finite sums.

children.title: Structured-Component Nonconvex Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for nonconvex averages with stronger component structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Component Nonconvex Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex averages whose components satisfy stronger curvature control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable finite sum \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) belongs to a structured-component nonconvex regime with parameters \((L_i,ho_i)_{i=1}^n\) if \(F\) is nonconvex and, for every \(i\),
\[\|
abla f_i(x)-
abla f_i(y)\|_2\le L_i\|x-y\|_2\quad	ext{and}\quad f_i(y)\ge f_i(x)+\langle
abla f_i(x),y-xangle- rac{ho_i}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2\]
for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), with \(0\leho_i<L_i\). Thus each component is smoother than a fully unrestricted \(L_i\)-smooth nonconvex component through a strictly smaller weak-convexity parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The average is nonconvex, while every component has a Lipschitz gradient and a weak-convexity constant strictly smaller than its smoothness bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable for every \(i\).
\(0\le \rho_i<L_i<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is nonconvex and every \(f_i\) is both \(L_i\)-smooth and \(\rho_i\)-weakly convex.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The title and navigation role do not uniquely select componentwise weak convexity with the strict restriction rho_i<L_i. An authoritative source is required to establish that this particular condition is the intended structured-component nonconvex regime.

children.title: Fully Nonconvex Component Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for nonconvexity at both component and aggregate levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Nonconvex Component Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sums allowing nonconvexity in every component and the average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable finite sum \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) is in the fully nonconvex component regime with bounds \((L_i)_{i=1}^n\) if every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies
\[\|\nabla f_i(x)-\nabla f_i(y)\|_2\le L_i\|x-y\|_2\quad\text{for all }x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d,\]
while neither the components nor \(F\) are assumed convex. In a worst-case class, admissible instances include families for which each \(f_i\) and their average \(F\) are nonconvex. No componentwise curvature restriction stronger than gradient Lipschitz continuity is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every component is smooth but may be nonconvex, the average may also be nonconvex, and no stronger componentwise curvature structure is assumed.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\)
Each \(f_i\) is differentiable with finite gradient-Lipschitz constant \(L_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity is not required for any \(f_i\) or for \(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\).

children.title: Finite-Sum Objective Structure
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum component organization relevant to incremental-oracle lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Objective Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable average objective accessed through indexed components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable finite-sum objective has the form
\[F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^d,\]
where \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\) and each component \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable. An indexed first-order oracle accepts a pair \((i,x)\) and returns \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\), or only \(\nabla f_i(x)\) when values are excluded. One full gradient is
\[\nabla F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla f_i(x),\]
requiring \(n\) component-gradient evaluations in the basic indexed-oracle accounting model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective is an average of differentiable components; an indexed oracle reveals one component gradient per query, while a full gradient aggregates all components.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\in\mathbb{N}\)
Every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\) and \(\nabla F=n^{-1}\sum_i\nabla f_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Output Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic and randomized first-order stationarity conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a differentiable objective \(F:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\), a deterministic output \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary under the gradient-norm criterion if
\[\|
abla F(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon.\]
Under the squared-gradient convention it satisfies \(\|
abla F(x)\|_2^2\le\varepsilon\). For a randomized output \(X\), the corresponding expected criteria are \(\mathbb{E}\|
abla F(X)\|_2\le\varepsilon\) and \(\mathbb{E}\|
abla F(X)\|_2^2\le\varepsilon\), respectively. These conventions are not numerically interchangeable without replacing the tolerance: the squared-norm threshold \(\varepsilon\) corresponds to gradient-norm scale \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity may be measured by gradient norm or squared gradient norm, deterministically or in expectation; complexity claims must identify the chosen convention.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
Any expectation is taken over all algorithmic and oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output criterion is one explicitly chosen inequality involving \(\nabla F\), with its stated deterministic or expected interpretation.

children.title: Objective–Criterion Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries between finite-sum objectives and stationarity certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective–Criterion Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity must be evaluated for the aggregate objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), with every \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) differentiable. A first-order stationarity criterion for the finite-sum optimization problem is compatible with its objective when it is stated using
\[
abla F(x)= rac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
abla f_i(x).\]
Thus \(\|
abla F(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon\), or its declared randomized analogue, certifies aggregate stationarity. Requiring every \(\|
abla f_i(x)\|_2\) to be small is generally a different and stronger condition. Conversely, a small sampled component gradient does not by itself certify that \(x\) is stationary for \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-sum stationarity guarantee must concern the average gradient; small individual or sampled component gradients generally express different conditions.
assumptions_latex: Every component \(f_i\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Aggregate stationarity is measured using \(\nabla F=n^{-1}\sum_i\nabla f_i\), not an unaggregated component gradient.

children.title: Batch-Processing Cost Baselines
children.top_down_role: Navigation for comparisons against batch processing.

children.title: Full-Gradient Baselines
children.top_down_role: Reference costs measured through complete gradient evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Gradient Baselines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed-oracle cost of batch gradient iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), suppose a batch first-order method performs \(T\) iterations and at each iteration computes \(\nabla F(x_t)\) by querying every component gradient once. In the serial indexed first-order oracle model, its component-gradient cost is exactly
\[Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}=nT,\]
excluding initialization, function-value queries, and line-search retries. If an additional final full gradient is computed to verify the output criterion, the cost is \(n(T+1)\). Consequently, any iteration bound \(T(\varepsilon)\) for the batch method induces the component-oracle baseline \(nT(\varepsilon)\), subject to the same accuracy convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A batch method using one complete gradient per iteration spends n component-gradient queries per iteration, plus any separately counted verification gradient.
assumptions_latex: Each full gradient is formed from all \(n\) component gradients.
Oracle calls are counted serially, without parallel-time discounting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{IFO}}=nT\), or \(n(T+1)\) when one final full-gradient verification is included.

children.title: Data-Pass Baselines
children.top_down_role: Reference costs measured through complete passes over component data.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Pass Baselines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Serial component-access cost normalized by dataset size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite sum with \(n\) indexed components, one equivalent data pass is defined as \(n\) component-oracle evaluations. If an algorithm makes \(Q\) such evaluations, its fractional pass count is
\[P_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{Q}{n}.\]
When only completed or initiated scans are reportable, the corresponding integer counts are \(\lfloor Q/n\rfloor\) completed passes and \(\lceil Q/n\rceil\) initiated passes. This normalization measures total serial component access; it does not imply that indices are visited in order, exactly once, or without replacement, and it does not measure parallel wall-clock time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One equivalent data pass equals n component accesses; dividing total indexed-oracle calls by n gives a fractional pass count independent of access order.
assumptions_latex: The finite sum contains \(n\) indexed components.
Every counted component-oracle evaluation has unit serial cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{eq}}=Q/n\), with floor or ceiling used only for explicitly integer pass conventions.

children.title: Gradient-to-Pass Accounting
children.top_down_role: Comparability boundaries between gradient counts and data-pass counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-to-Pass Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between component-gradient queries, full gradients, and equivalent passes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a finite sum with \(n\) components. If an execution uses \(G\) explicitly formed full gradients and \(S\) additional single-component gradient evaluations, with no overlap credited twice, then its indexed component-gradient count and equivalent-pass count are
\[Q=nG+S,\qquad P_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{Q}{n}=G+\frac{S}{n}.\]
More generally, a mini-batch evaluation of size \(b_t\) contributes \(b_t\) to \(Q\), so \(Q=\sum_t b_t\). The identities are serial-work accounting equalities; parallel evaluation may alter elapsed time but does not change \(Q\) unless a different cost model is declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count each full gradient as n component gradients and each mini-batch by its size; dividing the resulting serial query total by n gives equivalent passes.
assumptions_latex: Component-gradient evaluations are the unit resource.
No evaluation is counted simultaneously as full-gradient and additional component work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q=nG+S=\sum_t b_t\) under the applicable decomposition, and \(P_{\mathrm{eq}}=Q/n\).

notation.meaning: number of explicitly formed full gradients

children.title: Variance-Reduction Matching Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for finite-sum classes with sharp variance-reduced counterparts.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduction Matching Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classes where variance-reduced upper bounds attain oracle lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an instance class \(\mathcal{F}\), an indexed first-order oracle, an output criterion at tolerance \(\varepsilon\), and a permitted algorithm class. The tuple is a variance-reduction matching regime if a variance-reduced method has worst-case oracle cost \(U(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\) and every permitted method has worst-case cost at least \(L(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\), where
\[U(n,\varepsilon,\theta)=\widetilde{\Theta}\bigl(L(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\bigr).\]
Here \(\theta\) collects the declared regularity and initial-error parameters, and \(\widetilde{\Theta}\) permits only the explicitly stated logarithmic factors. Matching is invalid if the upper and lower bounds use different oracle powers, randomization models, component assumptions, or output criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variance-reduced method matches a lower bound only when upper and lower complexities agree, up to declared logarithms, under the same class, oracle, randomness, and criterion.
assumptions_latex: The instance, oracle, algorithm, and output-criterion classes are fixed identically for both bounds.
All suppressed logarithmic factors are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=\widetilde{\Theta}(L)\) under one common complexity model.

notation.meaning: declared problem parameters other than size and tolerance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement supplies a generic definition of matching but identifies no actual finite-sum class, variance-reduced method, or corresponding upper and lower bounds. Sources are required before this navigation container can assert the existence or scope of matching regimes.

children.title: Finite-Sum Open Complexity Gaps
children.top_down_role: Navigation for unresolved distinctions involving component structure, randomization, and oracle power.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Open Complexity Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal boundary between proved matching and unresolved complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a finite-sum class \(\mathcal{F}\), oracle model \(\mathcal{O}\), algorithm class \(\mathcal{A}\), and output criterion. Let \(L(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\) be a proved lower bound and \(U(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\) a proved upper bound under exactly these conventions. A finite-sum complexity gap is present on a parameter domain \(D\) when
\[L(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\le U(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\quad\text{but}\quad U(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\notin\widetilde{\Theta}\bigl(L(n,\varepsilon,\theta)\bigr)\quad\text{on }D.\]
The gap is attributable to component structure, randomization, or oracle power only after holding all other conventions fixed. Absence of a known matching theorem is not itself a mathematical proof that the gap is intrinsic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An open gap exists when comparable proved upper and lower bounds do not match; its cause cannot be assigned while other model conventions also differ.
assumptions_latex: Upper and lower bounds concern the same instance parameters and accuracy convention.
Their oracle and algorithm models are explicitly identified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonmatching comparable bounds define an unresolved interval, not an intrinsic separation theorem.

notation.meaning: parameter domain on which bounds are compared

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic boundary between matching and nonmatching bounds is sensible and failure_boundary fits the container, but the record supplies no current primary sources or concrete finite-sum gap. Claims about what remains open are time-sensitive and require authoritative evidence.

children.title: Gradient-Regular Nonconvex Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for baseline smooth nonconvex stationarity lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Regular Nonconvex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Baseline smooth, possibly nonconvex class for first-order stationarity complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L>0\) and \(\Delta>0\). The gradient-regular nonconvex regime consists of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), together with an initial point \(x_0\) such that \(f(x_0)-\inf_x f(x)\le\Delta\). A first-order oracle returns \((f(x),
abla f(x))\). Under the squared-norm convention, an output \(\widehat x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \(\|
abla f(\widehat x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2\), and complexity counts oracle calls required to guarantee such an output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiable objectives have Lipschitz gradients and bounded initial optimality gap; complexity counts first-order queries needed to return a point with gradient norm at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and bounded below.
\(L>0\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\nabla f(\widehat x)\|\le\varepsilon\) is the stationarity target in the \((L,\Delta)\)-gradient-regular regime.

notation.meaning: upper bound on the initial objective gap

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Lipschitz-gradient smoothness, bounded initial gap, and gradient-norm stationarity are standard first-order nonconvex complexity conventions.

children.title: Higher-Smoothness First-Order Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for first-order algorithms operating on objectives with additional derivative regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Smoothness First-Order Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional derivative regularity without granting higher-order oracle access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an integer \(p\ge2\). The order-\(p\) higher-smoothness first-order regime consists of functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) that are \(p\)-times continuously differentiable and satisfy \(\|
abla^p f(x)-
abla^p f(y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L_p\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The algorithm nevertheless accesses only a first-order oracle returning \((f(x),
abla f(x))\); derivatives of orders \(2,\ldots,p\) are regularity assumptions, not oracle outputs. Complexity is the number of first-order calls needed to return \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(\|
abla f(\widehat x)\|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective has a Lipschitz p-th derivative, but the algorithm may query only values and gradients when seeking an epsilon-stationary point.
assumptions_latex: \(p\ge2\) is an integer and \(f\in C^p(\mathbb{R}^d)\).
\(L_p>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Higher derivative regularity may restrict the instance class while the computational resource remains first-order oracle calls.

notation.meaning: p-th derivative tensor of the objective
induced operator norm on derivative tensors
Lipschitz constant of the p-th derivative

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Higher-smoothness first-order lower-bound classes conventionally impose Lipschitz higher derivatives while withholding higher-order oracle access.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

In particular, it is unclear whether this regime is intended to retain the baseline Lipschitz-gradient and bounded-gap assumptions in addition to Lipschitz continuity of the p-th derivative; that choice materially changes the lower-bound class.

children.title: Deterministic Nonconvex Scope
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound coverage for deterministic nonconvex first-order algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Nonconvex Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic adaptive first-order oracle model for nonconvex stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A deterministic first-order method is a sequence of fixed maps \(\Phi_t\) such that, after querying \(x_0,\ldots,x_{t-1}\), it selects \(x_t=\Phi_t((x_i,f(x_i),\nabla f(x_i))_{i<t})\). Its output after \(T\) calls is another fixed function of the same transcript. A worst-case deterministic lower bound of \(N\) calls means that for every such method producing an \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point on every function in a specified class \(\mathcal F\), there exists \(f\in\mathcal F\) for which the method makes at least \(N\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each query is a deterministic function of the previous first-order transcript, and worst-case complexity maximizes the required calls over the objective class.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is a fixed class of differentiable objectives.
The oracle response at \(x\) is \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_\varepsilon(A,f)\ge N\) expresses the deterministic lower bound.

notation.meaning: class of deterministic adaptive first-order methods
queries used by method A to meet the stationarity criterion on f
deterministic query-selection map at iteration t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Transcript-adaptive deterministic oracle algorithms and infimum-supremum query complexity are standard information-based complexity definitions.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transcript-based deterministic model is plausible, but the exact algorithm class, output convention, and lower-bound quantifiers require an authoritative nonconvex oracle-complexity source. The prose also alternates between at least N and the displayed greater-than-N event elsewhere in the shard.

children.title: Randomized Nonconvex Scope
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound coverage for randomized nonconvex first-order algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Nonconvex Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random-seed first-order oracle model with an explicit probabilistic success criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A randomized first-order method draws an internal seed \(U\), independent of the objective and oracle, and conditionally follows deterministic transcript maps \(x_t=\Phi_t(U,(x_i,f(x_i),\nabla f(x_i))_{i<t})\). For a declared failure level \(\delta\in(0,1)\), its worst-case query complexity is the least \(N\) such that every \(f\in\mathcal F\) yields an output \(\widehat x\) after at most \(N\) calls with \(\mathbb P_U(\|\nabla f(\widehat x)\|\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\). Expected-query or expected-stationarity criteria define different models and must be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queries may depend on an independent random seed; complexity must specify whether success is high-probability, expected-stationarity, or expected-query based.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is independent of the fixed instance \(f\in\mathcal F\).
\(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\mathbb P_U(\|\nabla f(\widehat x)\|>\varepsilon)\le\delta\) is the declared high-probability success requirement.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Conditioning on an independent seed represents randomized adaptive oracle algorithms as distributions over deterministic algorithms.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The high-probability model is internally coherent, but randomized lower bounds depend materially on the success, stopping-time, and worst-case conventions. An authoritative locator is needed to establish that this is the intended randomized nonconvex scope.

children.title: Deterministic-to-Randomized Transfer Boundary
children.top_down_role: Conditions limiting extensions from deterministic hard instances to randomized classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic-to-Randomized Transfer Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary between deterministic hard instances and randomized lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The assertion \(\forall A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}\ \exists f_A\in\mathcal F:T_\varepsilon(A,f_A)>N\) does not alone imply \(\forall R\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{rand}}\ \exists f\in\mathcal F:\mathbb P_U(T_\varepsilon(R_U,f)>N)\ge c\), because the deterministic hard instance may depend on the realized seed. A distributional lower bound supplies a transfer route: find one distribution \(\mathcal D\) over \(\mathcal F\) such that every deterministic \(A\) satisfies \(\mathbb P_{f\sim\mathcal D}(T_\varepsilon(A,f)>N)\ge c\). Under the applicable minimax hypotheses, this yields the corresponding randomized worst-case lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Seed-dependent deterministic hard instances do not establish randomized hardness; transfer requires a common hard distribution and appropriate minimax conditions.
assumptions_latex: The distributional problem satisfies the minimax or finite-support conditions required for transfer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A pointwise deterministic lower bound is insufficient; a uniform hard distribution can imply \(\inf_R\sup_f\mathbb P_U(T_\varepsilon(R_U,f)>N)\ge c\).

notation.meaning: deterministic algorithm obtained by fixing the randomized method's seed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The warning about seed-dependent hard instances is sound, but the claimed distributional-to-randomized transfer is conditional on unspecified minimax or finite-support hypotheses. Those hypotheses and the precise transfer conclusion require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Controlled Negative-Curvature Regimes

children.title: Near-Convex Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity behavior under small departures from convex geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex objectives with uniformly limited negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mu\ge 0\). A twice continuously differentiable function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d	o\mathbb{R}\) is \(\mu\)-near-convex when \(
abla^2 f(x)\succeq-\mu I\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Equivalently, the function \(x\mapsto f(x)+(\mu/2)\|x\|^2\) is convex. If \(
abla f\) is additionally \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \(-\min\{\mu,L\}I\preceq
abla^2 f(x)\preceq LI\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The endpoint \(\mu=0\) is convex, whereas \(\mu>0\) permits negative curvature of magnitude at most \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable objective is mu-near-convex when its Hessian eigenvalues are at least minus mu, equivalently when adding a quadratic of curvature mu makes it convex. If its gradient is also L-Lipschitz, its Hessian eigenvalues lie between minus the smaller of mu and L and plus L.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d)\).
When gradient regularity is invoked, \(L>0\) and \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq-\mu I\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\) if and only if \(f+(\mu/2)\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex.

notation.meaning: uniform upper bound on negative-curvature magnitude
gradient Lipschitz constant when that additional regularity is imposed
A minus B is positive semidefinite

children.title: Weakly Convex Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity behavior under controlled lower curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Convex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratically convexifiable functions, including nonsmooth objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be convex and let \(\rho\ge0\). A proper lower-semicontinuous function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex when \(x\mapsto f(x)+(\rho/2)\|x\|^2\) is convex on \(C\). Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in C\) and every limiting subgradient \(v\in\partial f(x)\), it satisfies \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle v,y-x\rangle-(\rho/2)\|y-x\|^2\), whenever the stated subdifferential calculus applies. The case \(\rho=0\) reduces to convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is rho-weakly convex when adding a quadratic of curvature rho makes it convex; rho zero recovers ordinary convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is \(\rho\)-weakly convex exactly when \(f+(\rho/2)\|\cdot\|^2\) is convex on \(C\).

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization
source_refs.locator: 2.3 Convex Functions p. 21

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Quadratic convexification is the standard definition of weak convexity.

children.title: Negative-Curvature Transition
children.top_down_role: Changes in lower-bound behavior as permitted negative curvature increases.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp transition from convexity to classes admitting negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge1\) and \(\rho\ge0\), let \(\mathcal C_\rho\) be the class of twice continuously differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq-\rho I\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The class \(\mathcal C_0\) consists of convex functions, while for every \(\rho>0\), the class \(\mathcal C_\rho\) contains nonconvex functions. In particular, \(f_\rho(x)=-(\rho/2)x_1^2\) belongs to \(\mathcal C_\rho\) and is nonconvex. Thus membership in \(\mathcal C_\rho\) implies convexity exactly at the boundary value \(\rho=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero negative-curvature allowance enforces convexity, whereas every positive allowance admits nonconvex functions, including a concave quadratic in one coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ge1\) and \(\rho\ge0\).
\(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(\mathcal C_\rho\) implies convexity when \(\rho=0\), but not for any \(\rho>0\).

notation.meaning: class whose Hessians are bounded below by minus rho times the identity

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The Hessian criterion characterizes convexity at rho zero, and the displayed quadratic is a direct standard counterexample for every positive rho.

children.title: Stochastic Nonconvex Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Organizes stationarity barriers under noisy first-order information.

children.title: Bounded-Variance Nonconvex Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for classical stochastic stationarity lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Variance Nonconvex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical unbiased stochastic-gradient model with uniformly bounded noise variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\mathbb E_\xi[f(x;\xi)]\) be differentiable. A bounded-variance stochastic first-order oracle returns \(g(x;\xi)\) satisfying \(\mathbb E_\xi[g(x;\xi)]=
abla F(x)\) and \(\mathbb E_\xi\|g(x;\xi)-
abla F(x)\|^2\le\sigma^2\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). With \(F\) additionally having an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, stochastic stationarity complexity counts oracle samples required to output \(\widehat x\) such that \(\mathbb E\|
abla F(\widehat x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2\). Bounded variance alone does not impose samplewise smoothness on \(g(\cdot;\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stochastic gradient is unbiased with uniformly bounded variance; expected squared gradient norm defines the stated stationarity target.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
Oracle samples are distributed according to the declared stochastic access model.
\(\sigma\ge0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(\widehat x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2\) is measured using the number of stochastic-gradient samples.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Unbiasedness plus a uniform second-moment noise bound is the classical bounded-variance stochastic-gradient model.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-variance condition is standard and internally consistent, but the combined unbiasedness, uniform variance, smooth population objective, and expected-squared-stationarity criterion define a particular stochastic complexity model. A nonconvex stochastic-complexity source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Mean-Squared Smoothness Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for stronger stochastic regularity used by variance-reduced estimators.

knowledge_statements.title: Mean-Squared Smoothness Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled-sample stochastic-gradient regularity stronger than smoothness of the mean objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A stochastic gradient oracle \(g(x;\xi)\) is mean-squared smooth with constant \(L_{\mathrm{ms}}\) when \(\mathbb E_\xi\|g(x;\xi)-g(y;\xi)\|^2\le L_{\mathrm{ms}}^2\|x-y\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d\), where the same sample \(\xi\) is used in both oracle values. If \(\mathbb E[g(x;\xi)]=
abla F(x)\), Jensen's inequality gives \(\|
abla F(x)-
abla F(y)\|\le L_{\mathrm{ms}}\|x-y\|\). The coupled condition additionally controls stochastic gradient differences used by variance-reduced estimators and is not implied by bounded variance alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Using the same sample at two points, the expected squared gradient difference is Lipschitz-controlled; this implies smoothness of the population gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x;\xi)\) has finite second moments for every \(x\).
\(\mathbb E[g(x;\xi)]=\nabla F(x)\).
\(L_{\mathrm{ms}}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E\|g(x;\xi)-g(y;\xi)\|^2\le L_{\mathrm{ms}}^2\|x-y\|^2\) implies that \(\nabla F\) is \(L_{\mathrm{ms}}\)-Lipschitz.

notation.meaning: shared random sample in the coupled difference

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: The coupled same-sample second-moment inequality is the standard mean-squared smoothness condition.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The same-sample mean-squared smoothness inequality and its implication for the mean gradient are mathematically consistent. However, its role as the stronger oracle regularity used in the intended lower-bound taxonomy, including access to coupled evaluations, requires an authoritative variance-reduction or lower-bound locator.

children.title: Sampling-Reuse Access Boundary
children.top_down_role: Navigation for distinctions between fresh-sample and reusable-component access.

children.title: Online Nonconvex Access
children.top_down_role: Fresh-sample nonconvex information models.

knowledge_statements.title: Online Nonconvex Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fresh-sample population-oracle model without indexed component reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In online nonconvex access, the objective is \(F(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[f(x;\xi)]\). At query \(t\), the algorithm chooses \(x_t\) from its previous transcript, and the oracle independently draws \(\xi_t\sim P\) and returns \(g(x_t;\xi_t)\), optionally together with \(f(x_t;\xi_t)\). The algorithm cannot request a named sample, revisit a previous sample, or evaluate one realized component at a second point. Complexity counts fresh draws, and stationarity is assessed using \(\nabla F\), not an individual sampled gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each oracle call draws a fresh independent sample; the algorithm cannot select or revisit components, and stationarity concerns the population objective.
assumptions_latex: \((\xi_t)_{t\ge0}\) are independent draws from a fixed distribution \(P\).
Each \(x_t\) is measurable with respect to the transcript before \(\xi_t\) is drawn.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The online resource count is the number of fresh stochastic-oracle draws used to meet a stationarity criterion for \(F\).

notation.meaning: fresh sample drawn at query t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fresh independent samples with no component-index control define the standard online stochastic-oracle boundary.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fresh-sample model is coherent, but online stochastic oracle conventions differ on whether sample identities are visible, whether repeated evaluation under the same randomness is available, and whether values accompany gradients. A specific lower-bound source is needed to support this exact access boundary.

children.title: Finite-Sum Nonconvex Access
children.top_down_role: Reusable-component nonconvex information models.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Nonconvex Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indexed component-oracle model permitting repeated access and information reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In finite-sum nonconvex access, \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\) for fixed differentiable components \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\). An incremental first-order oracle accepts an adaptively selected pair \((i,x)\) and returns \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\). The algorithm may query the same index at multiple points, revisit earlier pairs, store component information, and correlate later choices with the full transcript. Complexity counts component-oracle calls required to output \(\widehat x\) satisfying the declared stationarity criterion for \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed finite collection of components is accessed by chosen indices; components may be revisited and stored information reused across queries.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge1\) is fixed and each \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
The algorithm may adaptively choose \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-sum complexity is measured in indexed component evaluations, with repeated access to any \(f_i\) permitted.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Adaptive indexed component queries with permitted reuse define the standard incremental first-order finite-sum oracle.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The indexed incremental first-order oracle is a plausible finite-sum model, but lower-bound results may use different index-selection, value-return, and reuse conventions. An authoritative finite-sum nonconvex lower-bound locator is needed for this exact terminal scope.

children.title: Fresh-Sample-to-Reuse Boundary
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions caused by replacing fresh samples with reusable components.

knowledge_statements.title: Fresh-Sample-to-Reuse Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes online stochastic access from persistent finite-sum access by whether a previously revealed component may be queried again.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an oracle query at time \(t\) return \(G(x_t;\xi_t)\), where \(\mathbb{E}[G(x;\xi)]=\nabla f(x)\). In the fresh-sample model, \(\xi_t\) is drawn independently of the query history and the algorithm cannot request the same realization again. The reuse model instead exposes persistent labels \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and permits repeated queries of \(G_i(x)\). Thus a lower bound proved by constructing independent oracle noise at every call does not automatically apply under reuse: repeated evaluations at a fixed label can reveal correlations or cancel persistent noise. Transferring such a bound requires a construction valid for adaptive repeated-label queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fresh sampling hides each realization after one call; reuse permits adaptive repeated component queries. Noise-based online lower bounds therefore need an additional persistent-oracle argument before applying to finite sums.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G(x;\xi)]=\nabla f(x)\) for every admissible query point \(x\).
The algorithm chooses queries adaptively from its previously observed oracle transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{fresh-sample lower bound}\not\Rightarrow\text{reuse-model lower bound}\) without a reuse-stable hard instance.

notation.meaning: persistent component-oracle response with reusable label i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematical distinction are plausible, but the transfer claim depends on precise fresh-sample and persistent-label oracle models. No citation supports those models or the asserted limitation on transferring lower bounds.

children.title: Affinely Constrained Convex Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Organizes feasibility and objective-complexity barriers induced by linear constraints.

children.title: Smooth Affinely Constrained Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for smooth convex objectives with first-order constraint information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-Representation Scaling Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation boundary for affine-operator conditioning in lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every invertible \(S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m\), \[\{x:Ax=b\}=\{x:SAx=Sb\}.\] Nevertheless, \(\|SA\|\) and its nonzero singular values can change under the row transformation. A representation-independent complexity claim therefore cannot depend on these quantities without fixing the exposed representation, norms, and normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible row transformations preserve the feasible set while changing ordinary matrix-conditioning parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear.
\(S\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is invariant under \((A,b)\mapsto(SA,Sb)\), but ordinary conditioning parameters need not be.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Representation Scaling Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Free Nullspace-Parametrization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Access-model boundary for affine-constrained lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x_0\) with \(Ax_0=b\) and \(N\) with \(\operatorname{range}N=\ker A\) are freely supplied, then \[\min_{Ax=b}f(x)=\min_u f(x_0+Nu).\] If \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the ambient Euclidean norm, the reduced objective has gradient-Lipschitz constant at most \(L\|N\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free affine parametrization reduces the constrained instance to an unconstrained smooth problem, so access to such a parametrization must be specified or charged.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{range}N=\ker A\).
\(f\) is \(L\)-smooth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{f\circ(x_0+N\cdot)}\le L\|N\|^2.
knowledge_statements.title: Free Nullspace-Parametrization Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Accuracy Alone Does Not Certify Affine Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of a bicriteria output condition in affine-constrained complexity statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \min_x f(x) subject to Ax=b, objective accuracy alone need not bound feasibility. If f\equiv0, A=1, and b=0, every \hat x has f(\hat x)-f^\star=0 while |A\hat x-b|=|\hat x| is arbitrarily large. Any theorem permitting infeasible outputs must separately specify feasibility tolerance or a combined residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfect objective value can coexist with arbitrarily large affine infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Infeasible candidate outputs are permitted.
Objective accuracy has no explicit feasibility penalty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\hat x)-f^\star=0\centernot\Longrightarrow\|A\hat x-b\|\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Accuracy Alone Does Not Certify Affine Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bicriteria Success for Possibly Infeasible Outputs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-accuracy convention required when an affine-constrained lower-bound model permits infeasible candidates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix norms on the decision and constraint spaces and tolerances \(\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_{m feas}\ge0\). For \(f^\star=\min\{f(x):Ax=b\}\), a possibly infeasible output \(\hat x\) is bicriteria-accurate when \[f(\hat x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon_f,\qquad \|A\hat x-b\|\le\varepsilon_{\rm feas}.\] Any oracle-complexity claim using this criterion must declare both tolerances and the norm used for the feasibility residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A possibly infeasible output must meet separately declared objective and affine-feasibility tolerances.
assumptions_latex: The affine-constrained optimum is finite and attained.
The norm on the constraint space is fixed.
Possibly infeasible outputs are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(\hat x)-f^\star\le\varepsilon_f\ \text{and}\ \|A\hat x-b\|\le\varepsilon_{\rm feas}.
knowledge_statements.title: Bicriteria Success for Possibly Infeasible Outputs
Smooth Affinely Constrained Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the smooth convex problem class used when classifying affine-constrained first-order lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem belongs to this regime when it has the form \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and differentiable; and its gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(X\): \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in X\). The feasible set \(X\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\) must be nonempty. Complexity is measured using first-order objective information together with the specified access to \(A\), \(A^{\mathsf T}\), and feasibility operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime consists of convex differentiable objectives with Lipschitz gradients, minimized over a nonempty convex set intersected with affine equality constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(X\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth on \(X\), with feasibility determined by \(Ax=b\).

children.title: Strongly Convex Affinely Constrained Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for curvature-sensitive constrained complexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Uniqueness Does Not Imply Multiplier Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally relevant distinction between objective curvature and affine-constraint identifiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even when strong convexity makes the attained feasible minimizer \(x^\star\) unique, an equality multiplier need not be unique. If \(\nabla f(x^\star)+A^{\mathsf T}\lambda^\star=0\), then every \(\lambda^\star+q\) with \(q\in\ker A^{\mathsf T}\) is another multiplier. For example, minimizing \(x^2/2\) subject to \((x,x)=(0,0)\) has unique primal solution \(0\) and multiplier set \(\{(t,-t):t\in\mathbb R\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity can ensure a unique primal optimizer while redundant affine rows leave multipliers nonunique.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and strongly convex.
The equality-constrained optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal uniqueness does not imply \(\ker A^{\mathsf T}=\{0\}\) or multiplier uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Uniqueness Does Not Imply Multiplier Uniqueness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible Objective Gap Certifies Primal Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-convexity conversion for feasible candidates in the affine-constrained subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be \mu-strongly convex and let x^\star minimize f over the nonempty convex affine-feasible set C=\{x:Ax=b\}. Then x^\star is unique and every x\in C satisfies f(x)-f(x^\star)\ge\frac{\mu}{2}\|x-x^\star\|^2. Hence f(x)-f(x^\star)\le\varepsilon implies \|x-x^\star\|\le\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For feasible outputs, strong convexity converts objective accuracy into distance from the unique constrained optimizer.
assumptions_latex: f is \mu-strongly convex on a convex set containing C.
C is nonempty and the minimum is attained.
x\in C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)-f(x^\star)\le\varepsilon\Longrightarrow\|x-x^\star\|\le\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\mu}.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Objective Gap Certifies Primal Distance
Strongly Convex Affinely Constrained Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the curvature-sensitive subclass of smooth affine-constrained convex problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A problem belongs to this regime when it has the form \(\min_{x\in X}\,f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\), the feasible set is nonempty, and \(f\) is differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex on the closed convex set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\). Explicitly, for all \(x,y\in X\), \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) and \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle+ rac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2\), with \(0<\mu\le L\). Curvature-sensitive bounds may be parameterized by \(\kappa=L/\mu\), alongside conditioning introduced by the affine operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This is the affine-constrained smooth regime with a positive strong-convexity modulus; objective conditioning is summarized by the ratio L divided by μ.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is closed and convex, and \(X\cap\{x:Ax=b\}\ne\varnothing\).
\(0<\mu\le L<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective condition number is \(\kappa=L/\mu\), while affine constraints may contribute separate operator conditioning.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and strong-convexity formulas fit the terminal regime, but no source supports the affine-constrained complexity class or the convention separating objective conditioning from affine-operator conditioning.

children.title: Bilinear Convex–Concave Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Organizes lower bounds for bilinearly coupled saddle problems.

children.title: General Convex–Concave Bilinear Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for primal–dual gap and residual complexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unrestricted Saddle Gap May Be Infinite
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain boundary for gap-based complexity in the general bilinear regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi(x,y)=xy\) on \(X=Y=\mathbb R\), \[G(\hat x,\hat y)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R}\Phi(\hat x,y)-\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}\Phi(x,\hat y)\] is infinite whenever \((\hat x,\hat y)\ne(0,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrestricted bilinear saddle gap on unbounded domains can be infinite at every nonsolution candidate.
assumptions_latex: \(X=Y=\mathbb R\).
\(\Phi(x,y)=xy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(\hat x,\hat y)=+\infty\quad\text{for }(\hat x,\hat y)\ne(0,0).
knowledge_statements.title: Unrestricted Saddle Gap May Be Infinite

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scale-Invariant Bilinear Coupling Parameter
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic invariant parameter for bounded bilinear domains in fixed compatible norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_X=\sup_{x\in X}\|x\|\), \(R_Y=\sup_{y\in Y}\|y\|\), and let \(\|K\|\) be the induced norm. Under \(x=\alpha\tilde x\), \(y=\beta\tilde y\) with \(\alpha,\beta>0\), the transformed quantities satisfy \(\tilde K=\alpha\beta K\), \(R_{\tilde X}=R_X/\alpha\), and \(R_{\tilde Y}=R_Y/\beta\). Hence \[\|\tilde K\|R_{\tilde X}R_{\tilde Y}=\|K\|R_XR_Y.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupling norm times the two domain radii is invariant under scalar coordinate rescaling.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are bounded in the declared norms.
\(\alpha,\beta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|K\|R_XR_Y\) is invariant under the stated rescaling.

notation.meaning: domain radii in the declared norms

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Invariant Bilinear Coupling Parameter

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Restricted Primal–Dual Gap Criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite comparison-set accuracy criterion for the uncurved bilinear lower-bound regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_0\subseteq X\) and \(Y_0\subseteq Y\) be declared comparison sets and let \((\hat x,\hat y)\in X_0\times Y_0\). Whenever both extrema are finite, define \[G_{X_0,Y_0}(\hat x,\hat y)=\sup_{y\in Y_0}\Phi(\hat x,y)-\inf_{x\in X_0}\Phi(x,\hat y).\] Then \(G_{X_0,Y_0}\ge0\); it vanishes exactly when \((\hat x,\hat y)\) is a saddle pair relative to \(X_0\times Y_0\). An \(\varepsilon\)-accurate restricted-gap output satisfies \(G_{X_0,Y_0}(\hat x,\hat y)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Declared comparison sets yield a finite primal–dual gap criterion when both comparison extrema are finite.
assumptions_latex: \(X_0\subseteq X\) and \(Y_0\subseteq Y\) are nonempty and declared as part of the accuracy model.
\((\hat x,\hat y)\in X_0\times Y_0\).
The displayed supremum and infimum are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\le G_{X_0,Y_0}(\hat x,\hat y)\le\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: declared primal and dual comparison sets

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted Primal–Dual Gap Criterion
General Convex–Concave Bilinear Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the uncurved bilinear saddle class for primal–dual gap and residual lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A saddle problem belongs to this regime when \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb{R}^q\) are nonempty convex sets and \(\Phi(x,y)=g(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h(y)\), where \(g\) and \(h\) are proper closed convex functions and \(K\) is linear. The task is \(\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\Phi(x,y)\). No positive strong-convexity modulus is assumed for either \(g\) or \(h\). For bounded \(X\) and \(Y\), an output \((\hat x,\hat y)\) may be assessed by the primal–dual gap \(\sup_{y\in Y}\Phi(\hat x,y)-\inf_{x\in X}\Phi(x,\hat y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This regime covers bilinearly coupled convex–concave saddle problems with no strong curvature on either side, assessed by a primal–dual gap or specified residual.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty convex sets.
\(g\) and \(h\) are proper closed convex functions, and \(K\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(\cdot,y)\) is convex and \(\Phi(x,\cdot)\) is concave, with zero required strong-curvature moduli.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind and bilinear convex–concave formulation fit the regime, but no source supports the exact problem class or its primal–dual gap convention. A source must also clarify bounded domains or restricted test sets for a finite gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone Saddle-Operator Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic operator representation proposed for the bilinear lower-bound taxonomy leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \Phi(x,y)=g(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h(y), define T(x,y)=[\partial g(x)+K^{\mathsf T}y+N_X(x);\partial h(y)-Kx+N_Y(y)]. Under valid subdifferential sum rules, T is monotone and 0\in T(x^\star,y^\star) exactly at saddle points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear convex-concave saddle problem is a zero of a monotone operator with skew coupling.
assumptions_latex: g and h are proper closed convex functions.
X and Y are nonempty closed convex sets.
The displayed subdifferential sum rules are valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in T(x^\star,y^\star)\iff(x^\star,y^\star)\text{ is a saddle point}.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Saddle-Operator Representation

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns the uncurved bilinear lower-bound class, its scale-invariant coupling size, and the finite-gap boundary. The proposed monotone-operator statement was deferred as generic saddle representation already owned elsewhere. A fixed oracle-class definition and the landmark quantitative lower bound remain missing; strong-curvature regimes were excluded as sibling content.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bilinear Saddle-Point Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the bilinear convex–concave model form; closedness is assumed, but attainment, compactness, and equality of primal and dual values are not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q_p\) and \(Q_d\) be closed convex sets, let \(A\) be a linear operator, and let \(b,c\) have compatible dimensions. The associated bilinear saddle-point problem is
\[
\min_{x\in Q_p}\max_{w\in Q_d}\bigl\{\langle Ax,w\rangle+\langle c,x\rangle+\langle b,w\rangle\bigr\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bilinear saddle-point problem minimizes over a closed convex primal set and maximizes over a closed convex dual set an objective consisting of a bilinear coupling plus linear primal and dual terms.
assumptions_latex: Q_p\text{ and }Q_d\text{ are closed and convex}
A\text{ is linear}
b\text{ and }c\text{ have dimensions compatible with }A,Q_p,Q_d
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in Q_p}\max_{w\in Q_d}\left\{\langle Ax,w\rangle+\langle c,x\rangle+\langle b,w\rangle\right\}\text{ is the associated bilinear saddle-point problem.}

children.title: One-Sided Strong-Curvature Regime
children.top_down_role: Navigation for asymmetric strongly convex or strongly concave structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Curvature Does Not Ensure a Unique Saddle Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp uniqueness boundary for asymmetric curvature assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R\), \(Y=[-1,1]\), and \(\Phi(x,y)=x^2/2\), so \(g(x)=x^2/2\), \(K=0\), and \(h(y)=0\). Then \[\operatorname{Sad}(\Phi)=\{0\}\times[-1,1].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly convex primal block can coexist with an entire interval of dual saddle coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(Y=[-1,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One assumed curved side does not guarantee uniqueness of the saddle pair.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Curvature Does Not Ensure a Unique Saddle Pair

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness on an Assumed Curved Best-Response Side
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence under the inclusive one-sided-curvature convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g\) is \(\mu_x\)-strongly convex with \(\mu_x>0\), then for every fixed \(y\), \(x\mapsto g(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle\) has at most one minimizer. Dually, if \(h\) is \(\mu_y\)-strongly convex, then for every fixed \(x\), \(y\mapsto\langle Kx,y\rangle-h(y)\) has at most one maximizer. No conclusion about the other coordinate follows without additional curvature or coupling assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature makes the corresponding conditional best response unique but does not by itself ensure uniqueness of the other coordinate or saddle pair.
assumptions_latex: At least one of \(g\) and \(h\) has a positive strong-convexity modulus.
The relevant conditional optimum is attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Sided Curvature as an Assumption Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies the inclusive convention used for asymmetric bilinear lower-bound assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi(x,y)=g(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h(y)\), a one-sided strong-curvature assumption requires a positive strong-convexity modulus for one designated block while requiring only convexity for the other. Thus either \(\mu_x>0\) is assumed and no positive lower bound on \(\mu_y\) is required, or conversely. The unrequired side may possess additional curvature; writing its required modulus as zero denotes absence of an assumption, not failure of strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-sided curvature means that positive curvature is required on one designated block but not on the other; it does not assert that the other block has zero actual curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are proper convex functions on convex domains.
\(K\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_x>0,\ \mu_y\ge0\text{ unprescribed})\quad\text{or}\quad(\mu_y>0,\ \mu_x\ge0\text{ unprescribed}).

notation.meaning: available strong-convexity moduli for the primal and dual-side convex terms

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Curvature as an Assumption Regime
One-Sided Strong-Curvature Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines bilinear saddle problems with strong curvature on exactly one primal–dual side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\Phi(x,y)=g(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h(y)\) on convex sets \(X\times Y\). The problem lies in the one-sided strong-curvature regime when exactly one of the following holds: \(g\) is \(\mu_x\)-strongly convex on \(X\) with \(\mu_x>0\), while no positive strong-convexity modulus is imposed on \(h\); or \(h\) is \(\mu_y\)-strongly convex on \(Y\) with \(\mu_y>0\), while none is imposed on \(g\). Because \(-h\) is then strongly concave in \(y\), the two alternatives are primal–dual mirrors. Complexity claims must identify which side is curved and how \(K\) couples the uncurved side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly one side of the bilinear saddle problem is strongly curved. Bounds must state whether curvature is primal or dual and retain the asymmetry.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are proper closed convex functions on convex domains.
\(K\) is a linear coupling operator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \((\mu_x>0,\mu_y=0)\) or \((\mu_x=0,\mu_y>0)\), but not \((\mu_x>0,\mu_y>0)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the one-sided-curvature leaf, but no source supports the classification. Moreover, writing the uncurved-side modulus as zero must be identified as a class convention meaning that positive curvature is not required, rather than as a claim that the function cannot be strongly convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coupling and Curvature Enter Operator Conditioning Separately
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning structure of a differentiable two-sided bilinear saddle operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable \(g,h\), define \[T(x,y)=(
abla g(x)+K^{\mathsf T}y,
abla h(y)-Kx).\] In the Euclidean product norm, if \(
abla g\) and \(
abla h\) are respectively \(L_g\)- and \(L_h\)-Lipschitz, then \[\operatorname{Lip}(T)\le \max\{L_g,L_h\}+\|K\|.\] If \(g,h\) are respectively \(\mu_x\)- and \(\mu_y\)-strongly convex, the guaranteed strong-monotonicity modulus is at least \(\min\{\mu_x,\mu_y\}\). Thus coupling regularity and block curvature are distinct condition parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coupling norm affects operator Lipschitzness, whereas the guaranteed strong-monotonicity modulus comes from the two block curvatures.
assumptions_latex: The product space uses Euclidean norms.
\(g,h\) are differentiable with Lipschitz gradients.
\(g,h\) have positive strong-convexity moduli.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_T\le\max\{L_g,L_h\}+\|K\|\) and \(\mu_T\ge\min\{\mu_x,\mu_y\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Sided Strong-Curvature Bilinear Class

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\Phi(x,y)=g(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-h(y)\), two-sided strong curvature means that \(g\) is \(\mu_x\)-strongly convex and \(h\) is \(\mu_y\)-strongly convex for constants \(\mu_x,\mu_y>0\). Equivalently, \(\Phi(\cdot,y)\) is \(\mu_x\)-strongly convex for every \(y\), and \(\Phi(x,\cdot)\) is \(\mu_y\)-strongly concave for every \(x\). If a saddle point exists, it is unique.

children.title: Monotone Lipschitz Regime
