knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Lipschitz Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the monotone Lipschitz operator class underlying baseline variational-inequality lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. An operator \(F:Z\to\mathbb{R}^d\) lies in the monotone Lipschitz regime when, for all \(z,w\in Z\), \(\langle F(z)-F(w),z-w\rangle\ge0\) and \(\|F(z)-F(w)\|_*\le L\|z-w\|\). The associated variational inequality is to find \(z^\star\in Z\) satisfying \(\langle F(z^\star),z-z^\star\rangle\ge0\) for every \(z\in Z\). No positive strong-monotonicity modulus is assumed. Gap or residual complexity must additionally state the norm, output criterion, and any boundedness required to make that criterion finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The operator is monotone and Lipschitz on a closed convex domain but need not be strongly monotone; complexity depends on the chosen gap or residual criterion.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(F:Z\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is monotone and \(L\)-Lipschitz, with no required modulus \(\mu>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Comparison Sets Can Give Infinite Dual Gap

On \(Z=\mathbb R\), the constant operator \(F(w)=1\) is monotone and Lipschitz, but \[G_Z(z)=\sup_{w\in\mathbb R}(z-w)=+\infty.\]

children.title: Strongly Monotone Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Monotone Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the condition-sensitive Lipschitz variational-inequality class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. An operator \(F:Z\to\mathbb{R}^d\) lies in the strongly monotone Lipschitz regime if constants \(\mu>0\) and \(L\ge\mu\) satisfy, for all \(z,w\in Z\), \(\langle F(z)-F(w),z-w\rangle\ge\mu\|z-w\|^2\) and \(\|F(z)-F(w)\|_*\le L\|z-w\|\). If a variational-inequality solution exists, strong monotonicity makes it unique. Condition-sensitive oracle bounds may be expressed through \(\kappa=L/\mu\), subject to the selected norm, oracle model, and accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The operator is both Lipschitz and strongly monotone. Its variational-inequality solution is unique when it exists, and complexity may scale with L divided by μ.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
A solution to the associated variational inequality exists.
\(0<\mu\le L<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution is unique and the operator condition number is \(\kappa=L/\mu\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-Call Adaptive Operator Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the one-new-operator-value-per-iteration information regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method is in the single-call information regime when, at iteration \(t\), it adaptively selects at most one new query \(q_t\), obtains at most one previously unavailable value \(F(q_t)\), and forms its next state from the prior transcript, that response, and permitted internal randomness. Hence \(N_F(t+1)-N_F(t)\le1\). Reusing a stored value is permitted; two new sequential or parallel evaluations, a multi-point batch response, or an uncharged auxiliary evaluation is outside this regime unless the oracle explicitly declares that response to be one atomic call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration may reveal at most one new operator value; cached values are reusable, but multi-point or auxiliary evaluations are not free.
assumptions_latex: The operator oracle and its atomic response are declared in advance.
Queries may depend on the preceding transcript and internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_F(t+1)-N_F(t)\le1\quad\text{for every }t.

notation.meaning: new operator query selected at iteration t
number of new operator responses obtained before iteration t

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Call Adaptive Operator Interface
Single-Call Information Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an iteration model permitting at most one new operator evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an operator oracle returning \(F(z)\), a method is in the single-call information regime if iteration \(t\) selects at most one new query point \(q_t\), receives at most one previously unavailable value \(F(q_t)\), and computes its next state and output from the accumulated transcript \(\mathcal{H}_t=\{(q_s,F(q_s)):0\le s\le t\}\) together with permitted deterministic or randomized internal operations. Reusing a stored value does not constitute a new oracle call. Batch queries, two sequential evaluations at distinct newly chosen points within one iteration, and uncharged auxiliary operator evaluations fall outside this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration obtains at most one new operator value. Stored values may be reused, but two new evaluations or an uncharged auxiliary call violate the model.
assumptions_latex: The oracle response to query \(q\) is \(F(q)\).
Queries may depend adaptively on the preceding transcript and internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_F(t+1)-N_F(t)\le1\) for every iteration \(t\), where \(N_F(t)\) counts new operator evaluations.

notation.meaning: operator query point at iteration t
cumulative number of new operator evaluations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this information-regime leaf, and the transcript model is precise, but no source establishes this particular meaning of a single-call iteration or its treatment of stored values, batch calls, and randomized adaptive queries.

children.title: Extragradient Information Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Extragradient Information Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the two-stage information pattern used by extragradient-type variational-inequality methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current state \(z_t\in Z\), the extragradient information regime permits a first evaluation \(F(z_t)\), constructs an auxiliary point \(y_t=P_Z(z_t-\gamma_tF(z_t))\), then evaluates \(F(y_t)\) before forming the next state, for example \(z_{t+1}=P_Z(z_t-\gamma_tF(y_t))\). Thus one logical iteration may use two sequential operator evaluations, with the second query depending on the first response. Any lower bound stated per iteration in this regime must be converted to operator-evaluation complexity by charging both new evaluations unless one value is already stored or the oracle model explicitly assigns another cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extragradient iteration evaluates the operator, forms a predictive point, evaluates there, and then updates. Its two adaptive calls must normally both be charged.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is a closed convex set admitting the projection or prox map \(P_Z\).
\(\gamma_t>0\), and the second query may depend on the first oracle response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A standard extragradient iteration incurs up to two new evaluations of \(F\).

notation.meaning: permitted projection or prox mapping onto Z

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conversion from Iterations to Operator Evaluations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalizes iteration guarantees by newly charged operator-oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If iteration \(t\) requests \(c_t\) previously unavailable operator values, then the number of operator evaluations through \(T\) iterations is \[N_F(T)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c_t.\] Consequently, \(c_-T\le N_F(T)\le c_+T\) whenever \(c_-\le c_t\le c_+\). Reuse of a stored value is not a new call. Batch, parallel, or weighted calls require separately declared accounting rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluation complexity is the number of new operator values requested, not the number of iteration labels; uniform per-iteration call bounds convert between the two counts.
assumptions_latex: Each newly requested operator value has unit cost under the declared scalar accounting convention.
The accuracy criterion and stopping iteration are fixed independently of how calls are relabeled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_F(T)=\sum_{t<T}c_t,\qquad c_-T\le N_F(T)\le c_+T.

notation.meaning: new operator evaluations charged during iteration t
cumulative operator-evaluation count through T iterations

knowledge_statements.title: Conversion from Iterations to Operator Evaluations
Operator-Evaluation Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalizes iteration bounds by the actual number of charged operator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let iteration \(t\) make \(c_t\) new calls to the operator oracle, and define \(N_F(T)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c_t\). An accuracy guarantee achieved after \(T(\varepsilon)\) iterations has operator-evaluation complexity \(N_F(T(\varepsilon))\), not merely \(T(\varepsilon)\). If \(c_t\le c\) uniformly, then \(N_F(T(\varepsilon))\le cT(\varepsilon)\); if each completed iteration necessarily uses \(c_t\ge c_0>0\), then \(N_F(T(\varepsilon))\ge c_0T(\varepsilon)\). Stored-value reuse is uncharged, whereas every newly requested \(F(q)\) is charged unless the oracle model explicitly specifies batch or parallel accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle complexity counts new operator calls, not iteration labels. A method using at most c calls per iteration converts an iteration bound into at most c times as many evaluations.
assumptions_latex: The accuracy criterion defining \(T(\varepsilon)\) is fixed.
Each newly requested operator value has unit cost unless another accounting rule is stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_F(T)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}c_t\), with \(c_0T\le N_F(T)\le cT\) whenever \(c_0\le c_t\le c\).

knowledge_statements.title: General Compact-Domain Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the baseline compact-domain class for linear-minimization-oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem lies in the general compact-domain LMO regime when it is \(\min_{x\in D} f(x)\), where \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and access to \(D\) is provided through a linear minimization oracle \(\operatorname{LMO}_D(g)\in\arg\min_{v\in D}\langle g,v\rangle\). The objective is convex and is assigned a stated first-order regularity class, such as \(L\)-smoothness or bounded subgradients. No polytope, atomic sparsity, strong convexity, or enhanced oracle operation is assumed. Complexity must separately count objective first-order calls and LMO calls and must specify the criterion for \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible set is an arbitrary compact convex domain accessed only by linear minimization. Extra atomic geometry, strong curvature, and enhanced oracle operations are not assumed.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and has an explicitly stated first-order regularity class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{LMO}_D(g)\in\arg\min_{v\in D}\langle g,v\rangle\) is the baseline domain oracle, and its calls are counted separately from objective-oracle calls.

notation.meaning: linear objective supplied to the LMO

children.title: Polytope Geometry Regime
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound effects tied to polyhedral feasible domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Polytope Geometry Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex sparsity imposed by ordinary linear-minimization-oracle access to a compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(V\) is finite. Suppose an algorithm starts from a convex combination of at most \(s_0\) vertices and, at each oracle call, obtains one vertex \(v_t\in\arg\min_{v\in V}\langle g_t,v\rangle\). If every iterate is formed from previously available vertices, then after \(t\) calls its iterate belongs to the convex hull of at most \(s_0+t\) vertices. Consequently, any accuracy requirement forcing every admissible output to have vertex-support size at least \(s_\varepsilon\) entails at least \(\max\{0,s_\varepsilon-s_0\}\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordinary LMO supplies at most one new vertex per call, so any required vertex-support size directly yields an oracle-call lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polytope with finite vertex set \(V\).
Iterates use only vertices already available to the algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\varepsilon\geq\max\{0,s_\varepsilon-s_0\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum support required for the target accuracy

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: each ordinary LMO call exposes at most one new vertex, giving the stated support-counting obstruction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-growth argument is mathematically coherent under the stated atom-restricted iterate model and fits the polytope-geometry regime. However, the resulting oracle lower bound has no inspectable authoritative citation; standard-field rationale alone is insufficient to resolve the model-specific lower-bound claim.

children.title: Atomic-Domain Regime
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound effects tied to atomic domain representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Atomic-Domain Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic-support growth under an LMO over a compact atomic convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be compact and let \(D=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\). An atomic LMO queried with \(g_t\) returns \(a_t\in\arg\min_{a\in\mathcal A}\langle g_t,a\rangle\). If the initial point has an atomic representation using at most \(s_0\) atoms and each iterate lies in the convex hull of the initial atoms and returned atoms, then the atomic support of the iterate after \(t\) calls is at most \(s_0+t\). Thus a target set whose points all require at least \(s_\varepsilon\) atoms cannot be reached in fewer than \(s_\varepsilon-s_0\) calls when this quantity is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For atom-restricted methods, one oracle call adds at most one atom; necessary atomic support therefore becomes an LMO lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\operatorname{conv}(\mathcal A)\) for a compact atom set \(\mathcal A\).
The method constructs iterates only from atoms it has obtained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\varepsilon\geq\max\{0,s_\varepsilon-s_0\}\).

notation.meaning: minimum atomic support at the requested accuracy

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: oracle-exposed atomic support grows by at most one per ordinary LMO call

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The atomic-support growth statement is plausible and internally consistent, but it depends on a restricted oracle model in which iterates use only revealed atoms. No source with a specific locator supports that model and its lower-bound consequence.

children.title: Sparsity–Facial Structure Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity–Facial Structure Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of facial geometry into generic vertex-support requirements and LMO-call barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an \(r\)-dimensional face of a polytope \(P=\operatorname{conv}(V)\). Every point of \(F\) is a convex combination of at most \(r+1\) vertices of \(F\). Moreover, outside the finite union of convex hulls of at most \(r\) vertices, a point in \(\operatorname{relint}(F)\) requires at least \(r+1\) vertices. Hence, for such a generic target, a method beginning with \(s_0\) available vertices and acquiring at most one new vertex per LMO call requires at least \(\max\{0,r+1-s_0\}\) calls before representing the target exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generic point of an r-dimensional polytope face needs r+1 vertices, converting facial dimension into an exact-representation LMO barrier.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polytope and \(F\) is an \(r\)-dimensional face.
The method gains at most one previously unavailable vertex per LMO call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{exact}}\geq\max\{0,r+1-s_0\}\) for generic targets in \(\operatorname{relint}(F)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Caratheodory's theorem on an affine face and generic avoidance of lower-dimensional vertex simplices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The facial-dimension and generic-support claims are plausible applications of Carathéodory-type geometry, and the exact-representation qualification is appropriate. A source is still required for the finite-union genericity statement and its conversion into an LMO-call barrier.

children.title: Enhanced LMO Access Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for away, pairwise, local, and corrective oracle enhancements.

knowledge_statements.title: Enhanced LMO Access Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle models that reveal more feasible-set information than one global minimizing atom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a compact convex set \(D\), an enhanced LMO access regime augments the standard response \(s(g)\in\arg\min_{x\in D}\langle g,x\rangle\) with at least one of the following operations: selection of an away atom from a maintained active set, minimization of a pairwise direction over active and feasible atoms, minimization over a prescribed local feasible region, or corrective reoptimization over the convex hull of all revealed atoms. Complexity bounds in such a regime count each enhanced operation explicitly and are not directly comparable with bounds charging only standard LMO calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enhanced LMO models add away, pairwise, local, or corrective operations; their lower bounds must charge the extra information separately.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonempty compact convex set.
The oracle model specifies which enhanced responses and stored atoms are accessible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_{\mathrm{enh}}\supseteq\mathcal O_{\mathrm{LMO}}\), with complexity measured in explicitly declared enhanced-oracle operations.

notation.meaning: standard LMO response to direction g

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: away-step, pairwise, local, and fully corrective methods expose distinct enhancements of standard LMO access

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record matches the navigation role, but it combines away-atom selection, pairwise access, local minimization, and corrective reoptimization into one enhanced interface without a cited formal oracle definition. The inclusion notation and comparability claim remain model-dependent.

children.title: Partial-Information Oracle Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Organizes information limits for partial-gradient and subspace-restricted access while leaving method construction to the owning chapters.

children.title: Coordinate-Oracle Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Navigation for uniform, importance-sampled, and anisotropic coordinate information.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Oracle Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information lower bound for optimization when a query reveals only one gradient coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(d\geq2\), \(L>0\), and \(R>0\). For the family \(f_\sigma(x)=\tfrac{L}{2}\lVert x-R\sigma/\sqrt d\rVert_2^2\), where \(\sigma\) is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}^d\), suppose each query reveals only one chosen coordinate of \(\nabla f_\sigma(x)\). After \(t\leq d\) distinct-coordinate queries, every possibly randomized method satisfies \(\mathbb E[f_\sigma(x_t)-f_\sigma^*]\geq\tfrac{LR^2}{2}(1-t/d)\). Therefore achieving expected error at most \(\varepsilon<LR^2/2\) requires \(t\geq d(1-2\varepsilon/(LR^2))\) coordinate queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable quadratic with hidden coordinate signs forces nearly d coordinate queries whenever the required error is substantially below its initial scale.
assumptions_latex: A query returns one selected partial derivative and no full function value or other coordinates.
The expectation includes the uniform hidden sign vector and algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\varepsilon\geq\left\lceil d\left(1-\frac{2\varepsilon}{LR^2}\right)\right\rceil\).

source_refs.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
source_refs.locator: 5 Randomized coordinate update methods p. 113

source_witnesses.source_title: Large-Scale Convex Optimization: Algorithms & Analyses via Monotone Operators
source_witnesses.locator: 5 Randomized coordinate update methods p. 113

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hidden-sign quadratic calculation is plausible, but the cited coordinate-method chapter does not specifically establish this adaptive coordinate-oracle lower bound, its constant, or its randomized quantifiers. A directly supporting theorem or derivation source is required.

children.title: Block-Subspace Coverage Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Navigation for block coverage, overlap, and neglected-direction limitations.

children.title: Block-Access Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information limits determined by blockwise access patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Access Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-coverage lower bound when each oracle call reveals one coordinate block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(\mathbb R^d\) into disjoint blocks of dimensions at most \(b\). For \(f_\sigma(x)=\tfrac{L}{2}\lVert x-R\sigma/\sqrt d\rVert_2^2\), let each query reveal gradient coordinates in one selected block and no other information. Under a uniform hidden \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^d\), after \(t\) block queries the expected number of unrevealed coordinates is at least \((d-bt)_+\). Consequently, every randomized method satisfies \(\mathbb E[f_\sigma(x_t)-f_\sigma^*]\geq\tfrac{LR^2}{2d}(d-bt)_+\), implying a linear block-coverage lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one query covers at most b new coordinates, hidden separable directions force error proportional to the dimension still uncovered.
assumptions_latex: The blocks are disjoint and each has dimension at most \(b\).
A block query reveals only partial derivatives within its selected block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\varepsilon\geq\left\lceil\frac{d}{b}\left(1-\frac{2\varepsilon}{LR^2}\right)\right\rceil\) when \(0\leq\varepsilon<LR^2/2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the hidden-sign coordinate construction extends by counting newly exposed block coordinates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coverage calculation is coherent for a fixed disjoint partition and a response revealing no information outside the selected block. The exact randomized lower bound and oracle restrictions lack an authoritative source.

children.title: Overlapping-Subspace Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information limits determined by overlap among accessible subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Overlapping-Subspace Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage lower bound governed by the span of queried, possibly overlapping subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each oracle query expose the orthogonal projection of the gradient onto a selected subspace \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). For an execution using \(S_{i_1},\ldots,S_{i_t}\), define \(U_t=S_{i_1}+\cdots+S_{i_t}\) and \(r_t=\dim U_t\). On an isotropic hidden-center quadratic family with minimizer norm \(R\), rotational symmetry leaves the component in \(U_t^\perp\) unidentified. The minimax expected objective gap is therefore at least \(\tfrac{LR^2}{2}(1-r_t/d)\). Overlap can only reduce \(r_t\), so counting queried dimensions with multiplicity cannot improve this bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For overlapping block queries, progress depends on the dimension of their union span, not the sum of individual block sizes.
assumptions_latex: Each response is restricted to the queried subspace projection of the gradient.
The hidden minimizer is isotropically distributed on the Euclidean sphere of radius \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x_t}\sup_f\mathbb E[f(x_t)-f^*]\geq\frac{LR^2}{2}\left(1-\frac{r_t}{d}\right)\).

notation.meaning: sum of all queried subspaces through time t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: orthogonal invariance leaves energy in the unqueried complement statistically unidentified

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The union-span intuition fits the container, but rotational symmetry alone does not settle the stated minimax constant when subspaces may be selected adaptively. The displayed conclusion also mixes an execution-dependent dimension with an infimum-supremum formulation. A precise sourced oracle model and quantifier statement are needed.

children.title: Neglected-Direction Barriers
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds arising from directions omitted by block or subspace coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Neglected-Direction Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indistinguishability caused by a direction outside the span of all queried subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_T\) be the span of all subspaces queried through time \(T\), and suppose \(u\in U_T^\perp\) is a unit vector. Consider \(f_\pm(x)=\tfrac L2\lVert x\mp Ru\rVert_2^2\). Projected-gradient responses on every queried subspace coincide for \(f_+\) and \(f_-\). Hence the transcript cannot identify the sign, and for any common output \(x_T\), at least one instance satisfies \(f_\pm(x_T)-f_\pm^*\geq LR^2/2\). Uniform accuracy below this threshold is impossible until the query span covers every possible hidden direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A completely unqueried direction can hide either of two opposite minimizers, preventing uniform error below half the quadratic energy scale.
assumptions_latex: Oracle responses contain only projections onto queried subspaces.
A unit direction \(u\) remains orthogonal to the entire query span.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: two opposite quadratic centers are indistinguishable under projections orthogonal to their separating direction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two opposite-center quadratics do produce identical projected-gradient transcripts when the neglected direction is orthogonal to every queried subspace, and the failure-boundary kind fits. The adaptive transcript assumptions and exact uniform lower bound nevertheless require an authoritative partial-information-oracle source.

children.title: Polynomial Krylov Information Barriers
children.top_down_role: Navigation for span-restricted quadratic and spectral lower bounds.

children.title: Krylov-Span Barriers
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds induced by iterates confined to Krylov-generated spans.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov-Span Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial restriction imposed by iterates confined to a Krylov subspace for quadratic optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Hx-b^\top x\) with symmetric positive-definite \(H\), let \(r_0=b-Hx_0\). Any method satisfying \(x_t-x_0\in\mathcal K_t(H,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,Hr_0,\ldots,H^{t-1}r_0\}\) has an error of the form \(x_t-x_*=p_t(H)(x_0-x_*)\), where \(p_t\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(t\) with \(p_t(0)=1\). Thus its worst-case progress is bounded by the best degree-\(t\) polynomial approximation to zero on the admissible spectrum of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Krylov-span iterates can only apply low-degree polynomials to the initial error, so hard spectra impose polynomial-approximation barriers.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is symmetric positive definite.
The iterate displacement belongs to the order-t Krylov subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_t-x_*\rVert_H\geq\inf_{\substack{p\in\mathbb R_t[z]\\p(0)=1}}\max_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(H)}|p(\lambda)|\,\lVert x_0-x_*\rVert_H\) for a worst-case spectral initialization.

notation.meaning: square root of z transpose H z

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Krylov vectors are polynomial images of the initial residual and quadratic error is spectral

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Krylov residual-polynomial representation is standard and correctly stated. The final norm lower bound requires precise quantifiers over the method, polynomial, spectrum, and initialization; no source is supplied to validate that worst-case formulation.

children.title: Polynomial-Information Barriers
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds governed by restricted polynomial access to problem information.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Information Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree limitation on information obtainable through repeated matrix-vector products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm start from \(v\neq0\) and obtain information only through linear combinations and at most \(t\) sequential products by a fixed matrix \(H\). Every vector it can construct lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{v,Hv,\ldots,H^tv\}\) and hence equals \(p(H)v\) for some polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(t\). If a target operator is \(\phi(H)\), then the attainable error on an eigencomponent with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is controlled by \(|p(\lambda)-\phi(\lambda)|\); indistinguishable or poorly approximated spectral values yield an information lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After t matrix-vector products, constructed vectors contain only degree-t polynomial information about the matrix, limiting approximation of spectral operators.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm accesses \(H\) only by sequential matrix-vector products.
No independent spectral decomposition or factorization of \(H\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_t=p(H)v\) for some \(p\in\mathbb R_t[z]\), and \(\lVert y_t-\phi(H)v\rVert_2\geq\min_{p\in\mathbb R_t[z]}\lVert(p(H)-\phi(H))v\rVert_2\).

notation.meaning: real polynomials of degree at most t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: closure under linear combinations and matrix-vector multiplication generates a Krylov polynomial space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polynomial-span conclusion is valid for a strict linear-combination and sequential matrix-vector-product model. The record needs a source formalizing that model, especially the exclusion of independently generated query directions and other matrix information.

children.title: Spectral Approximation Interface
children.top_down_role: Connections between span restrictions and spectral approximation difficulty.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Approximation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of Krylov approximation error into a weighted scalar polynomial problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d)Q^\top\) be symmetric, let \(v=Qc\), and let \(y_t=p(H)v\) with \(p\) of degree at most \(t\). For any scalar function \(\phi\) defined on \(\operatorname{spec}(H)\), the approximation error satisfies \[\lVert y_t-\phi(H)v\rVert_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d c_i^2\bigl(p(\lambda_i)-\phi(\lambda_i)\bigr)^2.\] Therefore the best Krylov approximation is exactly a weighted discrete polynomial-approximation problem on the spectrum; uniform spectral approximation gives the corresponding worst-case bound over \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonalizing the matrix turns Krylov error into weighted scalar polynomial error at its eigenvalues, linking oracle complexity to spectral approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is real symmetric.
\(\phi\) is defined at every eigenvalue of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{p\in\mathbb R_t[z]}\lVert p(H)v-\phi(H)v\rVert_2^2=\min_{p\in\mathbb R_t[z]}\sum_i c_i^2|p(\lambda_i)-\phi(\lambda_i)|^2\).

notation.meaning: coordinates of v in the eigenbasis

children.title: Sketch Fidelity-Cost Interface
children.top_down_role: Navigation for when sketch construction, embedding failure, or approximation error changes the effective lower-bound model.

children.title: Sketch-Construction Cost
children.top_down_role: Resource costs incurred when constructing or applying sketches.

knowledge_statements.title: Sketch-Construction Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic and input-access cost that must accompany iteration bounds for sketched methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\) and let a method explicitly construct \(SA\) for a sketching matrix \(S\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). In the standard RAM model, any construction that must inspect every nonzero entry of an arbitrary sparse input has cost at least \(\Omega(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\). Dense multiplication costs \(O(mnd)\), while a sketch admitting input-sparsity-time multiplication has cost \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+\operatorname{poly}(m,d))\). Consequently, total complexity equals sketch construction plus optimization on the sketch, and an iteration count alone does not bound end-to-end work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sketched optimizer must charge for forming the sketch—at least input-reading cost when every nonzero may affect the result—plus subsequent optimization.
assumptions_latex: The input matrix is explicitly stored and arbitrary nonzeros may affect \(SA\).
Arithmetic and memory accesses have unit cost in the RAM model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{total}}=C_{\mathrm{sketch}}+C_{\mathrm{opt}}\) with \(C_{\mathrm{sketch}}=\Omega(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) under full input inspection.

notation.meaning: number of nonzero entries of A
cost of optimization after sketch construction

children.title: Model-Fidelity Loss
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound changes caused by mismatch between the sketch model and the original problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Fidelity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case discrepancy between a full first-order oracle and a decoded sketched oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a query set, \(S:X\to Z\) a sketch, \(\mathcal F\) an objective class, \(O_f:X\to Y\) the full oracle, and \(\widehat O_{f,S}:Z\to W\) the sketched oracle. For a decoder \(D:W\to Y\) and metric \(d_Y\), define the model-fidelity loss by \[\Delta_{[1m[0m\mathcal F}(S,D)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sup_{x\in X}d_Y\!\left(O_f(x),D(\widehat O_{f,S}(Sx))\right).\] The optimal loss of the sketch is \(\Delta_{[1m[0m\mathcal F}^{\star}(S)=\inf_D\Delta_{[1m[0m\mathcal F}(S,D)\), where the infimum ranges over admissible decoders. A fidelity requirement at tolerance \(\eta\ge0\) is satisfied exactly when \(\Delta_{[1m[0m\mathcal F}^{\star}(S)\le\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model-fidelity loss is the smallest worst-case error with which any decoder can reconstruct full oracle responses from sketched responses.
assumptions_latex: \(O_f(x)\) and \(D(\widehat O_{f,S}(Sx))\) belong to the same metric space \((Y,d_Y)\).
\(\mathcal F\) and the admissible decoder class are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_{[1m[0m\mathcal F}^{\star}(S)\le\eta\) characterizes fidelity at tolerance \(\eta\).
review_flags: Exact sketch-oracle fidelity formulation lacks a matching supplied source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed fidelity functional is mathematically plausible but is a bespoke sketch-oracle definition with no supplied source locator. In addition, the ANSI fragments `[1m[0m` corrupt every occurrence of the fidelity-loss symbol and make the LaTeX invalid.

children.title: Embedding-Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where an embedding ceases to preserve the information needed by the lower-bound model.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedding-Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricted near-isometry failure on the model’s secant set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(S:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear, and define the normalized secant set \(T=\{(x-y)/\|x-y\|_2:x,y\in K,\ x\ne y\}\). Its restricted distortion is \[\delta_T(S)=\sup_{u\in T}\left|\|Su\|_2^2-1\right|.\] A target \(\delta\in[0,1)\) fails exactly when \(\delta_T(S)>\delta\). In particular, if \(\ker(S)\cap T\ne\varnothing\), then \(\delta_T(S)\ge1\), so no distortion target below one can hold and distinct feasible points are collapsed by the sketch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embedding fails when some normalized feasible secant is distorted beyond tolerance; a secant in the sketch kernel forces complete failure.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) contains at least two distinct points.
\(S:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear.
\(0\le\delta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker(S)\cap T\ne\varnothing\) implies \(\delta_T(S)\ge1>\delta\).

notation.meaning: normalized secant set of the model class

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses restricted embeddings or their failure boundary.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The secant-set distortion definition and kernel-collapse implication are precise and fit the failure-boundary container, but no inspectable source is supplied for the restricted-embedding formulation.

children.title: Parallel Oracle-Round Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Navigation for batched queries and limited adaptivity.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Oracle-Round Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indistinguishability lower bound for deterministic batched first-order oracle algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider deterministic algorithms making at most \(q\) simultaneous oracle queries per round. Suppose that for every such algorithm using \(R\) rounds there exist \(f_0,f_1\in\mathcal F\) whose complete oracle transcripts are identical through round \(R\), while their \(\varepsilon\)-solution sets \(X_\varepsilon(f_i)=\{x:f_i(x)-\inf f_i\le\varepsilon\}\) are disjoint. The algorithm must then return the same output on both instances, so it fails on at least one. Consequently the worst-case parallel oracle-round complexity satisfies \[R_{\varepsilon,q}(\mathcal F)>R.\] The resource counted is adaptive rounds; all queries within a round are chosen before that round’s responses are observed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two instances remain indistinguishable for R batches but have disjoint epsilon-solution sets, every q-parallel deterministic method needs more than R rounds.
assumptions_latex: Algorithms are deterministic and issue at most \(q\) queries per round.
The oracle transcript includes every query and corresponding response.
The two \(\varepsilon\)-solution sets are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\varepsilon,q}(\mathcal F)>R\).
review_flags: A precise lower-bound source for batched first-order oracle rounds is not supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic indistinguishability argument is stated coherently and the complexity-bound kind fits the terminal container, but a source specific to batched first-order oracle-round lower bounds is required.

children.title: Network Communication-Round Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Navigation for topology-sensitive distributed complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Communication-Round Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-sensitive lower bound obtained from finite information-propagation speed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a synchronous communication graph in which one round transmits messages only across edges. After \(R\) rounds, a node \(v\)'s state depends only on inputs within its radius-\(R\) neighborhood \(B_G(v,R)\). If two distributed optimization instances agree on \(B_G(v,R)\) but require disjoint admissible output sets at \(v\), then no deterministic protocol terminating in \(R\) rounds is correct on both. Hence its worst-case communication-round complexity \(C_\varepsilon(G)\) obeys \[C_\varepsilon(G)>R.\] In particular, dependence on data at distance \(D\) yields a lower bound of at least \(D\) rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node cannot use information farther than R hops after R synchronous rounds, yielding distance-based lower bounds when remote data changes its required output.
assumptions_latex: Communication is synchronous and restricted to graph edges.
Nodes initially know only their local inputs.
Correct outputs for the indistinguishable local views are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_\varepsilon(G)>R\), and remote dependence at distance \(D\) implies \(C_\varepsilon(G)\ge D\).

notation.meaning: closed radius-R graph neighborhood of node v

children.title: Computation-Communication Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Navigation for separately priced local queries and inter-node communication.

children.title: Local-Computation Cost
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound accounting for queries or processing performed within individual nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Computation Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate and maximum per-node arithmetic or oracle work in a distributed first-order execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a distributed execution with a finite node set \(V\) and rounds \(r=1,\ldots,R\), let \(c_{v,r}\ge 0\) count the prescribed local primitive operations performed by node \(v\) in round \(r\), including local oracle calls when designated. Define the aggregate local-computation cost and maximum per-node local-computation cost by \[C_{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sum_{v\in V}c_{v,r},\qquad C_{\mathrm{node}}=\max_{v\in V}\sum_{r=1}^{R}c_{v,r}.\] The first measures total local work over all nodes; the second measures the largest accumulated workload assigned to any node. Neither quantity alone necessarily equals elapsed parallel time, and the primitive-operation accounting convention must be fixed before algorithms are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local-computation cost can record either aggregate primitive work over all nodes or the maximum accumulated primitive work assigned to one node; neither metric alone necessarily equals elapsed parallel time.
assumptions_latex: The node set \(V\) and number of rounds \(R\) are finite.
A fixed primitive-operation and local-oracle accounting convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{sum}}\) measures aggregate local work, while \(C_{\mathrm{node}}\) measures maximum accumulated work per node.

notation.meaning: local primitive-operation count at node v in round r

children.title: Communication Cost
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound accounting for information exchanged between nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate or critical-link communication charged by messages, bits, or transmitted scalars.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rounds \(r=1,\ldots,R\) on a directed communication edge set \(E\), let \(b_{e,r}\ge0\) be the charged size in bits of the message sent over edge \(e\) during round \(r\), with \(b_{e,r}=0\) when no message is sent. Define \[B_{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sum_{e\in E}b_{e,r},\qquad B_{\mathrm{max}}=\max_{e\in E}\sum_{r=1}^{R}b_{e,r}.\] Here \(B_{\mathrm{sum}}\) is aggregate communication and \(B_{\mathrm{max}}\) is critical-link congestion. Message-count or scalar-count models are obtained by replacing \(b_{e,r}\) with the corresponding fixed charge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication cost measures either all transmitted bits or the largest cumulative traffic on one link, under a fixed charging convention.
assumptions_latex: The communication graph and execution horizon are finite.
Message encodings and the unit of communication charge are fixed.

children.title: Computation–Communication Frontier

knowledge_statements.title: Computation–Communication Frontier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto boundary of achievable local-computation and communication costs at fixed accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance class \(\mathcal F\), accuracy \(\varepsilon\), and success requirement. Let \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\subseteq\mathbb R_+^2\) contain every pair \((C,B)\) achieved by an admissible distributed algorithm, where \(C\) is local-computation cost and \(B\) is communication cost. The computation–communication frontier is \[\mathcal P_\varepsilon=\{(C,B)\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon:\nexists(C',B')\in\mathcal A_\varepsilon\text{ with }C'\le C,\ B'\le B,\ (C',B')\ne(C,B)\}.\] Thus every frontier point is Pareto-efficient: neither resource can be reduced without increasing the other or violating the accuracy requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The frontier consists of achievable cost pairs for which no other correct method uses no more computation and communication and strictly less of one.
assumptions_latex: The instance class, accuracy criterion, and success requirement are fixed.
Computation and communication use fixed accounting conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \((C,B)\in\mathcal P_\varepsilon\) is Pareto-minimal in \(\mathcal A_\varepsilon\).

children.title: Message-Size Limits

knowledge_statements.title: Message-Size Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-message conditional-support constraint for a synchronous distributed protocol.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b,m,R\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). A protocol obeys a \(b\)-bit message-size limit if, for every directed edge \(e\), round \(r\), and feasible prior transcript \(h\), the conditional support of the message random variable satisfies \[\left|\operatorname{supp}(M_{e,r}\mid H_{r-1}=h)\right|\le 2^b.\] Equivalently, conditional on the known prior transcript, every possible message can be represented injectively by a fixed-length binary word of at most \(b\) bits. If at most \(m\) directed messages are transmitted in each of at most \(R\) rounds, then the encoded transcript uses at most \(bmR\) transmitted bits and has at most \(2^{bmR}\) possible binary encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-bit message limit permits at most 2^b possible messages after any fixed prior transcript; at most m messages per round for R rounds use at most bmR transmitted bits.
assumptions_latex: \(b,m,R\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\).
Messages use fixed-length binary encodings conditional on the prior transcript.
At most \(m\) directed messages are transmitted in each of at most \(R\) rounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The encoded transcript uses at most \(bmR\) bits and has at most \(2^{bmR}\) possible binary encodings.

children.title: Quantization Limits

knowledge_statements.title: Quantization Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case Euclidean distortion forced by a finite reconstruction alphabet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q:B_2^d\to\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a deterministic quantizer of the Euclidean unit ball, with at most \(2^b\) reconstruction points. Its worst-case error \(e(Q)=\sup_{x\in B_2^d}\|x-Q(x)\|_2\) satisfies \[e(Q)\ge 2^{-b/d}.\] Indeed, covering \(B_2^d\) by \(|\mathcal C|\) Euclidean balls of radius \(e(Q)\) requires \(|\mathcal C|e(Q)^d\ge1\). Consequently, guaranteeing error at most \(\eta\in(0,1)\) requires \(b\ge d\log_2(1/\eta)\) bits in this worst-case model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quantizing a d-dimensional unit ball with b bits incurs worst-case error at least 2^{-b/d}; error eta requires at least d log2(1/eta) bits.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is deterministic and has at most \(2^b\) reconstruction points.
Distortion is measured in Euclidean norm on \(B_2^d\).
\(b\ge0\) and \(d\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(Q)\ge2^{-b/d}\), hence \(e(Q)\le\eta<1\) implies \(b\ge d\log_2(1/\eta)\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean unit ball in d dimensions

children.title: Bit–Round Complexity Interface
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between communicated bits and counted communication rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit–Round Complexity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion between total-bit lower bounds and communication-round lower bounds under bounded nonempty messages.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b,m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). Suppose a synchronous protocol transmits at most \(m\) messages per round and each message contains at most \(b\) bits. A protocol running for \(R\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) rounds therefore transmits at most \(bmR\) bits. If every protocol satisfying a fixed \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy and success requirement must transmit at least \(B_\varepsilon\ge0\) bits, then every protocol subject to these per-round and per-message limits satisfies \[R\ge\left\lceil\frac{B_\varepsilon}{bm}\right\rceil.\] In the reverse direction, if every counted communication round is required to contain at least one transmitted bit, then an \(R_\varepsilon\)-round lower bound implies only the baseline total-bit bound \(B\ge R_\varepsilon\); stronger bit lower bounds require additional information arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With at most m messages of b bits per round, a B-epsilon-bit lower bound yields at least ceiling of B-epsilon divided by bm communication rounds. A round lower bound alone gives only one bit per required nonempty round unless stronger information constraints are available.
assumptions_latex: \(b,m\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\).
At most \(m\) messages are transmitted per round.
Every message contains at most \(b\) bits.
\(B_\varepsilon\ge0\) lower-bounds total transmitted bits for the fixed task.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\ge\left\lceil B_\varepsilon/(bm)\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: required total transmitted bits at accuracy epsilon

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Basis Resisting Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transcript-dependent oracle construction revealing at most one new orthogonal direction per query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the revealed subspace as \(V_0=\{0\}\). At query \(x_t\), choose a unit vector \(v_t\) orthogonal to \(V_{t-1}+\operatorname{span}\{x_t\}\), set \(V_t=V_{t-1}+\operatorname{span}\{x_t,v_t\}\), and return a first-order response \((f_t,g_t)\) whose vector component satisfies \(g_t\in V_t\). Choose the scalar and vector responses so that the accumulated transcript is realizable by one objective in the target class. Continue until the query budget is exhausted, then output any realizing objective. For a linear-span method, every subsequent iterate lies in the revealed subspace, while unrevealed orthogonal directions remain unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle adaptively selects orthogonal hidden directions, returns consistent first-order data, and limits a linear-span method to the progressively revealed subspace.
assumptions_latex: The ambient dimension is large enough to select each required orthogonal direction.
The algorithm is deterministic and satisfies the linear-span restriction.
Every finite response transcript produced by the rule is realizable in the target objective class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\in V_t\) for a linear-span method, while directions in \(V_t^\perp\) remain unrevealed.

notation.meaning: first-order oracle response at query t

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No objective decrease during the first resisting-oracle steps

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Transcript Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite interpolation criterion for exact value-subgradient transcripts of closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite and let \((x_i,a_i,g_i)\in\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\) for \(i\in I\). The transcript is consistent with a proper closed convex function exactly when \[a_i\ge a_j+\langle g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\qquad\text{for every }i,j\in I.\] Under these inequalities, the function \(f(x)=\max_{j\in I}\{a_j+\langle g_j,x-x_j\rangle\}\) is proper, closed, and convex, and satisfies \(f(x_i)=a_i\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for every \(i\). Thus the inequalities are both the consistency predicate and an explicit realization certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite value-subgradient data are convexly realizable exactly when every recorded affine support lies below every recorded function value.
assumptions_latex: The index set \(I\) is finite.
Each \(x_i,g_i\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(a_i\in\mathbb R\).
Oracle responses are exact value-subgradient pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transcript is realizable if and only if \(a_i\ge a_j+\langle g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\) for all \(i,j\in I\).

notation.meaning: recorded objective value at query x_i

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Instance Realizability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Realizability of a finite first-order oracle transcript by one objective in a prescribed function class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\mathcal O_f(x)\) denote the admissible first-order oracle outputs for \(f\) at \(x\). A finite transcript \(\mathcal T=((x_i,y_i))_{i=0}^{T-1}\) is objective-instance realizable over \(\mathcal F\) if there exists one function \(f\in\mathcal F\) such that \(y_i\in\mathcal O_f(x_i)\) for every \(i\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\). In the value-subgradient model, where \(y_i=(v_i,g_i)\), this means \(v_i=f(x_i)\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) simultaneously for all queried points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transcript is realizable when a single objective in the chosen class produces every recorded value and first-order response at the corresponding query.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is a specified function class on \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(\mathcal T\) is a finite oracle transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal T\text{ is realizable}\iff\exists f\in\mathcal F\;\forall i<T:\;y_i\in\mathcal O_f(x_i).\)

notation.meaning: set of admissible first-order outputs at x

knowledge_statements.title: Nonrealizable Transcript Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact obstruction to interpolating finite value-subgradient data by a proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \((x_i,v_i,g_i)_{i=1}^m\subset\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\), a proper closed convex function \(f\) satisfying \(f(x_i)=v_i\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for every \(i\) exists if and only if \(v_i\ge v_j+\langle g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\) for all \(i,j\). Consequently, the transcript is nonrealizable precisely when at least one ordered pair violates this inequality. When all inequalities hold, an interpolant is \(f(x)=\max_{1\le j\le m}\{v_j+\langle g_j,x-x_j\rangle\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite convex value-subgradient data are nonrealizable exactly when some recorded affine support plane lies strictly above another recorded value.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\) and \(x_i,g_i\in\mathbb R^d\), \(v_i\in\mathbb R\).
The target class is the proper closed convex functions on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{nonrealizable}\iff\exists i,j:\;v_i<v_j+\langle g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle.\)

children.title: Randomized-Algorithm Extensions
children.top_down_role: Navigation for hard distributions and randomized oracle constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized-Algorithm Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Yao-type transfer from hard input distributions to worst-case lower bounds for randomized first-order algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an oracle budget \(T\), an instance class \(\mathcal I\), and a nonnegative terminal loss \(L(A,I)\). Let \(\mathfrak D_T\) be the deterministic algorithms using at most \(T\) oracle calls and \(\mathfrak R_T\) their randomized mixtures. Then
\[\inf_{R\in\mathfrak R_T}\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\mathbb E[L(R,I)]\ge \sup_{P\in\mathcal P(\mathcal I)}\inf_{A\in\mathfrak D_T}\mathbb E_{I\sim P}[L(A,I)].\]
Thus, if one distribution \(P\) forces expected loss at least \(\varepsilon\) for every deterministic \(T\)-query algorithm, every randomized \(T\)-query algorithm has some instance with expected loss at least \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributional lower bound against every deterministic bounded-query method yields a worst-case expected lower bound for every randomized method with the same budget.
assumptions_latex: \(L(A,I)\ge0\) is measurable and expectations are defined.
Algorithms in \(\mathfrak R_T\) randomize over deterministic \(T\)-query procedures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists P\;\forall A\in\mathfrak D_T:\mathbb E_P L(A,I)\ge\varepsilon\Rightarrow\forall R\in\mathfrak R_T\;\exists I:\mathbb E L(R,I)\ge\varepsilon.\)

notation.meaning: deterministic and randomized algorithms with oracle budget T

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower-bound direction is a plausible Yao-type principle and the content kind fits the navigation topic, but the precise algorithm-mixture, measurability, and minimax formulation has no supporting source. Those modeling details materially determine the theorem's scope.

children.title: Convex Zero Chains

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Zero Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable convex zero chains relative to an ordered orthonormal coordinate system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((e_1,\ldots,e_d)\) be an ordered orthonormal basis and define \(E_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\), with \(E_0=\{0\}\). A differentiable convex function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is a first-order convex zero chain in this basis if, for every \(r\in\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\), \[x\in E_r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nabla f(x)\in E_{r+1}.\] Thus, whenever a method queries a point in \(E_r\), the resulting gradient is supported in at most the first \(r+1\) basis directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex zero chain has the property that a query supported on the first r basis directions produces a gradient supported on at most the first r+1 directions.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex.
\((e_1,\ldots,e_d)\) is an ordered orthonormal basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall r<d:\;\nabla f(E_r)\subseteq E_{r+1}.\)

notation.meaning: span of the first r ordered basis vectors

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical first-order zero-chain predicate specialized to convex functions

children.title: Nonconvex Zero Chains

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Zero Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable nonconvex zero chains used to delay discovery of coordinates needed for stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((e_1,\ldots,e_d)\) be an ordered orthonormal basis and let \(E_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\), with \(E_0=\{0\}\). A differentiable, not necessarily convex function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is a first-order nonconvex zero chain if \[x\in E_r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nabla f(x)\in E_{r+1}\qquad(0\le r<d).\] A stationarity-obstructing zero chain additionally has a threshold \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\ge\varepsilon\) for every \(r<d\) and every \(x\in E_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex zero chain reveals at most one new basis direction at a prefix-supported query and, under an additional uniform condition, keeps every such partially revealed point at least epsilon away from first-order stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable.
\((e_1,\ldots,e_d)\) is an ordered orthonormal basis.
For the stationarity-obstruction variant, \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall r<d:\;\nabla f(E_r)\subseteq E_{r+1}\), and under the obstruction condition \(\inf_{x\in E_r}\|\nabla f(x)\|\ge\varepsilon\) for every \(r<d\).

notation.meaning: subspace spanned by the first r revealed basis directions

children.title: Block Zero Chains

knowledge_statements.title: Block Zero Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-chain propagation with ordered vector blocks replacing scalar coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb R^d=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m\) be an orthogonal block decomposition and set \(W_r=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_r\), with \(W_0=\{0\}\). A differentiable function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is a first-order block zero chain if
\[x\in W_r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nabla f(x)\in W_{r+1}\qquad(0\le r<m).\]
Thus one first-order response can activate at most the next entire block. The scalar zero-chain definition is recovered when every \(V_r\) is one-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block zero chain permits each gradient query to reveal at most one new ordered coordinate block.
assumptions_latex: \(V_1,\ldots,V_m\) form an orthogonal direct-sum decomposition of \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(f\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall r<m:\;\nabla f(W_r)\subseteq W_{r+1}.\)

notation.meaning: sum of the first r blocks

children.title: Component Zero Chains
children.top_down_role: Sequential-revelation constructions adapted to component-oracle access.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Zero Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum zero chains whose individual component gradients obey the ordered support restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(x)\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(E_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\) for an ordered orthonormal basis. The family \((f_j)_{j=1}^n\) is a component first-order zero chain if, for every component \(j\) and every \(r<d\),
\[x\in E_r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nabla f_j(x)\in E_{r+1}.\]
Accordingly, even an oracle that returns a selected component gradient cannot expose a coordinate beyond the immediate successor of the currently supported prefix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a component zero chain, every individual finite-sum component gradient reveals at most the next coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^n f_j\) and every \(f_j\) is differentiable.
An ordered orthonormal basis of \(\mathbb R^d\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall j\le n\;\forall r<d:\;\nabla f_j(E_r)\subseteq E_{r+1}.\)

children.title: Distributed Zero Chains

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Zero Chains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-indexed zero chains combining local gradient revelation with neighbor-to-neighbor propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a communication graph, let \(F(x)=\sum_{v\in V}f_v(x)\), and let \(E_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\). A distributed zero-chain execution assigns each node a revealed level \(r_v^t\) such that a local gradient computation at node \(v\) maps states in \(E_{r_v^t}\) into \(E_{r_v^t+1}\), while one communication round permits
\[r_v^{t+1}\le \max_{u\in N[v]}r_u^t.\]
Thus information about coordinate \(e_k\) can reach node \(v\) only after local sequential revelation and transmission along a graph path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributed zero chain restricts new coordinates to local one-step revelation and subsequent propagation through neighboring nodes.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is the allowed communication graph.
Each node \(v\) accesses only its differentiable local function \(f_v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{local computation increases }r_v^t\text{ by at most }1\), while \(\text{communication replaces it by at most }\max_{u\in N[v]}r_u^t\).

notation.meaning: largest coordinate level revealed at node v by time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Distributed zero-chain models depend on the ordering and power of local computation and communication rounds. The displayed communication update does not specify how a same-round local level increase interacts with communication, so the exact mathematical variant cannot be validated without a source defining the execution model.

knowledge_statements.title: Chain-Structured Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted path-energy representation of convex quadratic hard instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A weighted chain-structured quadratic on \(\mathbb R^d\) has the representation
\[q(x)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\alpha_i(x_i-x_{i+1})^2+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^d\beta_i x_i^2-\gamma x_1+c,\]
where \(\alpha_i\ge0\) and \(\beta_i\ge0\). Its Hessian is the weighted path Laplacian plus \(\operatorname{diag}(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_d)\), hence is positive semidefinite and tridiagonal. Moreover, if \(x\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\), then \(\nabla q(x)\in\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_{r+1}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chain quadratic is a weighted path energy with a tridiagonal positive-semidefinite Hessian and one-coordinate gradient propagation.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha_i\ge0\) and \(\beta_i\ge0\).
The linear term is supported on the first coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla^2q\succeq0\) is tridiagonal and \(\nabla q(E_r)\subseteq E_{r+1}\) for \(r<d\).

notation.meaning: span of the first r coordinate vectors

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted path-energy representation, positive-semidefinite tridiagonal Hessian, and prefix-support propagation are mathematically consistent. Representation is an appropriate content kind, but an inspectable lower-bound source is needed to establish this as the intended hard-instance family rather than merely an elementary quadratic class.

children.title: Tridiagonal Quadratics

knowledge_statements.title: Tridiagonal Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic objectives whose Hessians couple only equal or adjacent coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A quadratic function \(q:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), written as \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\) with symmetric \(A\), is tridiagonal in the chosen coordinate basis if
\[A_{ij}=0\qquad\text{whenever }|i-j|>1.\]
It is convex exactly when \(A\succeq0\), and it is \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient exactly when \(\mu I\preceq A\preceq LI\). Tridiagonality means each gradient coordinate depends only on the corresponding coordinate and its immediate neighbors, together with the matching entry of \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tridiagonal quadratic couples each coordinate only to itself and its immediate neighbors; spectral bounds determine convexity and smoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) is symmetric.
\(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_{ij}=0\) for \(|i-j|>1\), with \(\mu I\preceq A\preceq LI\) characterizing \(\mu\)-strong convexity and \(L\)-smoothness.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary quadratic and spectral characterization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and spectral characterizations are correct under the stated symmetric-Hessian setting, and definition fits the leaf. No authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infinite-dimensional tridiagonal quadratic-chain construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of an ℓ2 quadratic-chain instance and its associated tridiagonal operator for condition-dependent lower-bound constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb R^\infty\equiv\ell_2\) consist of sequences \(x=(x^{(i)})_{i=1}^\infty\) satisfying \(\|x\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^\infty(x^{(i)})^2<\infty\). For \(\mu>0\) and \(Q_f>1\), define \[f_{\mu,Q_f}(x)=\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}8\left((x^{(1)})^2+\sum_{i=1}^\infty(x^{(i)}-x^{(i+1)})^2-2x^{(1)}\right)+\frac\mu2\|x\|^2,\] set \(L=\mu Q_f\), and let \(A\) be the infinite tridiagonal operator with diagonal entries \(2\) and adjacent off-diagonal entries \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On ℓ2, the construction is a regularized quadratic chain involving adjacent-coordinate differences and a linear term in the first coordinate. Its associated infinite tridiagonal operator has 2 on the diagonal and −1 on the adjacent diagonals.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb R^\infty\equiv\ell_2
\mu>0
Q_f>1
L=\mu Q_f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{\mu,Q_f}(x)=\frac{\mu(Q_f-1)}8\left((x^{(1)})^2+\sum_{i=1}^\infty(x^{(i)}-x^{(i+1)})^2-2x^{(1)}\right)+\frac\mu2\|x\|^2,\qquad A=\operatorname{tridiag}(-1,2,-1).

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Information Propagation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prefix-support invariance for linear-span methods applied to tridiagonal quadratic instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q(x)=	frac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x+c\), where \(A\) is tridiagonal and \(b\in E_1\), and set \(E_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_r\}\). Then
\[x\in E_r\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
abla q(x)=Ax-b\in E_{r+1}.\]
Consequently, if \(x_0=0\) and a linear-span first-order method satisfies \(x_t\in x_0+\operatorname{span}\{
abla q(x_0),\ldots,
abla q(x_{t-1})\}\), induction gives \(x_t\in E_t\). After \(t\) oracle calls, coordinates beyond \(t\) therefore remain unrevealed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a tridiagonal quadratic, a linear-span first-order method starting at zero can activate at most one additional coordinate per oracle call.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is tridiagonal and \(b\in E_1\).
\(x_0=0\) and the method obeys the stated linear-span restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_t\in E_t\) for every admissible iteration \(t\le d\).

notation.meaning: span of the first r coordinate vectors

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct support propagation for tridiagonal matrix-vector products

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The prefix-support induction is mathematically correct for the stated linear-span method and property is the correct role for this leaf. A source is still required for the precise iteration convention and its use as a first-order lower-bound mechanism.

children.title: Polynomial-Approximation Barriers
children.top_down_role: Navigation for spectral and Krylov lower-bound mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial-Approximation Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Krylov lower bound for minimizing strongly convex quadratics through uniform polynomial approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x\), where \(\mu I\preceq A\preceq LI\), and a linear-span first-order method with \(x_0=0\). After \(t\) oracle calls, \(x_t=p_{t-1}(A)b\) for some polynomial \(p_{t-1}\) of degree at most \(t-1\). Its residual polynomial \(r_t(\lambda)=1-\lambda p_{t-1}(\lambda)\) satisfies \(r_t(0)=1\). In sufficiently large dimension, the worst-case relative energy-norm error is bounded below by
\[\min_{\substack{r\in\mathbb R_t[\lambda]\\r(0)=1}}\max_{\lambda\in[\mu,L]}|r(\lambda)|=\frac{1}{\left|T_t\!\left(\frac{L+\mu}{L-\mu}\right)\right|}.\]
Thus achieving relative error \(\varepsilon\) requires \(t=\Omega(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Krylov iterates correspond to low-degree polynomials, and Chebyshev approximation forces order square-root condition-number times log accuracy oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\mu<L\) and \(\mu I\preceq A\preceq LI\).
The method is linear-span, starts at \(x_0=0\), and the adversarial dimension is sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t=\Omega\!\left(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon)\right)\) oracle calls are necessary for worst-case relative energy-norm error at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind of degree t
real polynomials of degree at most t
lower and upper spectral bounds for A

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Krylov-polynomial and Chebyshev mechanism is classical, and complexity_bound is compatible with the barrier topic. However, the exact equality, relative energy-norm interpretation, sufficient-dimension condition, and resulting oracle lower bound require an authoritative theorem-level source; the current standard-field rationale is insufficient to validate those linked claims.

children.title: Finite-Sum Matrix Partitioning

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Matrix Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitions a quadratic hard instance among component-gradient oracles without changing its aggregate objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) be positive semidefinite and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^d\). A finite-sum matrix partitioning of \((H,b)\) consists of positive-semidefinite matrices \(H_1,\ldots,H_n\) and vectors \(b_1,\ldots,b_n\) satisfying \(H=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n H_i\) and \(b=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\). Defining \(f_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}H_i x-b_i^{\mathsf T}x\) gives
\[
f(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx-b^{\mathsf T}x,
\qquad \nabla f_i(x)=H_i x-b_i.
\]
Thus a component query reveals only the assigned matrix-vector action while the average objective retains the original hard quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split a hard quadratic’s Hessian and linear term among components so their average recovers the original objective, while each component oracle reveals only its assigned matrix action.
assumptions_latex: \(H\succeq 0\).
\(H_i\succeq 0\) for every \(i\).
The oracle returns one selected component gradient per query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\) and \(\nabla f_i(x)=H_i x-b_i\).

notation.meaning: Matrix and linear term assigned to component i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: algebraic finite-sum decomposition of a convex quadratic
Exact lower-bound source for hard-matrix partitioning is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic decomposition is correct and representation fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports its use as a lower-bound construction. The claim that a component query reveals only a matrix-vector action also ignores the linear term and depends on the precise component-oracle interface.

children.title: Two-Point Constructions
