knowledge_statements.title: Two-Point Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Le Cam’s binary reduction for a metric-separated pair of optimization instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) be the transcript laws under two oracle instances with solutions \(x_0^\star,x_1^\star\) in a metric space \((\mathcal X,\rho)\), and suppose \(\rho(x_0^\star,x_1^\star)\ge 2s\). For every transcript-measurable estimator \(\widehat x\),
\[
\max_{v\in\{0,1\}}P_v\!\left(\rho(\widehat x,x_v^\star)\ge s\right)
\ge \frac{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)}{2}.
\]
Consequently, if every algorithm using at most \(T\) oracle calls induces \(\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)\le\alpha<1\), then its worst-case probability of failing to attain metric accuracy \(s\) is at least \((1-\alpha)/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two solution-separated instances whose transcript distributions have small total variation force every estimator to incur a fixed probability of error at the target accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho(x_0^\star,x_1^\star)\ge 2s\).
\(\widehat x\) is measurable with respect to the oracle transcript.
\(P_0,P_1\) are transcript laws under the same query budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_v P_v(\rho(\widehat x,x_v^\star)\ge s)\ge (1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1))/2\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Le Cam two-point testing reduction
An authoritative theorem locator for the optimization-transcript formulation is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Le Cam bound is mathematically standard, but no theorem or section locator is supplied. The leaf denotes a construction family, whereas complexity_bound describes the resulting inequality rather than the construction's mathematical role; an authoritative source should determine the intended formulation and kind.

children.title: Local-Alternative Constructions
children.top_down_role: Hard families formed from nearby competing objective instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Alternative Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contiguous alternatives whose solutions separate at the target optimization scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For statistical experiments \(\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), a sequence \(\theta_n\) is a local alternative to \(\theta_0\) at solution scale \(s_n>0\) when
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(P_{\theta_n}^{\otimes n}\middle\|P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\right)\le C
\quad\text{and}\quad
\rho\!\left(x^\star(\theta_n),x^\star(\theta_0)\right)\ge 2s_n
\]
for a constant \(C\) independent of \(n\). By Pinsker’s inequality and the two-point reduction, every estimator \(\widehat x\) then satisfies
\[
\max_{\theta\in\{\theta_0,\theta_n\}}P_\theta^{\otimes n}\!\left(\rho(\widehat x,x^\star(\theta))\ge s_n\right)
\ge \frac{1-\sqrt{C/2}}{2},
\]
whenever \(C<2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local alternative remains information-close to a base instance while moving its optimizer by twice the target scale, thereby producing a nonvanishing estimation-error probability.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{\theta_n}^{\otimes n}\ll P_{\theta_0}^{\otimes n}\).
The optimizer map \(x^star(\theta)\) is defined at both parameters.
\(C<2\) for a positive displayed lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded local divergence and \(2s_n\)-solution separation imply worst-case error probability at least \((1-\sqrt{C/2})/2\).

notation.meaning: Selected optimizer associated with parameter theta.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local asymptotic alternatives combined with Pinsker and Le Cam bounds
A source matching this optimizer-valued formulation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular optimizer-valued definition of a local alternative. Bounded product KL is one sufficient two-point construction, not a generally standard definition of local alternatives. The assumption also writes x^star instead of x^\star, so its TeX notation is malformed.

children.title: Pairwise Distinguishability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Information limits determined by the separation of paired alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Pairwise Distinguishability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact total-variation threshold separating binary indistinguishability from consistent testing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For probability measures \(P_0,P_1\) and tests \(\phi\) taking values in \(\{0,1\}\), the optimal equal-prior binary testing risk is
\[
\inf_\phi \frac{P_0(\phi=1)+P_1(\phi=0)}{2}
=\frac{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)}{2}.
\]
Hence a sequence of pairs \((P_{0,T},P_{1,T})\) is uniformly pairwise indistinguishable whenever \(\sup_T\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,T},P_{1,T})<1\), because its testing risk stays bounded away from zero. Conversely, tests with both error probabilities converging to zero exist precisely when \(\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,T},P_{1,T})\to1\). Thus pairwise lower-bound arguments cease to obstruct consistency at the total-variation boundary one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary testing error equals one half of one minus total variation; pairwise lower bounds remain effective below variation one and vanish as variation approaches one.
assumptions_latex: \(P_0\) and \(P_1\) are probability measures on a common measurable space.
Tests may be randomized.
The asymptotic claim concerns a sequence indexed by query budget \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistent pairwise testing is possible if and only if \(\operatorname{TV}(P_{0,T},P_{1,T})\to1\).

notation.meaning: Binary test based on the observed transcript.
Total variation distance between the two transcript laws.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact Bayes risk identity for binary hypothesis testing
A precise authoritative locator for the testing identity is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equal-prior total-variation identity is standard, but no authoritative locator is supplied. The equivalence involving tests with both errors tending to zero requires a sequence of tests and explicit allowance for randomized tests; its exact scope should be tied to a cited testing theorem.

children.title: Packing Constructions

knowledge_statements.title: Packing Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric packings used to encode many optimization instances with separated solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\Theta,\rho)\) be a metric space and let \(s>0\). A finite set \(\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_M\}\subseteq\Theta\) is a \(2s\)-packing if
\[
\rho(\theta_i,\theta_j)\ge 2s
\quad\text{for all distinct }i,j.
\]
An optimization packing construction additionally assigns an instance \(f_i\) and a selected optimizer \(x_i^\star\) to each codeword so that \(\rho(x_i^\star,x_j^\star)\ge2s\). Therefore every output \(\widehat x\) satisfying \(\rho(\widehat x,x_i^\star)<s\) identifies index \(i\) uniquely by nearest-neighbor decoding. The construction becomes information-theoretically hard when the associated transcript laws cannot reliably distinguish these indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A packing is a finite collection of pairwise separated parameters or optimizers; accuracy below half the separation uniquely reveals which packed instance generated the transcript.
assumptions_latex: \((\Theta,\rho)\) is a metric space.
Each packed optimization instance has a selected optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Metric error below \(s\) uniquely determines the index of a \(2s\)-separated optimizer.

notation.meaning: Selected optimizer of packed instance i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: metric packing and nearest-neighbor decoding
A source specifically connecting metric packings to optimization lower bounds is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric-packing definition and disjoint-ball argument are standard, but there is no cited locator connecting them to optimization lower-bound constructions. Nearest-neighbor decoding also needs a defined decoder and tie convention, although uniqueness inside an open s-ball follows from the stated separation.

children.title: Multiple-Hypothesis Constructions
children.top_down_role: Hard families requiring discrimination among many candidate instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Hypothesis Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fano reduction from optimization accuracy to recovery of a packed instance index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,M\}\), let \(Z\) be the transcript generated under instance \(V\), and suppose the selected optimizers satisfy \(\rho(x_i^\star,x_j^\star)\ge2s\) for \(i\ne j\). For every transcript-measurable output \(\widehat x\), nearest-neighbor decoding and Fano’s inequality give
\[
\Pr\!\left(\rho(\widehat x,x_V^\star)\ge s\right)
\ge 1-\frac{I(V;Z)+\log 2}{\log M}.
\]
Accordingly, any \(T\)-query oracle model satisfying \(I(V;Z)\le\beta\log M\) with \(\beta<1\) has average failure probability at least \(1-\beta-(\log2)/(\log M)\) at accuracy \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For many separated instances, Fano’s inequality converts limited transcript information about the hidden index into a lower bound on the probability of optimization error.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is uniform on \(M\ge2\) indices.
The optimizer family is \(2s\)-separated.
\(\widehat x\) is measurable with respect to transcript \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\rho(\widehat x,x_V^\star)\ge s)\ge1-(I(V;Z)+\log2)/\log M\).

notation.meaning: Mutual information between the instance index and transcript.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Fano inequality with packing-based decoding
An authoritative locator for the stated Fano form is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Fano inequality form is standard, but no authoritative theorem locator is supplied. This leaf is a construction family, while complexity_bound classifies the derived error inequality rather than the construction itself; the sourced formulation should fix the mathematical role.

children.title: Dimension-Sensitive Family Size

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Sensitive Family Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponential packing cardinality obtained from a binary code in dimension \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every integer \(d\ge8\), there exists a set \(\mathcal V\subseteq\{-1,1\}^d\) such that
\[
|\mathcal V|\ge 2^{d/8}
\quad\text{and}\quad
d_{\mathrm H}(u,v)\ge d/4
\quad\text{for all distinct }u,v\in\mathcal V.
\]
For any radius \(a>0\), the scaled points \(x_v=(a/\sqrt d)v\) lie on the Euclidean sphere of radius \(a\) and satisfy
\[
\|x_u-x_v\|_2=2a\sqrt{d_{\mathrm H}(u,v)/d}\ge a.
\]
Thus dimension \(d\) supports an \(a\)-separated family whose logarithmic cardinality is at least \((d/8)\log2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension-d binary code yields exponentially many points on a Euclidean sphere with constant-scale pairwise separation, so packing entropy grows linearly with dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ge8\) is an integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is an \(a\)-separated Euclidean family with \(\log|\mathcal V|\ge(d/8)\log2\).

notation.meaning: Hamming distance on binary sign vectors.
Euclidean radius and guaranteed separation scale.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Varshamov-Gilbert packing with conservative constants
The exact finite-dimensional coding constants require source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling from Hamming separation to Euclidean separation is correct, and property fits the leaf. The exact finite-dimension claim |\mathcal V|\ge 2^{d/8} with distance at least d/4 for every integer d\ge8 requires a precise coding-theorem source and locator.

children.title: Adaptive-Query Information Accounting

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Query Information Accounting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chain-rule decomposition of information revealed by a sequential adaptive oracle transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) index a random oracle instance. At round \(t\), let the query \(X_t\) be measurable with respect to the past transcript \(H_{t-1}=(X_1,Y_1,\ldots,X_{t-1},Y_{t-1})\) and independent internal randomness \(R\), and let \(Y_t\) be the oracle response. For \(Z_T=(R,X_1,Y_1,\ldots,X_T,Y_T)\), the mutual-information chain rule gives
\[
I(V;Z_T)=\sum_{t=1}^T I\!\left(V;Y_t\mid H_{t-1},X_t,R\right),
\]
provided \(V\) is independent of \(R\). Hence adaptively chosen queries create no additional information term by themselves; all information about the hidden instance enters through conditional response channels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an adaptive algorithm, total information about the hidden instance equals the sum of conditional information contributed by each oracle response given the preceding transcript.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is independent of algorithmic randomness \(R\).
Each \(X_t\) is determined by \((H_{t-1},R)\).
All displayed mutual informations are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(V;Z_T)=\sum_{t=1}^T I(V;Y_t\mid H_{t-1},X_t,R)\).

notation.meaning: Adaptive query and corresponding oracle response.
Complete randomized transcript through round T.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: mutual-information chain rule for adaptive experiments
A sequential-information source with the stated conditioning convention is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The information-chain principle is plausible, but no sequential-information source is cited. The text alternates between X_t being measurable with respect to H_{t-1} and being determined by (H_{t-1},R); the exact equality depends on the latter policy model and should be verified under a cited conditioning convention.

children.title: Hidden-Subspace Constructions
children.top_down_role: Hard instances whose informative directions lie in concealed subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden-Subspace Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embeds a lower-dimensional hard function in an unknown orthogonal subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\in\mathbb R^{d\times r}\) satisfy \(U^{\mathsf T}U=I_r\), and let \(g:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. The hidden-subspace embedding of \(g\) is
\[
f_U(x)=g(U^{\mathsf T}x),
\qquad
\nabla f_U(x)=U\nabla g(U^{\mathsf T}x).
\]
More generally, adding \(\tfrac\mu2\|(I-UU^{\mathsf T})x\|_2^2\) makes the objective \(\mu\)-quadratic off the hidden subspace while preserving \(g\) on \(\operatorname{range}(U)\). A first-order query can access the hard coordinates only through \(U^{\mathsf T}x\) and the returned vector in \(\operatorname{range}(U)\); orthogonal directions remain irrelevant until the transcript aligns with them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional hard objective is composed with an unknown orthogonal projection, restricting informative queries and gradients to a concealed subspace.
assumptions_latex: \(U^{\mathsf T}U=I_r\).
\(g\) is differentiable.
\(1\le r\le d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_U(x)=g(U^{\mathsf T}x)\) and \(\nabla f_U(x)=U\nabla g(U^{\mathsf T}x)\).

notation.meaning: Isometric embedding of the hidden r-dimensional subspace.
Embedded objective in the ambient space.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: orthogonal composition and gradient chain rule
A lower-bound reference for hidden-subspace embeddings is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The composition and gradient formulas are correct and representation fits the leaf, but no lower-bound source is supplied. The concluding concealment claim does not follow from the chain rule alone, and after adding the orthogonal quadratic term the oracle can return a nonzero orthogonal gradient component.

children.title: Random-Rotation Constructions
children.top_down_role: Hard instances randomized through rotations of informative directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Rotation Constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonal randomization of a hard instance while preserving its analytic parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}\) be orthogonal and let \(g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Define \(f_Q(x)=g(Q^{\mathsf T}x)\). Then
\[
\nabla f_Q(x)=Q\nabla g(Q^{\mathsf T}x),
\qquad
\|\nabla f_Q(x)-\nabla f_Q(y)\|_2
=\|\nabla g(Q^{\mathsf T}x)-\nabla g(Q^{\mathsf T}y)\|_2.
\]
Orthogonal rotation therefore preserves convexity, strong-convexity constants, gradient-Lipschitz constants, distances, and objective gaps. If \(Q\) is Haar distributed, the orientation of every fixed hard subspace is uniform, so a lower-bound distribution can conceal the coordinate system without altering the hard instance’s numerical parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing an objective with a Haar-random orthogonal map hides its coordinate orientation while preserving convexity, smoothness, distances, and objective gaps.
assumptions_latex: \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_d\).
\(g\) is differentiable.
Uniform-orientation claims use Haar-distributed \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Orthogonal composition preserves Euclidean first-order regularity parameters and randomizes the orientation of hard directions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: invariance of Euclidean geometry under orthogonal transformations
A source for the lower-bound use of Haar rotations is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Orthogonal invariance of the listed Euclidean quantities is standard, but the lower-bound use of a Haar rotation has no source. Because the leaf is Random-Rotation Constructions, representation or principle is more appropriate than property unless the terminal container is intended specifically for invariance properties.

children.title: Adaptive-Direction Concealment
children.top_down_role: Limits on preserving hidden directions against adaptive algorithm queries.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Direction Concealment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension condition permitting a resisting construction to choose fresh hidden directions online.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_{t-1}\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be the linear span of all query and oracle-response directions revealed before round \(t\). Adaptive-direction concealment is feasible through round \(T\) if, whenever a fresh direction is required, one can select
\[
v_t\in S_{t-1}^{\perp},
\qquad \|v_t\|_2=1.
\]
Equivalently, the construction requires \(\dim S_{t-1}<d\) at every such round. If at most \(k\) linearly independent directions are added per round and the initial revealed span has dimension \(r_0\), the sufficient budget \(d>r_0+k(T-1)\) guarantees a fresh orthogonal choice through round \(T\). Such choices leave all preceding inner products, function values, and gradients unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resisting construction can conceal one fresh direction per adaptive round while the span of all previously exposed query and response directions remains lower-dimensional than the ambient space.
assumptions_latex: Past oracle answers depend only on inner products with already selected directions.
At most \(k\) independent directions enter the revealed span per round.
The ambient dimension satisfies \(d>r_0+k(T-1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A unit vector \(v_t\in S_{t-1}^{\perp}\) can be selected whenever required for every \(t\le T\).

notation.meaning: Span of directions revealed before round t.
Initial span dimension and per-round dimension growth bound.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary orthogonal-complement dimension counting in resisting-oracle constructions
The consistency assumptions needed to preserve prior oracle answers require a specific resisting-oracle source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dimension-counting condition guarantees a fresh orthogonal vector, but it does not by itself guarantee that all prior function values and gradients remain unchanged. That assertion requires a specified resisting-oracle construction and consistency lemma with an inspectable source.

children.title: Zero-Respecting Reductions
children.top_down_role: Navigation for transferring zero-chain results to broader algorithm classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Respecting Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient simulation condition for transferring zero-chain lower bounds to general deterministic first-order methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A first-order method is zero-respecting on \(f:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) when every iterate satisfies
\[
\operatorname{supp}(x_t)
\subseteq \bigcup_{s<t}\operatorname{supp}(\nabla f(x_s)).
\]
Suppose a function class is invariant under orthogonal embeddings and, for every deterministic \(T\)-query method \(A\), there is an isometry \(U:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d\) such that the projected transcript of \(A\) on \(F(x)=f(U^{\mathsf T}x)\) coincides through round \(T\) with a zero-respecting transcript on \(f\). Then every \(T\)-query lower bound valid for zero-respecting methods on \(f\) also holds for arbitrary deterministic methods on the embedded class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an orthogonal embedding makes every deterministic method’s projected transcript zero-respecting, any zero-chain lower bound transfers to that broader deterministic algorithm class.
assumptions_latex: The objective class is closed under the stated orthogonal embedding.
The transcript simulation is exact through query \(T\).
The algorithm is deterministic; randomized transfer requires a distributional argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A \(T\)-query lower bound for zero-respecting methods transfers to every deterministic method admitting the embedding simulation.

notation.meaning: Set of nonzero coordinates of x.
Isometric embedding used in the transcript simulation.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: zero-respecting definition plus orthogonal transcript-simulation implication
A source specifying dimension requirements and randomized-algorithm extensions is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transfer implication is reasonable if exact transcript simulation and class closure hold, but no source specifies the necessary ambient-dimension budget, embedding construction, or deterministic scope. The record also combines a definition of zero-respecting methods with a conditional transfer theorem; principle is plausible for the navigation topic, but the sourced statement must clearly identify the terminal role.

children.title: Lifted-Embedding Dimension Budget
children.top_down_role: Navigation for ambient-dimension requirements of hard-instance transfers.

children.title: Dimension-Lifting Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Hard-instance transfers achieved through higher-dimensional representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Lifting Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Isometric lifting of a finite-dimensional resisting-oracle construction into a larger Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}\) be a hard instance and let \(U:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\) satisfy \(U^{\mathsf T}U=I_m\). Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(f(x)=h(U^{\mathsf T}x)\), optionally adding a term constant on \(\operatorname{range}(U)\). Then \(\nabla f(x)=U\nabla h(U^{\mathsf T}x)\) whenever \(h\) is differentiable, while distances, convexity, strong convexity on the embedded subspace, and gradient-Lipschitz constants are preserved. An adaptive resisting-oracle lift may choose unused orthogonal columns of \(U\) after each query, provided every answer remains consistent with one fixed completed embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isometric embedding transfers a hard instance to higher dimension while preserving its relevant geometry and oracle transcript; adaptive constructions may assign previously unused orthogonal directions as queries arrive.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ge m\) and \(U^{\mathsf T}U=I_m\).
The oracle answers are consistent with a single completed embedding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted problem reproduces the base-instance first-order information on \(\operatorname{range}(U)\) without changing the relevant Euclidean regularity constants.

notation.meaning: Isometric embedding from the hard-instance space into the lifted space.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The isometric composition formula and subspace regularity claims are standard, but the adaptive resisting-oracle completion claim is construction-dependent and has no inspectable citation. A source must establish fixed-objective transcript consistency and the precise scope of preserved class parameters.

children.title: Embedding-Dimension Budget
children.top_down_role: Ambient-dimension requirements imposed by hard-instance embeddings.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedding-Dimension Budget
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension required to realize an orthogonal-direction lower-bound transcript through a prescribed horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a lower-bound construction whose initialization occupies a subspace of dimension \(r_0\), and suppose each of the first \(T\) oracle interactions may require at most \(q\) new mutually orthogonal directions. A sufficient embedding budget is \[d\ge r_0+qT.\] Under this inequality, the construction can assign all directions while maintaining orthogonality to the previously exposed transcript. Consequently, a lower bound proved through iteration \(T\) is valid in every ambient dimension satisfying the budget. The inequality is sufficient rather than universally necessary; symmetry or shared-direction constructions can require fewer dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If initialization uses r₀ directions and each of T interactions needs at most q new directions, dimension d at least r₀+qT suffices for the lifted transcript.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb{N}\), \(r_0,q\in\mathbb{N}_0\).
At most \(q\) independent directions are introduced per oracle interaction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\ge r_0+qT\) is a sufficient ambient-dimension budget through interaction \(T\).

notation.meaning: Dimension occupied before the first interaction.
Maximum new orthogonal directions required per interaction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dimension count is plausible under the stated per-round direction assumption, and complexity_bound is suitable for this budget leaf. However, no source supports its use as a lower-bound transfer guarantee or specifies the oracle construction for which r_0+qT is sufficient.

children.title: Lifted-Transfer Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Regimes where the available dimension supports or obstructs a lifted lower bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Lifted-Transfer Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency conditions for transferring a finite-horizon lower bound by an isometric lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-horizon lower-bound transcript is lift-transfer feasible into \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) if there exist an isometry \(U:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}\) and a lifted objective \(f\) such that: \(U^{\mathsf T}U=I_m\); every lifted query and oracle answer projects to the corresponding base transcript; the full transcript is generated by one fixed admissible \(f\); and \(f\) belongs to the target objective class with the required parameter values. For an adaptive construction, the partially specified isometry after every round must admit a completion satisfying these conditions and the ambient-dimension budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transfer is feasible when one isometric embedding and one admissible lifted objective reproduce the complete base transcript while preserving the target class and allowing every adaptive partial embedding to be completed.
assumptions_latex: A base transcript of finite horizon \(T\) is specified.
The target oracle model and objective class are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility requires transcript preservation, global oracle consistency, class preservation, and sufficient dimension simultaneously.

notation.meaning: Single lifted objective consistent with the entire transcript.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the feasibility leaf, but the proposed criterion combines transcript projection, fixed-objective consistency, class preservation, adaptive completion, and dimension feasibility without an authoritative source or a fully specified oracle model.

children.title: Smooth Convex Complexity Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for classical and accelerated smooth convex behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Convex Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal deterministic first-order complexity for unconstrained smooth convex minimization with bounded initial distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(x_\star\in\operatorname{argmin}f\), and suppose \(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R\). In the exact first-order oracle model, accelerated gradient methods produce an iterate \(x_T\) satisfying \[f(x_T)-f(x_\star)\le \frac{2LR^2}{(T+1)^2}.\] Hence \(T=O(\!\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon}\!)\) oracle calls suffice for objective error at most \(\varepsilon\). Over this function class, the worst-case deterministic first-order oracle complexity has matching order \(\Theta(\!\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon}\!)\), subject to the usual dimension budget for the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex minimization has accelerated objective error proportional to LR²/T² and optimal deterministic first-order complexity of order √(LR²/ε).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable with \(\lVert\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\rVert\le L\lVert x-y\rVert\).
\(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R\).
The oracle returns exact function values and gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal worst-case oracle complexity is \(\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).

notation.meaning: Initial distance bound to a minimizer.

children.title: Strongly Convex Complexity Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for condition-sensitive geometric behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition-number-sensitive deterministic complexity for smooth strongly convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(0<\mu\le L\), unique minimizer \(x_\star\), and initial gap \(\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f(x_\star)\). Accelerated first-order methods attain \[f(x_T)-f(x_\star)\le C\Delta_0\exp\!\left(-cT\sqrt{\mu/L}\right)\] for universal constants \(C,c>0\). Thus objective error at most \(\varepsilon\) requires \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon))\) exact first-order calls. Matching resisting-oracle constructions give the same order in the worst case, with an adequate ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth strongly convex minimization has optimal exact first-order complexity proportional to the square root of the condition number times the logarithm of the relative objective accuracy.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with \(0<\mu\le L\).
\(0<\varepsilon<\Delta_0\).
The oracle is exact and deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal worst-case complexity is \(\Theta(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon))\), up to universal constants.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition-number dependence is standard, but no citation is supplied for either the accelerated estimate with the chosen initial-gap normalization or the matching resisting-oracle lower bound. The complete Theta statement therefore lacks required evidence.

children.title: Nonsmooth Complexity Family

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal deterministic first-order complexity for Lipschitz convex objectives on a bounded domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\) be closed and convex, let \(f:Q\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and \(G\)-Lipschitz, and suppose a minimizer \(x_\star\) satisfies \(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R\). Projected subgradient methods can return an averaged iterate \(\bar x_T\) with \[f(\bar x_T)-f(x_\star)\le \frac{GR}{\sqrt{T}}\] up to a universal constant. Therefore \(O(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) subgradient-oracle calls suffice. In the deterministic local first-order oracle model, the worst-case lower bound has the same order when the dimension is sufficiently large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz convex nonsmooth minimization has objective error of order GR/√T and optimal deterministic subgradient complexity of order G²R²/ε².
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and \(G\)-Lipschitz on the feasible region.
\(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R\).
Projection onto \(Q\) is available and not charged as an oracle call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal first-order oracle complexity is \(\Theta(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz bound for the objective, equivalently a subgradient bound under standard domain conditions.
Weighted or uniform average of subgradient iterates.

children.title: Nonconvex Stationarity Complexity Family

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Stationarity Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact-gradient complexity for first-order stationarity of smooth nonconvex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, bounded below by \(f_{\inf}\), and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Put \(\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\). Gradient descent with step \(1/L\) satisfies \[\min_{0\le k<T}\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert^2\le \frac{2L\Delta_0}{T}.\] Consequently, \(T=O(L\Delta_0/\varepsilon^2)\) exact-gradient evaluations suffice to obtain an iterate with \(\lVert\nabla f(x_k)\rVert\le\varepsilon\). For general smooth nonconvex functions, deterministic first-order lower bounds match the \(\varepsilon^{-2}\) dependence under the standard local-oracle and dimension conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth nonconvex objectives, gradient descent finds an ε-stationary point in order LΔ₀/ε² exact-gradient evaluations, and the ε⁻² dependence is worst-case optimal for deterministic first-order methods.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(f_{\inf}>-\infty\).
\(\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}<\infty\).
Stationarity means \(\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic exact-gradient complexity is \(O(L\Delta_0/\varepsilon^2)\), with matching dependence on \(\varepsilon\) in the worst case.

children.title: Full-Gradient Complexity Family

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Gradient Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource convention for deterministic methods querying complete first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\), a full-gradient oracle returns \(\mathcal{O}_f(x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x))\), or only \(\nabla f(x)\) when function values are immaterial. The full-gradient complexity \(N_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)\) of an algorithm is the smallest \(T\) such that, for every objective in the specified class, at most \(T\) adaptive oracle calls guarantee the prescribed \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy criterion. Arithmetic work, projections, proximal operations, and communication are excluded unless the model explicitly charges them; therefore this measure counts information rounds rather than total runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-gradient complexity counts adaptive queries returning the complete exact gradient, with accuracy, function class, and any separately charged computation specified by the oracle model.
assumptions_latex: The objective class and \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy criterion are fixed.
Each query returns exact complete first-order information at one point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{full}}(\varepsilon)\) counts full-gradient oracle calls required for a uniform worst-case guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Sample-Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource convention for fresh-sample or noisy unbiased first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\phi(x;\xi)]\). A stochastic first-order oracle call draws a fresh sample \(\xi_t\) and returns \(g(x_t,\xi_t)\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[g(x_t,\xi_t)\mid x_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\), with a stated variance or moment bound. The stochastic sample complexity \(N_{\mathrm{samp}}(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest number of sample-oracle calls sufficient to meet a specified expected or high-probability \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy criterion uniformly over the objective class. Mini-batch size counts multiplicatively in samples, even when its evaluations occur in one parallel round.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic sample complexity counts fresh noisy first-order samples needed for a stated expected or high-probability accuracy guarantee; every mini-batch element counts as one sample.
assumptions_latex: Samples are fresh under the specified filtration or independence convention.
The oracle bias and moment assumptions are stated explicitly.
The success criterion specifies expectation or confidence level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{samp}}(\varepsilon)\) counts individual stochastic-oracle samples, not merely iterations or parallel rounds.

notation.meaning: Fresh random sample used at interaction t.

children.title: Finite-Sum Component-Complexity Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for component queries, epochs, and data passes.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Component-Complexity Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource convention for indexed component-oracle access to a finite-sum objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\). A component first-order oracle accepts \((x,i)\) and returns \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\), or the gradient alone. The component complexity \(N_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest number of indexed component queries guaranteeing the prescribed \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy uniformly over the finite-sum class. One full gradient computed by visiting all components costs \(n\) component queries, and \(N_{\mathrm{comp}}/n\) is an epoch-equivalent count. This normalization does not identify adaptive sampling, random reshuffling, and with-replacement sampling unless their sampling rules are separately specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum component complexity counts indexed component evaluations; a complete data pass costs n queries, and dividing by n gives an epoch-equivalent count without fixing the sampling protocol.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x)\) with indexed component access.
The accuracy criterion and permitted sampling protocol are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A full component pass costs \(n\) queries, and the epoch-equivalent cost is \(N_{\mathrm{comp}}(\varepsilon)/n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the finite-sum component-complexity leaf, but no source is supplied for the indexed component-oracle model, full-pass normalization, or epoch-equivalent accounting convention. These conventions require an inspectable finite-sum complexity reference.

children.title: Structured Partial-Oracle Complexity Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for coordinate, block, proximal, LMO, subspace, and sketch-aware costs.

children.title: Coordinate–Block Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications for coordinatewise or blockwise information access.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate–Block Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case query complexity when an oracle reveals only one selected coordinate block per call.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) and let \(\{I_1,\ldots,I_m\}\) partition \(\{1,\ldots,d\}\). A coordinate–block first-order oracle queried at \((x,i)\) returns \(f(x)\) and \(\nabla_{I_i}f(x)\), but no unqueried gradient blocks. For an algorithm \(A\), problem class \(\mathcal F\), and accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), its coordinate–block oracle complexity is
\[
N_{\mathrm{cb}}(A,\mathcal F,\varepsilon)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf\{N:\mathbb{E}[f(x_N)-f_f^*]\leq\varepsilon\},
\]
where \(N\) counts block-oracle calls and the expectation covers algorithmic randomness. The optimal complexity is \(N_{\mathrm{cb}}^*(\mathcal F,\varepsilon)=\inf_A N_{\mathrm{cb}}(A,\mathcal F,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate–block complexity is the smallest worst-case number of partial-gradient block queries needed to attain the prescribed expected objective error.
assumptions_latex: \(f_f^*=\inf_x f(x)\) is finite for every \(f\in\mathcal F\).
Each oracle call reveals only the queried gradient block and permitted function information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{cb}}^*(\mathcal F,\varepsilon)\) measures optimal block-oracle query complexity at expected accuracy \(\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the coordinate–block oracle-complexity leaf, but no citation supports the particular information rule, function-value access, randomness convention, or optimal-complexity formulation. An authoritative locator defining the oracle model and its query accounting is required.

children.title: Proximal–LMO Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications for proximal or linear-minimization interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal–LMO Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-resource complexity for composite constrained optimization with proximal and linear-minimization oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x\in C}\{f(x)+g(x)\}\), where \(C\) is closed and convex. A proximal oracle for \(g\) returns \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda g}(v)=\arg\min_x\{g(x)+\|x-v\|^2/(2\lambda)\}\), while a linear-minimization oracle for \(C\) returns an element of \(\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle c,s\rangle\). For an algorithm \(A\), the proximal–LMO complexity at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is the worst-case resource pair
\[
\bigl(N_{\mathrm{prox}}(A,\varepsilon),N_{\mathrm{LMO}}(A,\varepsilon)\bigr)
\]
required to output \(x\) satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[f(x)+g(x)-F^*]\leq\varepsilon\). Comparisons between algorithms use componentwise order or an explicitly specified scalar cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal–LMO complexity records separately how many proximal and linear-minimization calls are needed to reach a target composite-objective error.
assumptions_latex: \(C\neq\varnothing\), and both displayed oracle subproblems attain solutions.
\(F^*=\inf_{x\in C}(f(x)+g(x))\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resource requirement is a two-dimensional oracle-count vector, not a single count unless costs are aggregated explicitly.

children.title: Subspace–Sketch Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity classifications for subspace-restricted or sketch-based information access.

knowledge_statements.title: Subspace–Sketch Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query complexity for randomized first-order information restricted to sampled or prescribed subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\). A subspace–sketch oracle queried with \((x,S)\), where \(S\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times q}\), returns information such as \(S^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x)\); the full gradient is unavailable unless \(\operatorname{range}(S)=\mathbb{R}^d\). For an admissible sketch distribution \(\mathcal D\), algorithm \(A\), and problem class \(\mathcal F\), define
\[
N_{\mathrm{sk}}(A,\mathcal F,\varepsilon;\mathcal D)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf\{N:\mathbb{E}[f(x_N)-f_f^*]\leq\varepsilon\}.
\]
The count \(N\) is the number of sketch-oracle calls; sketch dimension, sampling law, adaptivity, and any cost of forming \(S^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x)\) are part of the oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subspace–sketch complexity counts restricted projected-gradient queries, with the sketch distribution, dimension, and accuracy expectation fixed as part of the model.
assumptions_latex: Each \(S_k\) is drawn or selected according to the admissible model \(\mathcal D\).
The expectation includes sketch and algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{sk}}\) is meaningful only relative to a specified sketch model and per-query information rule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but “information such as” does not specify a unique oracle output, and no source supports the selected sketch model, sampling convention, adaptivity, or cost accounting. These choices materially determine the complexity notion.

children.title: Distributed Resource Complexity Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for adaptive rounds, network rounds, and message complexity.

children.title: Parallel-Round Complexity
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound classifications by adaptive parallel rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Round Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case number of synchronous adaptive rounds, allowing simultaneous oracle queries within each round.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a synchronous parallel first-order model, round \(t\) submits a batch \(Q_t=\{q_{t,1},\ldots,q_{t,b_t}\}\) whose queries may depend on all replies from rounds \(1,\ldots,t-1\), but not on replies within round \(t\). For algorithm \(A\), problem class \(\mathcal F\), and accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), the parallel-round complexity is
\[
R_{\parallel}(A,\mathcal F,\varepsilon)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf\{T:\mathbb{E}[f(x_T)-f_f^*]\leq\varepsilon\}.
\]
The definition must be accompanied by a bound on batch sizes \(b_t\), worker count, or total oracle calls; otherwise unbounded parallel querying can make round complexity degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel-round complexity counts sequential synchronization stages, while permitting bounded batches of simultaneous queries inside each stage.
assumptions_latex: Queries within a round are conditionally nonadaptive given the transcript of earlier rounds.
The permitted batch size or worker budget is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\parallel}\) measures adaptive depth rather than the total number of oracle evaluations.

notation.meaning: batch of queries in round t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its distinction between adaptive depth and query count fit the terminal container. However, no authoritative locator supports the synchronous batch model or the required worker, batch-size, or total-query restriction, all of which are essential to a nondegenerate round-complexity definition.

children.title: Communication Complexity
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound classifications by network rounds, messages, or bits.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case communicated information required by a distributed optimization protocol to attain prescribed accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let data be distributed among \(p\) parties connected by a specified communication network. For a protocol \(A\) and instance \(f\), let \(B_A(f)\) be the total number of transmitted bits, or let \(W_A(f)\) be the total number of transmitted scalar words under a fixed precision convention. For problem class \(\mathcal F\), communication complexity at accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is
\[
C_{\mathrm{comm}}(A,\mathcal F,\varepsilon)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf\{B_A(f):\mathbb{E}[f(\widehat x)-f_f^*]\leq\varepsilon\}.
\]
The network topology, message precision, broadcast accounting, and output location are part of the model and cannot be suppressed when comparing bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication complexity is the worst-case transmitted-bit or transmitted-word cost of producing an optimization solution with the required expected error.
assumptions_latex: The data allocation and communication graph are fixed by the problem model.
Messages have a specified bit or word accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}\) quantifies communication volume independently of local arithmetic unless a joint cost is declared.

notation.meaning: bits transmitted by protocol A on instance f

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but the displayed infimum is not a well-formed minimization of communication for a fixed protocol: \(B_A(f)\) is already a resource value, so the set is merely a singleton or empty unless an additional varying budget, transcript, or protocol is introduced. An authoritative communication model is also needed to settle random resource costs, precision, topology, and output conventions.

children.title: Parallel–Communication Resource Interaction
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes when parallelism and communication are jointly constrained.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel–Communication Resource Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of simultaneous round, communication, and local-oracle requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a distributed problem class \(\mathcal F\) and accuracy \(\varepsilon\), define the achievable resource region
\[
\mathcal R_\varepsilon(\mathcal F)=\left\{(T,B,N)\in\mathbb N^3:\exists A\ \forall f\in\mathcal F,\ \mathbb{E}[f(\widehat x_A)-f_f^*]\leq\varepsilon,\ R_A(f)\leq T,\ B_A(f)\leq B,\ N_A(f)\leq N\right\}.
\]
Here \(T\), \(B\), and \(N\) count synchronous rounds, communicated bits, and local oracle calls. The parallel–communication interaction is represented by the Pareto-minimal boundary of \(\mathcal R_\varepsilon(\mathcal F)\). A scalar complexity is obtained only after specifying a monotone cost function \(c(T,B,N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint distributed complexity is a Pareto frontier of rounds, transmitted bits, and local oracle calls, unless an explicit scalar cost combines them.
assumptions_latex: All protocols use the same network, precision, and oracle conventions.
Resource bounds hold uniformly over \(f\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pareto-minimal elements of \(\mathcal R_\varepsilon(\mathcal F)\) express tradeoffs that separate round and communication complexity alone cannot capture.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A Pareto resource region is an appropriate representation for this interaction leaf. No source supports this particular three-resource model, however, and for randomized protocols the record does not state whether the bounds on rounds, bits, and oracle calls hold almost surely, in expectation, or with high probability.

children.title: Lower-Bound Matching Method Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Maps lower-bound classes to method families establishing sharpness while leaving method mechanics to their owning chapters.

children.title: Smooth Method Matching Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for smooth convex and strongly convex matching families.

children.title: Gradient-Method Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships between gradient methods and smooth convex lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Method Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonaccelerated smooth-convex rate associated with fixed-step gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(x^*\in\arg\min f\), and suppose \(\|x_0-x^*\|\leq R\). Gradient descent with
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)
\]
satisfies
\[
f(x_k)-f(x^*)\leq \frac{L R^2}{2k}.
\]
Consequently, \(k\geq L R^2/(2\varepsilon)\) gradient evaluations suffice for objective error at most \(\varepsilon\). Quadratic instances give an \(\Omega(LR^2/k)\) worst-case error for this fixed-step gradient method, so its characteristic query dependence is \(\Theta(LR^2/\varepsilon)\), up to universal constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-step gradient descent has the characteristic nonaccelerated smooth-convex complexity proportional to L times squared initial distance divided by target error.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable with \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|\).
A minimizer \(x^*\) exists and \(\|x_0-x^*\|\leq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{GD}}(\varepsilon)=\Theta(LR^2/\varepsilon)\) for the stated fixed-step gradient method in worst case.

notation.meaning: gradient evaluations used by gradient descent

children.title: Acceleration Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships between accelerated families and improved smooth-regime rates.

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-optimal accelerated rate for smooth convex minimization in the deterministic first-order model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(x^*\in\arg\min f\), and suppose \(\|x_0-x^*\|\leq R\). An accelerated gradient method produces \(x_k\) satisfying
\[
f(x_k)-f(x^*)\leq \frac{C L R^2}{(k+1)^2}
\]
for a universal constant \(C\). Thus \(O(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) first-order oracle calls suffice. In the deterministic black-box model and dimension sufficiently large relative to \(k\), smooth convex instances force error \(\Omega(LR^2/(k+1)^2)\); hence the optimal complexity is \(\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Acceleration matches the smooth-convex first-order lower bound, reducing the error dependence from inverse epsilon to inverse square root epsilon.
assumptions_latex: The oracle returns exact function values and gradients.
The dimension is unrestricted or sufficiently large for the lower-bound construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N^*(\varepsilon)=\Theta(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) for deterministic smooth convex first-order optimization.

children.title: Restart Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships between restart families and curvature-sensitive complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Restart Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Periodic restart converts an accelerated convex rate into a linear strongly convex rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex, with \(0<\mu\leq L\), and set \(\kappa=L/\mu\). Suppose an accelerated method reduces the objective gap by a fixed factor whenever it is run for \(m=\lceil c\sqrt\kappa\rceil\) iterations, where \(c>0\) is universal. Restarting after every \(m\) iterations yields
\[
f(x_N)-f(x^*)\leq \rho^{\lfloor N/m\rfloor}\bigl(f(x_0)-f(x^*)\bigr)
\]
for some universal \(\rho\in(0,1)\). Therefore \(N=O(\sqrt\kappa\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon))\) gradient calls suffice, matching the deterministic strongly convex first-order lower bound up to constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restarting acceleration every order-square-root condition-number steps gives the optimal logarithmic strongly convex complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
The restart period uses a valid estimate of \(\kappa=L/\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N^*(\varepsilon)=\Theta(\sqrt\kappa\log(\Delta_0/\varepsilon))\) under the stated deterministic oracle model.

notation.meaning: condition number L divided by mu

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits restart correspondence, but neither the assumed fixed-factor contraction after \(O(\sqrt\kappa)\) iterations nor the matching lower bound has a source. The logarithmic formula also requires a convention such as \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta_0\) or a positive-part logarithm.

children.title: Nonsmooth Universal Method Matching Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for nonsmooth, stochastic, and intermediate-regularity matching families.

children.title: Subgradient Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships for subgradient-limited lower-bound regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal Lipschitz nonsmooth convex rate realized by projected subgradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex with subgradients satisfying \(\|g\|\leq G\). Suppose \(x^*\in\arg\min_C f\) and \(\|x_0-x^*\|\leq R\). Projected subgradient iterations
\[
x_{k+1}=\Pi_C(x_k-\alpha g_k),\qquad \alpha=\frac{R}{G\sqrt N},
\]
and the average \(\bar x_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x_k\) satisfy \(f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\leq GR/\sqrt N\). Hence \(N=O(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\), matching the nonsmooth first-order oracle lower bound up to constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected subgradient descent attains the optimal nonsmooth Lipschitz complexity proportional to the inverse square of objective accuracy.
assumptions_latex: Every queried subgradient has norm at most \(G\).
A minimizer exists within distance \(R\) of \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N^*(\varepsilon)=\Theta(G^2R^2/\varepsilon^2)\) in the deterministic Lipschitz convex first-order model.

children.title: Mirror-Method Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships for geometry-aware deterministic or stochastic regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror-Method Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry-adapted nonsmooth complexity realized by mirror descent with a strongly convex reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex, let \(h:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(1\)-strongly convex with respect to a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and suppose \(D_h(x^*,x_0)\leq D\). If \(f\) is convex and each selected subgradient satisfies \(\|g_k\|_*\leq G\), mirror descent
\[
x_{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in C}\left\{\alpha\langle g_k,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_k)\right\},\qquad \alpha=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{G\sqrt N},
\]
obeys \(f(\bar x_N)-f(x^*)\leq G\sqrt{2D/N}\). Thus \(N=O(G^2D/\varepsilon^2)\), with geometry encoded by the dual norm and Bregman radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror descent realizes the nonsmooth inverse-square accuracy rate while replacing Euclidean radius by a geometry-adapted Bregman radius.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and \(1\)-strongly convex in the chosen norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{MD}}(\varepsilon)=O(G^2D/\varepsilon^2)\) for the stated mirror-descent geometry.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The geometry-adapted mirror-descent bound fits the correspondence leaf, but no source is supplied. The statement also fails to declare \(x^*\in\arg\min_C f\) and does not define \(\bar x_N\), both of which are needed for the displayed objective bound.

u\in[0,1]\) and \(M_

children.title: Composite Splitting Method Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Navigation for composite and operator-oracle matching families.

children.title: Proximal Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships for composite problems with proximal access.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accelerated proximal-gradient matching for convex composite minimization in the gradient-plus-proximal oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=f+h\) on a Hilbert space, where \(f\) is convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(h\) is proper, closed, and convex, and \(x_0\) satisfies \(\|x_0-x^\star\|\le R\) for some minimizer \(x^\star\). In the oracle model returning \(\nabla f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}(v)\), accelerated proximal-gradient schemes attain \[F(x_k)-F(x^\star)\le \frac{2LR^2}{(k+1)^2}.\] Thus \(O(\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon})\) oracle rounds suffice for objective error at most \(\varepsilon\); this rate has the same dependence on \(L\), \(R\), and \(\varepsilon\) as the smooth first-order lower bound inherited by setting \(h=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated proximal gradient needs order square-root of LR²/ε gradient–proximal rounds, matching the smooth convex lower-bound dependence because the composite class contains the smooth subclass.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(h\) is proper, closed, convex, and its proximal map is available.
\(F\) has a minimizer \(x^\star\) with \(\|x_0-x^\star\|\le R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon=O(\!\sqrt{LR^2/\varepsilon}\!)\), with matching parameter dependence in the stated oracle model.

Number of gradient–proximal oracle rounds needed for error ε.

children.title: Splitting Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships for operator-splitting problem structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Splitting Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-preserving correspondence between qualified convex composite minimization and monotone-operator splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a Hilbert space and let \(f,h:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex. Assume a qualification ensuring \(\partial(f+h)=\partial f+\partial h\), for example that \(f\) is continuous at some point of \(\operatorname{dom}h\). Then \(x^\star\) minimizes \(f+h\) if and only if \(0\in\partial f(x^\star)+\partial h(x^\star)\). For every \(\gamma>0\), \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}=J_{\gamma\partial f}\) and \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}=J_{\gamma\partial h}\). Hence an iteration using only these proximal evaluations has the same oracle transcript and call count when written as the corresponding resolvent-splitting iteration. A complexity bound transfers without changing the counted oracle resource when the same accuracy measure and tolerance are used; quantitatively equivalent but different accuracy measures require the corresponding tolerance conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a subdifferential sum-rule qualification, convex composite minimization is equivalent to its subdifferential inclusion. Proximal calls are exactly the corresponding resolvent calls, so call counts transfer directly when the same accuracy measure is used and otherwise transfer after an explicit tolerance conversion.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a Hilbert space, and \(f\) and \(h\) are proper, lower-semicontinuous, and convex on \(\mathcal H\).
A qualification ensuring \(\partial(f+h)=\partial f+\partial h\) holds.
The compared algorithms use only the identified proximal or resolvent evaluations, and their accuracy measures and tolerances are explicitly identified or quantitatively translated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Proximal-call complexity for \(\min_x f(x)+h(x)\) transfers to resolvent-call complexity for \(0\in\partial f(x)+\partial h(x)\) with the same call count under identical accuracy conventions.

notation.meaning: Proximal map of f with parameter γ.

children.title: Composite–Operator Oracle Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Boundaries governing comparisons between composite and operator-oracle regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite–Operator Oracle Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate for transferring complexity between composite objectives and monotone inclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A composite formulation \(\min_x f(x)+h(x)\) and an operator formulation \(0\in A(x)+B(x)\) are oracle-compatible when \(A=\partial f\), \(B=\partial h\), and every primitive call counted in one model is implementable by at most a constant number of primitive calls in the other. In the fully proximal case this requires \(J_{\gamma A}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma f}\) and \(J_{\gamma B}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}\); in the forward–backward case, \(A=\nabla f\) must be queried by a gradient call while \(J_{\gamma B}=\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma h}\). Accuracy measures must also be mutually bounded with stated constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations are compatible when their gradient, proximal, or resolvent primitives simulate one another at constant cost and their accuracy measures are quantitatively comparable.
assumptions_latex: The formulations are linked by \(A=\partial f\) and \(B=\partial h\), with \(A=\nabla f\) when f is differentiable.
Primitive oracle calls and the accuracy measures are fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each formulation simulates the other's oracle transcript with constant-factor overhead, permitting complexity comparison after translating accuracy.

notation.meaning: Resolvent of A at scale γ.

children.title: Variance-Reduction Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Navigation for finite-sum matching families.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduction Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum strongly convex matching in the randomized incremental first-order oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), where every \(f_i\) is convex and \(L\)-smooth and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex. In the randomized incremental oracle model, one query selects \(i\) and returns \((f_i(x),\nabla f_i(x))\). Variance-reduced accelerated methods attain expected component-oracle complexity \[O\!\left(\left(n+\sqrt{nL/\mu}\right)\log\frac{F(x_0)-F^\star}{\varepsilon}\right)\] for \(\mathbb{E}[F(x)-F^\star]\le\varepsilon\). This dependence matches the standard randomized finite-sum lower bound up to universal constants in the usual regime and oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated variance reduction solves smooth strongly convex finite sums in order (n plus square-root nκ) log(1/ε) component-gradient queries, matching the standard randomized lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(F=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
Queries use the randomized incremental first-order oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon=O((n+\sqrt{nL/\mu})\log((F(x_0)-F^\star)/\varepsilon))\) component-oracle calls.

notation.meaning: Condition number of the finite-sum problem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-sum rate and matching claim depend on the precise incremental oracle, admissible randomization, component assumptions, and parameter regime. With no cited upper- or lower-bound source, the mathematical version of the correspondence cannot be verified.

children.title: Specialized Oracle Method Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Navigation for specialized-oracle matching families.

children.title: Conditional-Gradient Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships for linear-minimization-oracle lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Gradient Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-free smooth convex optimization under a linear minimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be compact and convex with diameter at most \(D\), and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. A conditional-gradient iteration queries \(\nabla f(x_k)\), obtains \(s_k\in\arg\min_{s\in C}\langle\nabla f(x_k),s\rangle\), and sets \(x_{k+1}=(1-\gamma_k)x_k+\gamma_k s_k\). With the standard diminishing steps, it achieves \(f(x_k)-f^\star=O(LD^2/k)\), hence \(O(LD^2/\varepsilon)\) gradient and linear-minimization calls. For the general smooth convex class in this oracle model, the \(1/\varepsilon\) dependence is lower-bound matched.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional gradient reaches ε objective error in order LD²/ε gradient and linear-minimization calls; this ε-dependence is sharp for the general projection-free oracle model.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and has diameter at most \(D\).
\(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(C\).
A linear minimization oracle over \(C\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon=O(LD^2/\varepsilon)\) paired gradient–linear-minimization rounds, with matched \(1/\varepsilon\) dependence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard conditional-gradient upper rate is plausible, but the sharp lower-bound statement is model-sensitive and unsupported. Authoritative sources must establish both the upper bound and the claimed lower bound for the same gradient-plus-linear-minimization oracle and feasible-set class.

children.title: Coordinate-Method Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships for coordinate or block information limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Method Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accelerated randomized coordinate matching under coordinate-wise smoothness and strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly convex in the Euclidean norm, and suppose coordinate \(i\) has Lipschitz constant \(L_i\). In an oracle call, an algorithm chooses one coordinate and observes the corresponding partial derivative. Accelerated randomized coordinate methods admit the bound \[O\!\left(\frac{\sum_{i=1}^d\sqrt{L_i}}{\sqrt{\mu}}\log\frac{f(x_0)-f^\star}{\varepsilon}\right)\] coordinate-derivative queries for expected objective error at most \(\varepsilon\). Under the corresponding randomized coordinate-oracle lower-bound model, this parameter dependence is the candidate matching rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated coordinate methods use order (sum of square-root coordinate smoothnesses)/square-root strong convexity times log(1/ε) coordinate queries in the stated model.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and \(\mu\)-strongly convex in the Euclidean norm.
Each coordinate derivative has coordinate-wise Lipschitz constant \(L_i\).
Each oracle call returns one chosen partial derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_\varepsilon=O((\sum_i\sqrt{L_i/\mu})\log((f(x_0)-f^\star)/\varepsilon))\) coordinate queries.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sum-of-square-roots rate varies with the norm defining strong convexity, coordinate smoothness conventions, sampling distribution, and whether coordinates are selected adaptively or randomly. No source fixes those conventions or supports the matching lower-bound claim.

children.title: Distributed-Method Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Matching relationships for network and communication lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed-Method Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Candidate decentralized smooth strongly convex rate separating optimization and network conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(F(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)\) over a connected undirected network, where every \(f_i\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(F\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex. Let \(W\) be a symmetric gossip matrix and let \(\chi\) denote its network condition number. In a model counting local-gradient rounds and neighbor-communication rounds separately, optimally accelerated decentralized methods target \[O\!\left(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\] gradient rounds and \[O\!\left(\sqrt{\chi L/\mu}\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)\] communication rounds. A sharp correspondence requires lower bounds in exactly the same synchrony, topology, and oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accelerated decentralized methods target square-root objective conditioning gradient rounds and an additional square-root network-conditioning factor in communication rounds, subject to a matched model.
assumptions_latex: The communication graph is connected, undirected, and represented by a symmetric gossip matrix \(W\).
Local objectives are \(L\)-smooth and their average is \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
Computation and communication rounds are counted separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Candidate rates are \(O(\sqrt{L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) gradient rounds and \(O(\sqrt{\chi L/\mu}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) communication rounds.

notation.meaning: Network condition number determined by the nontrivial spectrum of W.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated gradient and communication rates are highly sensitive to the definition of the gossip matrix and network condition number, synchrony, communication primitive, local objective assumptions, and output criterion. Those details and both matching bounds require authoritative sources.

children.title: Optimality Statuses
children.top_down_role: Classifies the structural status of lower and upper complexity comparisons.

children.title: Sharply Matched Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for coincident lower and upper complexity families.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharply Matched Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact asymptotic coincidence of lower and upper oracle complexity after fixing the problem and oracle models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem class \(\mathcal{P}\), oracle model \(\mathcal{O}\), accuracy criterion \(E\le\varepsilon\), and parameter vector \(\theta\). Let \(L(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be a valid minimax lower bound and \(U(\theta,\varepsilon)\) the complexity of a specified method. The regime is sharply matched on a domain \(\mathcal{D}\) when there exist universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of \((\theta,\varepsilon)\in\mathcal{D}\), such that \[cL(\theta,\varepsilon)\le U(\theta,\varepsilon)\le CL(\theta,\varepsilon).\] Oracle calls, success probability, initialization, and all normalized parameters must use the same conventions in both bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is sharply matched when a method’s upper complexity and the minimax lower bound differ only by universal constant factors under identical conventions.
assumptions_latex: The problem class, oracle, accuracy criterion, and parameter domain \(\mathcal{D}\) are fixed.
Lower and upper bounds count the same resource and use the same success convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U(\theta,\varepsilon)=\Theta(L(\theta,\varepsilon))\) uniformly on \(\mathcal{D}\).

notation.meaning: Parameter and accuracy regime under comparison.

children.title: Secondary-Factor Gaps
children.top_down_role: Navigation for logarithmic, dimension, probability, or accounting discrepancies.

knowledge_statements.title: Secondary-Factor Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconstant but explicitly designated secondary discrepancies between normalized lower and upper complexity bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a parameter domain \(\mathcal D\) and positive comparable bounds \(0<L(\theta,\varepsilon)\le U(\theta,\varepsilon)\) obtained in the same problem and oracle model. Define \(G(\theta,[0m\varepsilon)=U(\theta,\varepsilon)/L(\theta,\varepsilon)\). A secondary-factor gap occurs on \(\mathcal D\) when \(G\) is not uniformly bounded by a universal constant but there are a universal constant \(C<\infty\) and a declared factor \(q(\theta,\varepsilon)\ge 1\) such that \[G(\theta,\varepsilon)\le Cq(\theta,\varepsilon)\] throughout \(\mathcal D\), where \(q\) contains only discrepancies classified as secondary by the taxonomy, such as specified logarithmic, confidence, dimension, or non-universal accounting factors. After suppressing \(q\), the dependence on every parameter declared principal must be sharply matched; a discrepancy in a principal exponent or other principal scaling is not secondary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A secondary-factor gap is a genuinely nonconstant discrepancy that is bounded by an explicitly designated logarithmic, confidence, dimension, or accounting factor, while all principal parameter dependences remain matched.
assumptions_latex: The comparison domain \(\mathcal D\) is fixed, and \(0<L(\theta,\varepsilon)\le U(\theta,\varepsilon)\) throughout that domain.
Lower and upper bounds use the same problem class, oracle, counted resource, accuracy criterion, and success convention.
Principal parameters and the admissible secondary factor \(q(\theta,\varepsilon)\ge 1\) are declared before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ratio \(U(\theta,\varepsilon)/L(\theta,\varepsilon)\) is not uniformly \(O(1)\) but is \(O(q(\theta,\varepsilon))\), with only taxonomy-designated secondary dependence in \(q\).

notation.meaning: Parameter and accuracy domain of comparison.
Declared secondary discrepancy factor, bounded below by one.

children.title: Structural Open Gaps
children.top_down_role: Navigation for unresolved lower–upper separations that persist after normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural Open Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent lower–upper separations not attributable to declared secondary factors or incompatible conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(\theta,\varepsilon)>0\) and \(U(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be the best established compatible lower and upper complexity bounds after aligning the problem class, oracle, counted resource, success probability, initialization convention, and accuracy criterion. The regime has a structural open gap when the ratio \(U(\theta,\varepsilon)/L(\theta,\varepsilon)\) cannot be bounded, on the stated domain, by a universal constant times any discrepancy factor designated secondary by the taxonomy, and no established theorem closes the separation. The residual discrepancy must alter a dependence that the taxonomy declares principal, such as an accuracy, conditioning, connectivity, or oracle-strength exponent or scaling. This label records the current unresolved status and does not assert that matching is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural open gap remains after conventions and all taxonomy-designated secondary factors are normalized, and it changes a dependence declared principal. It records an unresolved status rather than impossibility.
assumptions_latex: The lower bound \(L(\theta,\varepsilon)\) is positive on the comparison domain.
The compared lower and upper bounds use compatible classes, oracles, resources, initialization, success, and accuracy conventions.
All factors designated secondary by the taxonomy have been identified before the residual gap is classified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual ratio \(U(\theta,\varepsilon)/L(\theta,\varepsilon)\) contains an unresolved dependence declared principal by the taxonomy.

notation.meaning: Best established positive compatible lower bound.
