knowledge_statements.title: Known Regularity Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonadaptive oracle-complexity regime with sufficient regularity information supplied to the method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P(\theta)\) be a problem class indexed by regularity parameters \(\theta\), such as a Lipschitz constant, smoothness constant, strong-convexity modulus, or Hölder exponent. A component of \(\theta\) is known to an algorithm when the algorithm is supplied, before its first decision that uses that component, with its exact value or with a certified bound having the direction and precision required by the stated tuning rule. Step sizes, momentum coefficients, smoothing levels, restart periods, and stopping thresholds may depend on this supplied information. The resulting complexity \(N(\theta,[0m\varepsilon)\) may depend explicitly on the actual regularity and on any declared quality of the supplied bounds. Parameters irrelevant to every algorithmic decision need not be classified as known.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularity parameter is known when the method receives its exact value or a sufficiently informative certified bound before making any decision that uses it. The complexity may depend on the actual regularity and on the quality of the supplied bound.
assumptions_latex: A regularity-indexed problem class \(\mathcal P(\theta)\) and an oracle model are fixed.
The algorithmic decisions that may use each component of \(\theta\), and the acceptable direction and precision of any supplied bound, are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method may use the supplied regularity information directly and is evaluated by the resulting bound \(N(\theta,\varepsilon)\), including any declared dependence on the quality of that information.

notation.meaning: Vector of actual regularity parameters relevant to the algorithm.
Problem class indexed by the regularity vector θ.
Oracle complexity at target accuracy ε.

children.title: Unknown Regularity Parameters

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Regularity Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive oracle-complexity regime in which tuning constants are withheld from the method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{P}(\theta)\) be indexed by regularity parameters \(\theta\). The unknown-parameter regime holds when the algorithm is not given one or more components of \(\theta\) before execution and may learn about them only through the permitted oracle transcript and verifiable tests. Its update and stopping rules must be measurable functions of the transcript, target accuracy, declared side information, and internal randomness, but not of the withheld values. Complexity is evaluated pointwise or uniformly as \(N_{\mathrm{ad}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\) over instances that actually possess regularity \(\theta\), including all oracle calls used for estimation, backtracking, or restart.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter is unknown when it is withheld and tuning may depend only on permitted observations; all adaptation, backtracking, and restart queries count toward complexity.
assumptions_latex: A regularity-indexed class \(\mathcal{P}(\theta)\), oracle, and allowed side information are fixed.
At least one algorithmically relevant component of \(\theta\) is withheld.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adaptive method's decisions exclude direct dependence on withheld \(\theta\), and \(N_{\mathrm{ad}}(\theta,\varepsilon)\) counts all adaptation overhead.

children.title: Regularity-Adaptation Gap
children.top_down_role: Complexity differences attributable to unknown regularity information.

knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Adaptation Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the multiplicative oracle-complexity price of not knowing the objective's regularity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\mathcal F_\alpha:\alpha\in A\}\) be regularity classes and let \(N_\alpha^\star(\varepsilon)\) be the minimax first-order oracle complexity when \(\alpha\) is known. For an algorithm \(M\) not given \(\alpha\), let \(N_M(\alpha,\varepsilon)\) be its worst-case complexity on \(\mathcal F_\alpha\). Its regularity-adaptation gap is \[G_M(\varepsilon)=\sup_{\alpha\in A}\frac{N_M(\alpha,\varepsilon)}{N_\alpha^\star(\varepsilon)}.\] The optimal gap is \(G^\star(\varepsilon)=\inf_M G_M(\varepsilon)\), where the infimum ranges over algorithms using the prescribed oracle without receiving \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gap is the worst-case ratio between an adaptive method's complexity and the class-specific minimax complexity available when regularity is known.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(N_\alpha^\star(\varepsilon)>0\) for every \(\alpha\in A\).
All algorithms are compared under the same first-order oracle and accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G^\star(\varepsilon)=\inf_M\sup_{\alpha\in A}N_M(\alpha,\varepsilon)/N_\alpha^\star(\varepsilon)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Known Noise Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic first-order regime in which quantitative oracle-noise bounds are supplied before optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a class of objectives \(f\), suppose a stochastic first-order oracle returns \(G(x,\xi)\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|G(x,\xi)-\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\|_*^2\mid x]\leq \sigma^2\). The known-noise-parameter regime means that the valid value \(\sigma\), together with any declared tail or bias parameters, is supplied to the algorithm before its first query. Stepsizes, batch sizes, and stopping rules may therefore depend explicitly on these parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm receives valid variance, tail, or bias bounds before querying the stochastic oracle and may tune all controls using them.
assumptions_latex: The oracle model and the norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\) are fixed.
The announced noise bounds hold uniformly over all admissible query points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithmic policy may depend on \(\sigma\) and every other announced noise parameter.

notation.meaning: subdifferential of the objective at the query point

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Noise Parameters
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic regime requiring tuning without numerical noise bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stochastic oracle conditions \(\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\in\partial f(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|G(x,\xi)-\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]\|_*^2\mid x]\leq \sigma^2<\infty\), the unknown-noise-parameter regime withholds \(\sigma\) and any declared tail or bias constants from the algorithm. Every query, stepsize, batch size, and stopping decision must be measurable with respect to past oracle observations and internal randomness, but not these hidden parameters. Performance is nevertheless evaluated separately for each admissible value of the hidden parameters.

Performance uses the same stochastic-oracle and accuracy conventions as the corresponding known-parameter benchmark.

children.title: Known Horizon

knowledge_statements.title: Known Horizon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-query regime in which the terminal query budget is announced in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a stochastic or deterministic first-order oracle and a query budget \(T\in\mathbb N\). In the known-horizon regime, \(T\) is supplied before the first oracle call. The algorithm may choose time-dependent parameters \(\eta_t(T)\), averaging weights, restarts, and batch allocations using \(T\), makes at most \(T\) calls, and returns a designated output \(\widehat x_T\). A complexity guarantee is assessed at this announced terminal time rather than requiring one parameter schedule to work simultaneously at every stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The final query budget is announced beforehand, so schedules, averaging, restarts, and sampling allocations may depend on it.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\) is fixed before any oracle observation.
Oracle calls are counted under a specified first-order oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(\widehat x_T\) and the policy generating it may depend explicitly on \(T\).

children.title: Unknown Horizon
children.top_down_role: Anytime complexity when the optimization horizon is not specified in advance.

knowledge_statements.title: Unknown Horizon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anytime regime in which stopping may occur without an advance terminal budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unknown-horizon regime, an algorithm generates outputs \((\widehat x_t)_{t\geq1}\) without being given a terminal budget. Its query and update rule at time \(t\) may depend only on \(t\), past oracle observations, and internal randomness. For every admissible stopping horizon \(T\), the prefix of length \(T\) must define a valid output \(\widehat x_T\) satisfying the stated performance guarantee. Thus a single policy, rather than a separately tuned policy for each \(T\), is evaluated across all horizons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One anytime policy must produce a valid output and guarantee at every possible stopping horizon without knowing the terminal budget.
assumptions_latex: Stopping does not reveal future oracle observations.
The guarantee specifies whether \(T\) is deterministic, data-dependent, or a stopping time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every admissible \(T\), the same horizon-independent policy returns \(\widehat x_T\) with the claimed guarantee.

notation.meaning: anytime output after t oracle calls

children.title: Adaptivity Cost-Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Navigation for unavoidable costs of simultaneous or parameter-free adaptation.

children.title: Adaptivity Overhead
children.top_down_role: Unavoidable complexity costs associated with parameter-free or adaptive guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the extra oracle cost relative to a benchmark supplied with hidden instance parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\in\Theta\) index problem parameters, let \(N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be the minimax oracle complexity when \(\theta\) is known, and let \(N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be the worst-case complexity of a single algorithm \(M\) that is not given \(\theta\). The multiplicative adaptivity overhead of \(M\) is \[H_M(\varepsilon)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\frac{N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)}{N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)}.\] An additive overhead may instead be recorded as \(A_M(\varepsilon)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}(N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)-N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon))\), under the same oracle and success criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptivity overhead compares one parameter-free algorithm with the minimax benchmark that may tune itself using the true parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)>0\) for each compared \(\theta\).
Adaptive and informed methods use identical oracle, accuracy, and success-probability conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimal multiplicative overhead is \(H^\star(\varepsilon)=\inf_M H_M(\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: hidden instance parameter or parameter vector

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas define multiplicative and additive overheads rather than state a complexity bound. A source is also required for the selected normalization and benchmark conventions; `definition` would better describe the record's mathematical role.

children.title: Adaptivity Impossibility
children.top_down_role: Regimes where the requested adaptive guarantee cannot be attained.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptivity Impossibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal boundary where no single parameter-blind method uniformly matches informed minimax complexities within a constant factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\mathcal F_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\) be problem classes with informed minimax complexities \(N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)>0\), and let \(N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be the worst-case oracle complexity of a single algorithm \(M\) that is not given \(\theta\). Constant-factor adaptation is impossible if \[\inf_{M}\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\frac{N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)}{N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)}=\infty,\] where each algorithm \(M\) is fixed across all \(\theta\) and \(\varepsilon\). Equivalently, for every such \(M\) and every \(C<\infty\), there exist \(\theta\in\Theta\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) for which \(N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)>C N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-factor adaptation is impossible when every single parameter-blind algorithm has an unbounded worst-case complexity ratio over the joint parameter and accuracy range.
assumptions_latex: \(N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)>0\) for every compared \(\theta\in\Theta\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
The informed and uninformed procedures use the same oracle, error criterion, and success criterion.
Each algorithm \(M\) is one policy fixed independently of \(\theta\) and used across the compared accuracies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_M\sup_{\varepsilon>0,\,\theta\in\Theta}N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)/N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)=\infty\).

notation.meaning: problem class indexed by the hidden parameter
worst-case complexity of the parameter-blind algorithm on the indexed class

children.title: Simultaneous-Adaptation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on adapting to multiple unknown problem features at once.

knowledge_statements.title: Simultaneous-Adaptation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates parameter collections admitting one near-optimal method from collections that do not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k)\in\Theta\) index several unknown features and let \(N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)\) be the fully informed minimax complexity. A family is simultaneously adaptable with overhead \(h\) if one algorithm \(M\), given none of the coordinates of \(\theta\), satisfies \(N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)\leq h(\theta,\varepsilon)N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon)\) for every \(\theta\) and \(\varepsilon\). The simultaneous-adaptation boundary is crossed when each coordinate can be adapted to separately, but no single algorithm achieves the prescribed overhead uniformly over their joint parameter space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The boundary occurs when separate adaptation to individual unknown features is possible but their joint informed benchmark cannot be matched uniformly.
assumptions_latex: All componentwise and joint comparisons use the same oracle and risk criterion.
The allowed overhead function \(h\) is fixed before assessing simultaneous adaptation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure means \(\inf_M\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}N_M(\theta,\varepsilon)/(h(\theta,\varepsilon)N^\star(\theta,\varepsilon))>1\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint-overhead inequality is meaningful, but the claimed boundary additionally requires a formal definition of adaptation to each coordinate separately. The conclusion only tests joint failure and does not encode that componentwise premise. A source and a precise componentwise benchmark are needed.

children.title: Lower-Bound Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Organizes conditions under which a lower bound cannot be transferred to another algorithm, oracle, dimension, metric, or structured problem class.

children.title: Dimension-Horizon Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Separates high-dimensional oracle lower bounds from finite-dimensional and long-horizon behavior.

children.title: Hard-Instance Dimension Requirements
children.top_down_role: Navigation for constructions whose ambient dimension grows with the query budget.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Instance Dimension Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-validity condition for lower bounds that reveal a fresh orthogonal direction at each query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a resisting-oracle or zero-chain lower-bound construction whose first \(T\) oracle answers require mutually orthogonal directions \(v_1,\ldots,v_T\), together with an additional direction carrying the unrevealed component of the minimizer. Such a construction embeds isometrically in \(\mathbb R^d\) only if \[d\geq T+1.\] More generally, if the proof uses \(m(T)\) linearly independent revealed and hidden directions, its stated hard instance requires \(d\geq m(T)\). Consequently, a lower bound proved by this construction cannot be transferred unchanged to a fixed dimension below that threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resisting-oracle construction needs enough dimensions for all revealed directions and any hidden minimizer direction; below that threshold its lower bound does not transfer unchanged.
assumptions_latex: Oracle answers enforce orthogonality of newly revealed directions.
The hard instance is embedded without identifying distinct construction directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The construction is dimension-valid only when \(d\geq m(T)\), with \(m(T)=T+1\) in the stated model.

notation.meaning: number of oracle queries covered by the construction
number of independent directions required by the hard instance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The general requirement `d >= m(T)` is structurally sound, but the specialization `m(T)=T+1` depends on the exact resisting-oracle or zero-chain construction. No authoritative construction or theorem locator is cited, so the precise dimension threshold cannot be verified.

children.title: Finite-Dimensional Oracle Escape Routes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for methods exploiting dimension or complete-data models.

children.title: Finite-Dimensional Localization Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods whose guarantees exploit a fixed finite ambient dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Localization Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic center-based localization using first-order separating halfspaces in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a compact convex set \(K_0\subset\mathbb R^d\) containing a minimizer of a convex function \(f\), fix a query budget \(T\in\mathbb N\). For \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), choose a center \(x_t\in K_t\), obtain \(f(x_t)\) and \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\) from a first-order oracle, and update \[K_{t+1}=K_t\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\langle g_t,x-x_t\rangle\leq0\}.\] Retain any \(\widehat x_T\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\leq t<T}f(x_t)\). Stop when the selected localization method's geometric tolerance is met or when the query budget is exhausted, and output \(\widehat x_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain a convex region containing a minimizer, query a prescribed center for a function value and subgradient, intersect the region with the resulting halfspace, and return a best queried point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex and attains a minimum in \(K_0\).
The first-order oracle returns \(f(x_t)\) and a valid \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\) at every query.
The center rule and geometric stopping tolerance are specified by the selected localization method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(K_{t+1}\) contains at least one minimizer contained in \(K_t\), and the algorithm outputs a best queried point \(\widehat x_T\).

notation.meaning: chosen center queried at iteration t
a queried point having the smallest observed objective value

children.title: Cutting-Plane Escape Mechanisms
children.top_down_role: Cutting-plane access patterns that evade baseline first-order lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane Escape Mechanisms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains how fixed-dimensional global cuts escape fresh-direction resisting-oracle behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex and attain its minimum, let \(x_t\in\mathbb R^d\) be a query point, and let \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\). Every global minimizer \(x^\star\) belongs to the halfspace \[H_t=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\langle g_t,x-x_t\rangle\leq0\}.\] Hence exact first-order answers provide globally valid cuts whose intersections continue to contain all minimizers. In fixed dimension, center-based cutting-plane methods can use these accumulated cuts to localize the solution without requiring a fresh independent direction for every query.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each exact subgradient defines a halfspace containing every minimizer, so a fixed-dimensional cutting-plane method can localize the solution by accumulating globally valid cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex and has at least one global minimizer.
The oracle returns an exact subgradient \(g_t\in\partial f(x_t)\) at each queried point.
The localization method retains the intersection of the valid halfspaces with its current region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every query \(t\), every global minimizer \(x^\star\) satisfies \(x^\star\in H_t\).

notation.meaning: exact subgradient returned at the query point
subgradient halfspace containing all global minimizers

children.title: Dimension-Dependent Crossover Regimes
children.top_down_role: Ranges where dimension-sensitive methods overtake horizon-based lower-bound predictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Crossover Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares a dimension-free iterative rate with a fixed-dimensional localization rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N_{\mathrm{iter}}(\varepsilon)\) be the query bound of a dimension-free first-order method and let \(N_{\mathrm{loc}}(d,\varepsilon)\) be that of a valid fixed-dimensional localization method. Their crossover threshold is any \(d_c(\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(N_{\mathrm{iter}}(\varepsilon)=N_{\mathrm{loc}}(d_c(\varepsilon),\varepsilon)\). For \(d\) with \(N_{\mathrm{loc}}(d,\varepsilon)<N_{\mathrm{iter}}(\varepsilon)\), localization supplies the smaller upper bound. A fresh-direction lower bound covering \(T=N_{\mathrm{iter}}(\varepsilon)\) queries is relevant only when its independent-direction requirement \(d\geq m(T)\) also holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The crossover occurs where fixed-dimensional localization becomes cheaper than the dimension-free iterative rate, subject to the hard instance's dimension requirement.
assumptions_latex: Both complexities use the same oracle, accuracy, and success criterion.
The localization method and lower-bound construction are valid in the compared dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The applicable comparison is \(N(\varepsilon,d)\leq\min\{N_{\mathrm{iter}}(\varepsilon),N_{\mathrm{loc}}(d,\varepsilon)\}\), while the fresh-direction lower bound additionally requires \(d\geq m(N_{\mathrm{iter}}(\varepsilon))\).

notation.meaning: dimension at which the two bounds coincide

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The upper-bound comparison is plausible, but an equality-defined crossover need not exist or be unique without monotonicity, continuity, or a generalized threshold definition. The dimension requirement and any concrete crossover also depend on selected methods and problem classes. No source is supplied to resolve these choices.

children.title: Horizon-Accuracy Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for lower bounds valid only within restricted accuracy or horizon ranges.

children.title: Preasymptotic Validity Windows
children.top_down_role: Accuracy or horizon ranges where the stated lower-bound rate remains informative.

knowledge_statements.title: Preasymptotic Validity Windows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite horizon–accuracy region in which a dimension-dependent lower bound is justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a problem dimension \(d\), horizon \(T\in\mathbb N\), and target accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\). Let \(L(d,T)\) be a claimed lower bound on the error after \(T\) oracle calls, and let \(V(d,T)\) collect every dimensional and oracle-model restriction used in its construction. The preasymptotic validity window is
\[
\mathcal W_d:=\{(T,\varepsilon):V(d,T)\ \text{holds and}\ L(d,T)>\varepsilon\}.
\]
Within \(\mathcal W_d\), the lower bound excludes attainment of accuracy \(\varepsilon\) by horizon \(T\). It makes no such assertion when \(V(d,T)\) fails, even if the displayed formula for \(L(d,T)\) remains positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The preasymptotic window consists of horizons satisfying the construction’s dimension restrictions and accuracies below its lower-bound error. The lower-bound conclusion is licensed only inside this window.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(T\in\mathbb N\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
\(L(d,T)\) is the error lower bound supplied by a fixed oracle construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((T,\varepsilon)\in\mathcal W_d\) implies that accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is unattainable by horizon \(T\) for the covered algorithm class.

notation.meaning: validity predicate containing dimension, horizon, and oracle restrictions
preasymptotic validity window at dimension d

review_flags: Exact lower-bound construction and dimension-horizon predicate are not identified by the supplied locators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no cited construction identifies the covered algorithm class, error criterion, lower-bound function, or validity predicate. Those omissions are evidentiary rather than safely repairable generically.

children.title: Terminal Accuracy Regimes
children.top_down_role: Late-stage ranges where finite dimension or exact recovery changes the rate taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies accuracies whose required horizon lies beyond a finite-dimensional lower-bound construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(T)\) be a nonincreasing positive lower-bound rate valid only for \(1\leq T\leq T_{\max}(d)\). Define the terminal scale by
\[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{term}}(d):=L\bigl(T_{\max}(d)\bigr).
\]
The terminal accuracy regime is \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{term}}(d)\). For such \(\varepsilon\), inversion of the rate requires a horizon strictly exceeding \(T_{\max}(d)\); consequently, the finite-horizon construction does not establish the extrapolated complexity bound. At the boundary \(\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{term}}(d)\), the largest valid horizon supplies the last certified point of the rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accuracies below the error at the largest valid horizon form the terminal regime. Reaching them requires extrapolating the lower-bound rate beyond the construction’s dimension-dependent horizon.
assumptions_latex: \(L:\mathbb N\to(0,\infty)\) is nonincreasing.
The lower-bound construction is valid exactly over \(1\leq T\leq T_{\max}(d)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{term}}(d)\) implies \(\inf\{T:L(T)\leq\varepsilon\}>T_{\max}(d)\).

notation.meaning: largest horizon certified by the dimension-dependent construction

review_flags: A source specifying the intended finite-dimensional lower-bound construction is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and finite-horizon inversion are coherent, with the infimum interpreted in the extended sense if the set is empty. A source is still required to identify the intended dimension-dependent construction and justify its terminal horizon.

children.title: Horizon-Driven Rate Crossovers
children.top_down_role: Transitions caused by the iteration horizon reaching a structural limit.

knowledge_statements.title: Horizon-Driven Rate Crossovers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a change in the dominant lower-bound term within a specified horizon-validity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb N\) be the horizon-validity set, and suppose that throughout \(I\),
\[
E_T\geq \max\{c_1r_1(T),c_2r_2(T)\},
\]
where \(c_1,c_2>0\) and \(r_1,r_2:I\to(0,\infty)\). A horizon-driven crossover from the first term to the second occurs at \(T_\times\in I\) when \(c_1r_1(T)\geq c_2r_2(T)\) for every \(T\in I\) with \(T<T_\times\), and \(c_1r_1(T)\leq c_2r_2(T)\) for every \(T\in I\) with \(T\geq T_\times\). If no such \(T_\times\) belongs to \(I\), the two displayed terms do not define this crossover within the certified horizon range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A horizon-driven crossover is a valid horizon at which the second of two simultaneous lower-bound terms begins to dominate the first. A formal crossing outside the certified horizon set does not define an applicable regime.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subseteq\mathbb N\) is the set of horizons on which both lower-bound terms are certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At a crossover \(T_\times\in I\), the dominant displayed lower-bound term changes from \(c_1r_1(T)\) to \(c_2r_2(T)\) according to the stated inequalities.

notation.meaning: worst-case error after T oracle calls

review_flags: The intended pair of first-order lower-bound rates and their common validity set are unspecified.

children.title: Algorithm-Class Transfer Failures

children.title: Span-Restriction Failure
children.top_down_role: Navigation for algorithms capable of leaving an oracle-generated span.

knowledge_statements.title: Span-Restriction Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks the failure of lower bounds proved only for iterates in the oracle-generated linear span.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A span-based lower bound does not automatically cover algorithms that add directions outside the span of previously returned first-order vectors.
assumptions_latex: The oracle transcript through round \(t\) contains first-order vectors \(g_0,\ldots,g_t\).
The original lower-bound induction uses membership in their linear span.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of an admissible \(v_t\notin\operatorname{span}\{g_0,\ldots,g_t\}\) blocks transfer of the span-restricted argument to the unrestricted algorithm class.

notation.meaning: first-order vector returned at round t
algorithm query or iterate at round t

children.title: Zero-Respecting Restriction Failure
children.top_down_role: Navigation for algorithms introducing unexplored coordinates or dense perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Respecting Restriction Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks when an algorithm activates coordinates absent from all previously observed first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(z\in\mathbb R^d\), let \(\operatorname{supp}(z):=\{i:z_i\neq0\}\). An algorithm is zero-respecting when every query satisfies
\[
\operatorname{supp}(x_{t+1})\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(x_0)\cup\bigcup_{s=0}^{t}\operatorname{supp}(g_s).
\]
The restriction fails if an admissible algorithm assigns a nonzero value to some coordinate outside this union, for example through a dense perturbation independent of the observed gradients. A zero-chain lower bound relying on delayed coordinate discovery consequently does not cover that algorithm without a rotation, randomization, or resisting-oracle argument extending the hard instance beyond zero-respecting queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero-respecting arguments fail to transfer when an algorithm can activate coordinates that have never appeared in its initial point or observed first-order vectors.
assumptions_latex: Queries and returned first-order vectors lie in \(\mathbb R^d\).
The lower-bound construction uses delayed revelation of coordinate support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A query with support outside the revealed-coordinate union invalidates direct transfer of the zero-respecting lower-bound induction.

notation.meaning: indices of nonzero coordinates of z
first-order vector observed at round s

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the zero-respecting definition or extension mechanisms.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The support-based restriction and its failure are stated consistently and fit the leaf. A source is required for the zero-respecting definition and for the listed mechanisms used to extend zero-chain lower bounds beyond that class.

children.title: Deterministic-to-Randomized Transfer Failure
children.top_down_role: Navigation for deterministic hard instances that do not control randomized algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic-to-Randomized Transfer Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses the quantifier mismatch between deterministic hard instances and randomized worst-case lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R(A,f)\geq0\) denote the error or cost of algorithm \(A\) on instance \(f\). A deterministic lower bound of the form
\[
\forall A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}\ \exists f_A\in\mathcal F:
R(A,f_A)\geq b
\]
does not imply
\[
\forall A\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{rand}}\ \exists f\in\mathcal F:
\mathbb E[R(A,f)]\geq b.
\]
The first hard instance may depend on the complete deterministic algorithm, whereas a randomized algorithm mixes many deterministic realizations. Transfer requires an additional distributional minimax argument or a hard-instance distribution controlling the expected performance of every deterministic realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance chosen separately against each deterministic algorithm does not by itself lower-bound randomized algorithms. A distributional or minimax argument is additionally required.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A_{\mathrm{det}}\subseteq\mathcal A_{\mathrm{rand}}\) and \(R(A,f)\geq0\).
Expectation is taken over the randomized algorithm’s internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic quantifier statement alone does not entail the randomized expected lower bound.

notation.meaning: hard instance allowed to depend on deterministic algorithm A

children.title: Sequential-to-Parallel Transfer Failure

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential-to-Parallel Transfer Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates adaptive sequential oracle rounds from batches whose queries are selected before within-round answers are known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a \(q\)-parallel first-order model, round \(r\) selects a batch \(x_{r,1},\ldots,x_{r,q}\) measurable with respect to transcripts from earlier rounds; all \(q\) oracle answers are then returned simultaneously. A sequential resisting-oracle argument may choose the answer at query \(t\) after observing every preceding query. It does not transfer directly when its construction adapts to queries within the same parallel batch, because those answers must be jointly consistent with a single instance chosen without an artificial within-batch order. The relevant adaptive resource is the number of rounds, not merely the total number \(qR\) of queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequential adversary cannot adapt between queries issued in the same batch. Lower bounds using such adaptation require a parallel-consistent construction and must count rounds separately from total queries.
assumptions_latex: Each parallel batch contains at most \(q\) queries.
Queries within a round are chosen before any answer from that round is observed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A sequential proof using within-batch adaptation does not establish the same bound for \(q\)-parallel algorithms.

notation.meaning: maximum number of simultaneous oracle queries
query j in parallel round r

children.title: Information-Cost Transfer Failures

children.title: Local-to-Structured Oracle Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Navigation for proximal, separation, linear-minimization, or complete-model access absent from the baseline.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Structured Oracle Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marks when a local first-order call lower bound cannot be transferred directly to an algorithm using stronger structured optimization primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a local oracle return \(O_{\mathrm{loc}}(x)=(f(x),g)\), where \(g\in\partial f(x)\), and let a structured oracle \(O_{\mathrm{str}}\) additionally solve a global subproblem, such as a proximal, separation, or linear-minimization query. A uniformly bounded-cost simulation of every structured response by local-oracle calls, preserving the relevant output guarantee over the same problem class, is sufficient to transfer a local-call lower bound with the corresponding simulation overhead. If no such simulation is established, the local-oracle proof does not by itself cover structured-oracle algorithms; transfer then requires a separate lower-bound argument for the structured model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local first-order lower bound does not automatically price proximal, separation, or linear-minimization calls. Transfer requires either a bounded-cost local simulation of those calls or a separate lower-bound argument for the structured oracle model.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) belongs to a fixed problem class on which both oracle models are defined.
The compared complexity measures count oracle calls and use the same performance criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absent a proved bounded-cost simulation or a separate structured-model lower bound, an \(O_{\mathrm{loc}}\)-call lower bound does not establish the corresponding claim for \(O_{\mathrm{str}}\)-algorithms.

children.title: Reusable Component Access
children.top_down_role: Finite-sum settings permitting repeated queries to identified components.

knowledge_statements.title: Reusable Component Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines indexed finite-sum access permitting repeated queries to previously selected component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,d\in\mathbb N\), let each \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and define
\[
F(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_i(x).
\]
A reusable component oracle accepts any adaptively chosen pair \((i,x)\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\times\mathbb R^d\) and returns \((f_i(x),g_i)\), where \(g_i\in\partial f_i(x)\). The algorithm may query the same index at multiple points, revisit an earlier pair, correlate future choices with all stored component answers, and retain arbitrary state derived from them. Oracle complexity counts each indexed query; the model does not require the selected index to be fresh or independently sampled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusable component access lets an algorithm choose and revisit finite-sum components, store their earlier answers, and adapt later component queries to the complete transcript.
assumptions_latex: \(n,d\in\mathbb N\) and each \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated adaptive access to every component index \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is permitted and charged once per indexed query.
review_flags: No supplied locator unambiguously defines reusable indexed component-oracle access.

children.title: Fresh-Sample Oracle Access
children.top_down_role: Stochastic settings where each query supplies a newly sampled observation.

knowledge_statements.title: Fresh-Sample Oracle Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines stochastic first-order access through a newly drawn sample at every query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[f(x;\xi)]\), and let \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\) denote the transcript available before query \(t\). A fresh-sample oracle receives an \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable query \(x_t\), draws \(\xi_t\) with conditional law \(P\) given \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\), and returns \(G(x_t;\xi_t)\) satisfying
\[
\mathbb E[G(x_t;\xi_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=g(x_t),\qquad g(x_t)\in\partial F(x_t).
\]
The algorithm may use the returned sample information in later queries but cannot request that an earlier realization be evaluated at a new point. Complexity counts fresh draws or oracle calls, and variance or moment restrictions are additional properties of the oracle class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fresh-sample access draws a new sample conditionally independently of the prior transcript at every adaptive query and returns an unbiased first-order estimate. The algorithm cannot deliberately reevaluate a previous realization at another point.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P}[f(x;\xi)]\) is well defined on the query domain.
The query \(x_t\) is \(\mathcal F_{t-1}\)-measurable, and the stated conditional expectation exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each call has \(\mathcal L(\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1})=P\) and satisfies \(\mathbb E[G(x_t;\xi_t)\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\in\partial F(x_t)\).

notation.meaning: fresh sample drawn at query t

review_flags: No supplied locator clearly specifies this fresh-sample oracle model.

children.title: Access-Model Transfer Failures
children.top_down_role: Comparisons that import rates across incompatible component-access models.

knowledge_statements.title: Access-Model Transfer Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when a lower-bound proof cannot be transferred directly between fresh-sample and reusable indexed-component access models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal O_a\) and \(\mathcal O_b\) be oracle models for the same objective class and performance criterion. If every \(t\)-call \(\mathcal O_b\)-algorithm can be simulated by an \(\mathcal O_a\)-algorithm using at most \(ct\) calls while preserving the relevant transcript distribution and output risk, then an \(\mathcal O_a\)-call lower bound transfers to \(\mathcal O_b\) with the corresponding factor \(c\). Fresh-sample and reusable component access do not automatically admit such a simulation: revisiting selected components can create correlations and stored information unavailable under forced fresh sampling. Without a suitable simulation, the source-model proof does not transfer directly; the target-model lower bound requires a separate argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-cost, risk-preserving simulation is sufficient to transfer a lower bound between access models. Component reuse prevents assuming equivalence with forced fresh sampling, so a missing simulation leaves the source proof model-specific unless a separate target-model proof is supplied.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal O_a\) and \(\mathcal O_b\) act on the same stated objective class.
Performance is measured by the same output-risk functional in both models.
\(c>0\) is uniform over the algorithms and instances covered by the comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absent a bounded-cost transcript-and-risk simulation, an \(\mathcal O_a\)-model proof does not by itself establish the corresponding \(\mathcal O_b\)-model lower bound.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly establishes a simulation or separation between these access models.

children.title: Hidden Computational Costs
children.top_down_role: Navigation for preprocessing or nested computation that changes the effective information model.

children.title: Unpriced Preconditioning Cost
children.top_down_role: Setup or maintenance costs incurred by transformations that improve effective conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Unpriced Preconditioning Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates iteration or oracle counts from the work required to construct and use a preconditioner.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose an algorithm constructs a preconditioner \(P\) and then performs \(T(P,\varepsilon)\) iterations to reach accuracy \(\varepsilon\). Let \(C_{\mathrm{build}}(P)\) be its construction cost, and let \(C_t(P)\) be the total arithmetic cost of iteration \(t\), including every application of \(P\) or \(P^{-1}\) and all other iteration work. Then
\[
C_{\mathrm{total}}(P,\varepsilon)=C_{\mathrm{build}}(P)+\sum_{t=1}^{T(P,\varepsilon)}C_t(P).
\]
An iteration bound reporting only \(T(P,\varepsilon)\) has unpriced preconditioning cost when the omitted construction or per-iteration terms depend nontrivially on dimension, sparsity, conditioning, or accuracy. Such an iteration bound therefore need not imply a corresponding runtime or arithmetic-complexity improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower iteration count does not establish lower runtime when constructing or using the preconditioner has omitted dimension-, sparsity-, conditioning-, or accuracy-dependent cost.
assumptions_latex: The implementation constructs or uses a preconditioner \(P\).
Arithmetic work is additive across preprocessing and completed iterations.
\(C_t(P)\) includes every preconditioner application and all other work performed in iteration \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Runtime comparison requires \(C_{\mathrm{total}}(P,\varepsilon)\), not merely \(T(P,\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: aggregate arithmetic cost of iteration t, including preconditioner use
number of iterations needed to reach accuracy epsilon with preconditioner P

children.title: Unpriced Sketch Construction
children.top_down_role: Resource costs associated with building or refreshing dimensionality-reduction sketches.

knowledge_statements.title: Unpriced Sketch Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of end-to-end complexity accounting when constructing a randomized sketch is excluded from the advertised cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an algorithm construct a random sketching operator \(S=S(A,\xi)\) at cost \(C_{\mathrm{sk}}(A,\xi)\), and then perform \(T\) iterations with costs \(c_1,\ldots,c_T\). Its end-to-end work is \[W(A,\xi)=C_{\mathrm{sk}}(A,\xi)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_t.\] A bound stated only as \(T\leq B(\varepsilon)\) does not imply \(W\leq O(B(\varepsilon))\) unless sketch construction is free in the declared model, the iteration costs are appropriately controlled, and \(C_{\mathrm{sk}}\) is bounded at the claimed work scale. Consequently, an end-to-end work comparison cannot silently identify the iteration count with total work while omitting \(C_{\mathrm{sk}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sketched method’s iteration count is not an end-to-end work bound unless both the iteration costs and the cost of constructing the sketch are free or explicitly controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\)
\(c_t\geq 0\) for \(1\leq t\leq T\)
\(C_{\mathrm{sk}}(A,\xi)\geq 0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=C_{\mathrm{sk}}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_t\), so omitting \(C_{\mathrm{sk}}\) can invalidate an end-to-end upper bound or work comparison.

notation.meaning: computational cost of constructing the sketch

children.title: Unpriced Inner-Solve Work
children.top_down_role: Nested computational effort omitted from outer-iteration comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Unpriced Inner-Solve Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of outer-iteration accounting when each nominal step contains a nontrivial iterative subproblem solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose outer iteration \(t\) invokes an inner algorithm for \(m_t\) primitive steps, with primitive costs \(d_{t,1},\ldots,d_{t,m_t}\), and let \(C_0\) denote all other work. The actual work is \[W=C_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{m_t}d_{t,j}.\] An outer bound \(T\leq B(\varepsilon)\) is not an end-to-end complexity bound unless the inner work is included or a uniform summable bound on \(m_t\) and \(d_{t,j}\) is supplied. Treating an inexact proximal, projection, linear-system, or subproblem solve as one free step therefore prevents direct transfer of primitive-operation lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer iteration counts can hide arbitrarily large work when proximal, projection, linear-system, or other inner solves are not priced.
assumptions_latex: \(T<\infty\)
\(m_t\in\mathbb{N}_0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\leq B(\varepsilon)\) alone gives no bound on \(W\) when the inner-work sums are uncontrolled.

notation.meaning: number of primitive inner steps during outer iteration t
cost of inner step j at outer iteration t

children.title: Effective Oracle-Model Inflation
children.top_down_role: Cases where auxiliary computation supplies information beyond the nominal oracle model.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Oracle-Model Inflation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary arising when one advertised oracle call uses multiple primitive calls or information unavailable in the baseline model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{O}\) be the primitive oracle used by a lower-bound model. If advertised call \(t\) is implemented using \(q_t\) calls to \(\mathcal{O}\), its effective primitive-query count is \[Q_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_t.\] If it additionally returns information not simulable from a uniformly bounded number of \(\mathcal{O}\)-calls, it constitutes a stronger oracle. A complexity statement counting only \(T\) advertised calls is comparable with an \(\mathcal{O}\)-oracle bound only when every advertised response is simulable in the baseline model and \(q_t\) is uniformly accounted for. Otherwise the oracle model has been effectively inflated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An advertised oracle count is incomparable with a primitive-oracle bound if each call hides multiple queries or supplies strictly stronger information.
assumptions_latex: \(q_t\in\mathbb{N}_0\) for \(1\leq t\leq T\)
\(T<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_t\), and comparison by \(T\) requires bounded simulation in the same oracle model.

notation.meaning: primitive queries used by advertised call t

children.title: Objective-Error Criteria

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Error Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute suboptimality criterion for minimization over a specified feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and suppose the finite optimal value \(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) is known conceptually. For \(\varepsilon\geq 0\), an output \(\widehat{x}\in X\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) satisfies the absolute \(\varepsilon\)-objective-error criterion precisely when \[f(\widehat{x})-f^*\leq\varepsilon.\] If an optimizer \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\) exists, the same predicate is \(f(\widehat{x})-f(x^*)\leq\varepsilon\). A complexity bound using this criterion must state whether error is absolute, relative, expected, or probabilistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible output has absolute objective error at most epsilon when its objective value exceeds the optimal value by at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\)
\(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\)
\(\varepsilon\geq 0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\widehat{x})-f^*\leq\varepsilon\) is the absolute objective-error predicate.

children.title: Stationarity Criteria
children.top_down_role: Complexity claims indexed by a stationarity measure.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized first-order stationarity criterion expressed through distance to a specified subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(F:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, and fix a declared subdifferential \(\partial F\). For \(\varepsilon\geq 0\), a point \(\widehat{x}\in\operatorname{dom}F\) is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary under this convention when \[\operatorname{dist}_{*}\!\left(0,\partial F(\widehat{x})\right)=\inf_{v\in\partial F(\widehat{x})}\|v\|_{*}\leq\varepsilon.\] If \(F\) is differentiable at \(\widehat{x}\) and the declared subdifferential satisfies \(\partial F(\widehat{x})=\{\nabla F(\widehat{x})\}\), this reduces to \(\|\nabla F(\widehat{x})\|_{*}\leq\varepsilon\). The comparison target is not fixed until the subdifferential, norm, and any constrained normal-cone term are specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a declared subdifferential convention, a point is epsilon-stationary when that subdifferential contains a vector whose dual norm is at most epsilon; the usual gradient criterion follows only for a compatible subdifferential at differentiability points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional
\(F\) is proper
\(\varepsilon\geq 0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_{*}(0,\partial F(\widehat{x}))\leq\varepsilon\) is the stationarity predicate under the declared convention.

notation.meaning: dual norm used to measure stationarity

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-distance criterion for approximate membership in a nonempty feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty. For \(\varepsilon\geq 0\), an output \(\widehat{x}\in X\) satisfies the \(\varepsilon\)-feasibility criterion when \[\operatorname{dist}(\widehat{x},C)=\inf_{z\in C}\|\widehat{x}-z\|\leq\varepsilon.\] Exact feasibility is the case \(\varepsilon=0\) when \(C\) is closed. If constraints are represented by residuals instead, the residual map, its norm, and its relation to distance from \(C\) must be specified before residual-based and distance-based complexity bounds are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An output is epsilon-feasible when its distance to the declared nonempty feasible set is at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\|\cdot\|)\) is a normed space
\(C\neq\varnothing\)
\(\varepsilon\geq 0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(\widehat{x},C)\leq\varepsilon\) is the distance-based feasibility predicate.

children.title: Cross-Criterion Comparability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring lower bounds between distinct output targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Criterion Comparability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic family showing that objective error and gradient norm are not uniformly interchangeable without conditioning assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), define \(f_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), with minimizer \(x^*=0\). Then \[f_{\lambda}(x)-f_{\lambda}(x^*)=\frac{\lambda x^2}{2},\qquad |f_{\lambda}'(x)|=\lambda|x|.\] At \(x=\sqrt{2\varepsilon/\lambda}\), the objective error equals \(\varepsilon\), while the gradient norm equals \(\sqrt{2\lambda\varepsilon}\), which is unbounded over \(\lambda\). At \(x=\varepsilon/\lambda\), the gradient norm equals \(\varepsilon\), while the objective error equals \(\varepsilon^2/(2\lambda)\), which is unbounded as \(\lambda\downarrow0\). Thus neither criterion uniformly implies the other without scale or curvature bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled quadratics show that objective error and gradient norm admit no uniform conversion unless smoothness, curvature, or scale parameters are controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\)
\(\lambda>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No conversion bound independent of \(\lambda\) exists between objective error and gradient norm on this family.

children.title: Expected-Error Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Rates evaluated through an expectation-based performance criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Error Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-based accuracy criterion for a randomized algorithm and a specified nonnegative error variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a randomized algorithm output \(X_T\), and let \(Z_T=E(X_T)\) be a measurable nonnegative error variable defined on its probability space. For \(\varepsilon\geq 0\), the algorithm has an expected-error guarantee after \(T\) iterations when \[\mathbb{E}[Z_T]\leq\varepsilon,\] where the expectation covers every declared source of algorithmic and oracle randomness. Its expected-error iteration complexity is the least \(T\), or an upper bound on such a \(T\), for which this inequality holds uniformly over the stated problem class. This criterion alone does not specify any confidence level for an individual run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized method has expected error at most epsilon when the mean of its declared nonnegative error variable is at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_T\geq 0\) almost surely
\(Z_T\) is measurable
\(\mathbb{E}[Z_T]<\infty\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[Z_T]\leq\varepsilon\) is the expected-error guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Guarantees

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a randomized algorithm output \(X_T\), and let \(Z_T=E(X_T)\) be a measurable nonnegative error variable. The associated complexity must display its dependence on both \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\), and the probability must cover every declared source of algorithmic and oracle randomness.

\(Z_T\) is measurable

children.title: Confidence-Dependence Gaps

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence-Dependence Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on converting expectation bounds into high-probability bounds without additional tail information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_T\geq0\) be the error of a randomized method. From an expected guarantee alone, Markov's inequality gives \[\mathbb{P}\{Z_T>\varepsilon\}\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[Z_T]}{\varepsilon}.\] Therefore, ensuring failure probability at most \(\delta\) by this conversion requires \(\mathbb{E}[Z_T]\leq\delta\varepsilon\), so an expected-complexity function \(T_{\mathrm{exp}}(\eta)\) yields only \(T_{\mathrm{hp}}(\varepsilon,\delta)\leq T_{\mathrm{exp}}(\delta\varepsilon)\). A claimed logarithmic dependence on \(1/\delta\), or any stronger tail rate, cannot be inferred from the mean alone; it requires concentration, bounded tails, amplification, or another explicit assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expectation alone yields only Markov-type confidence dependence; logarithmic dependence on inverse failure probability requires additional tail control or amplification.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_T\geq 0\) almost surely
\(\varepsilon>0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{hp}}(\varepsilon,\delta)\leq T_{\mathrm{exp}}(\delta\varepsilon)\) is the generic mean-to-tail conversion available from nonnegativity alone.

notation.meaning: iteration bound for a high-probability guarantee

direct source for the complexity-conversion formulation is missing

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case count of outer algorithmic updates required to meet a declared output criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a nonempty problem class \(\mathcal{P}\), an algorithm producing iterates \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\), and an accuracy predicate \(\mathcal{C}_{\varepsilon}(x)\). Its worst-case iteration complexity is \[T_{\mathrm{iter}}(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\inf\{t\in\mathbb{N}_0:\mathcal{C}_{\varepsilon}(x_t(P))\text{ holds}\}.\] For randomized algorithms, the predicate must specify the required expectation or probability statement. This resource counts declared outer updates only; it is not a bound on oracle calls, arithmetic operations, communication, preprocessing, or inner-solve work unless the model identifies those resources with one iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration complexity is the worst-case number of declared outer updates needed to satisfy a specified accuracy criterion.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{P}\neq\varnothing\)
\(x_t(P)\) is defined for each counted iteration
\(\mathcal{C}_{\varepsilon}\) is fixed before comparison

children.title: Per-Iteration Computational Cost

knowledge_statements.title: Per-Iteration Computational Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primitive-operation cost assigned to one declared iteration under a fixed computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a primitive-operation model and let iteration \(t\) execute operations with nonnegative costs \(c_{t,1},\ldots,c_{t,m_t}\). Its computational cost is \[C_t=\sum_{j=1}^{m_t}c_{t,j}.\] A uniform per-iteration bound \(C_t\leq C_{\mathrm{iter}}\) for \(0\leq t<T\) implies iterative work at most \(T C_{\mathrm{iter}}\). The bound is meaningful only if oracle evaluations, matrix-vector products, communication, memory access, and inner solves are either priced in the chosen model or explicitly excluded. It does not include one-time preprocessing unless that work is assigned to an iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Per-iteration cost is the priced sum of primitive operations in one update; multiplying it by the iteration count bounds only iterative work.
assumptions_latex: \(m_t\in\mathbb{N}_0\)
\(C_t\leq C_{\mathrm{iter}}\) for \(0\leq t<T\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}C_t\leq T C_{\mathrm{iter}}\).

notation.meaning: cost of primitive operation j in iteration t
uniform upper bound on one iteration's cost

children.title: Preprocessing Cost
children.top_down_role: One-time setup work excluded from iteration counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-time work performed before the first accuracy-dependent iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an algorithm and a computational resource unit. Its preprocessing cost is the resource count \(P(I)\) incurred on instance \(I\) before the first iterative update, including initialization, data transformation, factorization, indexing, or parameter estimation performed only once. Operations repeated during iterations are excluded. If preprocessing is randomized, the applicable convention—worst-case, expected, or high-probability cost—must be stated. Thus the reported preprocessing complexity over an instance class \(\mathcal I\) is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}P(I)\), or its explicitly declared probabilistic analogue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preprocessing cost counts one-time resource use before iterative updates, under a stated deterministic or probabilistic convention.
assumptions_latex: A computational resource unit and an instance class \(\mathcal I\) are fixed.
Preprocessing is separated from operations repeated within iterative updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The preprocessing complexity is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}P(I)\), subject to the declared probabilistic convention.

notation.meaning: preprocessing resource cost on instance I

children.title: End-to-End Work Complexity
children.top_down_role: Aggregate cost incorporating setup plus repeated computational effort.

knowledge_statements.title: End-to-End Work Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total work through production of an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_\varepsilon(I)\) be the first iteration at which an algorithm returns an output satisfying a declared accuracy criterion on instance \(I\). If \(P(I)\) is preprocessing work, \(W_k(I)\) is work in iteration \(k\), and \(R_\varepsilon(I)\) is termination and output-recovery work, then end-to-end work is \[C_\varepsilon(I)=P(I)+\sum_{k=0}^{T_\varepsilon(I)-1}W_k(I)+R_\varepsilon(I).\] A valid worst-case bound is a function \(B(\varepsilon)\) satisfying \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}C_\varepsilon(I)\le B(\varepsilon)\). Iteration complexity alone does not establish this bound unless all omitted work terms are uniformly controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: End-to-end complexity adds preprocessing, all per-iteration work, and output costs until the declared accuracy criterion is met.
assumptions_latex: The accuracy criterion and resource unit are fixed.
Every cost term is measured in the same resource unit.
The stopping time \(T_\varepsilon(I)\) is well-defined on \(\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A worst-case end-to-end bound satisfies \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}C_\varepsilon(I)\le B(\varepsilon)\).
