children.title: Resource-Unit Accounting Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Navigation for incompatible resource units.

children.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured by individual interactions with the designated oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy complexity measured by invocations of a specified information oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an oracle \(\mathcal O\), an instance class \(\mathcal I\), and an accuracy predicate \(E(x,I)\le\varepsilon\). If iteration \(k\) makes \(q_k(I)\) invocations of \(\mathcal O\), the oracle-call cost through the first accurate output is \[Q_\varepsilon(I)=\sum_{k=0}^{T_\varepsilon(I)-1}q_k(I).\] The worst-case oracle-call complexity is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}Q_\varepsilon(I)\). The oracle specification must identify the returned information, such as a value, gradient, subgradient, proximal point, or stochastic sample; calls to different oracle types are not interchangeable without a conversion theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call complexity counts invocations of a specified information oracle required to return an ε-accurate output.
assumptions_latex: The oracle interface \(\mathcal O\) is fixed.
Accuracy is defined by \(E(x,I)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case oracle-call complexity is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}Q_\varepsilon(I)\).

notation.meaning: calls through the first accurate output

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle-accounting idea and definition content kind fit the leaf, but no authoritative source is cited. The formula also uses T_ε(I) without explicitly defining that stopping index within the record, so a source-supported formulation must clarify it.

children.title: Data-Pass Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured by full traversals of the available data.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Pass Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy complexity normalized by the size of a finite dataset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a dataset of \(n\) records, suppose iteration \(k\) reads \(b_k(I)\) record occurrences, counting repeated reads with multiplicity. The effective number of data passes through the first \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output is \[D_\varepsilon(I)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{T_\varepsilon(I)-1}b_k(I).\] Its worst-case complexity over \(\mathcal I\) is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}D_\varepsilon(I)\). This convention measures logical record accesses; if physical I/O, caching, or parallel reads are intended, those resources require a separate accounting model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data-pass complexity divides total record accesses before an accurate output by the dataset size.
assumptions_latex: Each instance has a finite dataset of \(n\ge1\) records.
Record accesses, including repetitions, are countable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective-pass count is \(D_\varepsilon(I)=n^{-1}\sum_{k<T_\varepsilon(I)}b_k(I)\).

notation.meaning: record occurrences read in iteration k
effective data passes to accuracy ε

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conventional effective-pass accounting for finite-sum methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized record-access count is a plausible effective-pass convention, but conventions for epochs and data passes vary and no source is supplied. T_ε(I) is also used without an explicit local definition.

children.title: Communication-Round Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured by sequential synchronization or communication rounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Round Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential communication phases required by a distributed optimization method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a distributed computation, a communication round is one synchronous phase in which each participating processor may form outgoing messages from its current local state, messages are delivered according to the communication graph, and local states are then updated. If \(r_k(I)\) such phases occur during iteration \(k\), the communication-round cost through the first \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output is \[R_\varepsilon(I)=\sum_{k=0}^{T_\varepsilon(I)-1}r_k(I).\] The worst-case round complexity is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}R_\varepsilon(I)\); message volume, latency, and local computation are distinct resources unless explicitly incorporated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication-round complexity counts sequential synchronous message-exchange phases needed to produce an ε-accurate distributed output.
assumptions_latex: A synchronous distributed model and communication graph are fixed.
The location and accuracy requirement of the returned output are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case communication-round complexity is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}R_\varepsilon(I)\).

notation.meaning: rounds through the first accurate output

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly identifies a synchronous communication-round model and separates rounds from other resources, but round conventions are model-dependent and require an authoritative locator. T_ε(I) is not explicitly defined within the record.

children.title: Bit Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured by communicated or represented information volume.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision computational complexity in a specified bit-level machine model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a bit-level machine model and an encoding of each instance \(I\). If \(c_k^{\mathrm{bit}}(I)\) is the number of bit operations performed during iteration \(k\), including the cost induced by operand lengths, and \(P^{\mathrm{bit}}(I)\) and \(R_\varepsilon^{\mathrm{bit}}(I)\) are preprocessing and output costs, then \[B_\varepsilon(I)=P^{\mathrm{bit}}(I)+\sum_{k=0}^{T_\varepsilon(I)-1}c_k^{\mathrm{bit}}(I)+R_\varepsilon^{\mathrm{bit}}(I).\] Worst-case bit complexity is \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}B_\varepsilon(I)\). Unit-cost real arithmetic does not determine this quantity without bounds on representation length and numerical precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit complexity counts finite-precision bit operations, including operand-length, preprocessing, iteration, and output costs.
assumptions_latex: A finite encoding and bit-level machine model are fixed.
The required output accuracy and representation are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Worst-case bit complexity equals \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}B_\varepsilon(I)\).

notation.meaning: total bit cost to accuracy ε

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-precision accounting and definition content kind fit the bit-complexity leaf, but the claimed accounting convention requires a source for the selected machine model. The instance class 𝓘 used in the supremum is not explicitly introduced.

children.title: Resource-Unit Conversion Failures
children.top_down_role: Comparisons lacking a justified translation between resource measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Unit Conversion Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of dimension-free conversion between distinct complexity resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider finite-sum objectives \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). A component method reading one record per iteration has, after \(T\) iterations, component-oracle cost \(Q=T\) and effective-pass cost \(D=T/n\). A full-gradient method has per-iteration costs \(Q=n\) and \(D=1\). Consequently no constants independent of \(n\) can identify oracle calls with data passes in both models. Likewise, a serial implementation can use zero communication rounds while making arbitrarily many oracle calls. Therefore a bound in one resource unit transfers to another only under explicit uniform upper and lower conversion inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle calls, data passes, and communication rounds need not be comparable without dimension- and model-dependent conversion inequalities.
assumptions_latex: The finite-sum oracle returns information for one selected component per component call.
One effective pass is normalized as \(n\) record accesses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are no universal constants \(a,b>0\), independent of \(n\), satisfying both \(aQ\le D\le bQ\) across these methods.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct accounting counterexample in the stated finite-sum model
source needed for taxonomy-level transfer boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly illustrates the failure of dimension-independent two-sided conversion between component-oracle calls and normalized data passes, and failure_boundary is the correct role. A source is nevertheless required for this taxonomy-level transfer claim and its resource-model conventions.

children.title: Additional-Structure Escape Routes
children.top_down_role: Organizes structure that places a problem outside a baseline lower-bound class.

children.title: Enhanced Convex Geometry Classes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for geometry stronger than baseline convexity.

children.title: Error-Bound Geometry
children.top_down_role: Problem classes organized by error-bound structure beyond baseline convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local metric error bound expressed through the convex subdifferential residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, with nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}f\). The subdifferential error-bound condition holds on a set \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) with modulus \(\kappa>0\) when \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le \kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] If \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(X^*\), the condition is local; if \(U=\operatorname{dom}f\), it is global. The residual convention must remain fixed when comparing rates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Error-bound geometry controls distance to the solution set by a subdifferential residual, locally or globally.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
The minimizer set \(X^*\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in U\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard metric subregularity form of a convex error bound
source needed to confirm the intended residual among several error-bound conventions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent as a subdifferential-residual error bound, but error-bound geometry has several inequivalent residual conventions. An authoritative source is needed to establish that this is the intended condition for the leaf.

children.title: Growth Conditions
children.top_down_role: Problem classes organized by objective growth near the solution set.

knowledge_statements.title: Growth Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective growth away from a nonempty minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have finite minimum \(f^*\) and nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). For constants \(\mu>0\), \(p\ge1\), and a set \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\), the function satisfies \(p\)-th order growth on \(U\) when \[f(x)-f^*\ge \frac{\mu}{p}\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^p\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.\] The condition is local when \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(X^*\) and global when \(U=\operatorname{dom}f\). Quadratic growth is the case \(p=2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A growth condition lower-bounds objective error by a positive power of distance to the minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: The minimum \(f^*\) is finite and attained.
The exponent satisfies \(p\ge1\) and \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in U\), \(f(x)-f^*\ge(\mu/p)\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)^p\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Hölderian growth condition with explicit normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The p-th order growth condition is precise and condition is the appropriate content kind, but no source supports the selected exponent range and μ/p normalization. A specific definition or section locator is required.

children.title: Sharpness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where sharp local geometry changes attainable complexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear objective growth relative to distance from the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have finite minimum \(f^*\) and nonempty minimizer set \(X^*\). The objective is \(\mu\)-sharp on \(U\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) if \[f(x)-f^*\ge \mu\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\qquad\text{for every }x\in U,\] where \(\mu>0\). Local sharpness takes \(U\) to be a neighborhood of \(X^*\); global sharpness takes \(U=\operatorname{dom}f\). This is the linear-growth regime and is stronger near \(X^*\) than quadratic growth with a fixed positive modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sharpness is linear growth of objective error with distance from the minimizer set.
assumptions_latex: The minimum \(f^*\) is finite and attained.
The sharpness modulus satisfies \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in U\), \(f(x)-f^*\ge\mu\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sharpness is the first-order growth regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear-growth inequality is a standard sharpness condition and fits the leaf. A source is required, particularly for the statement comparing sharpness with quadratic growth, whose force depends on the local region and distance scale.

children.title: Geometry-Driven Rate Improvements
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound escape routes enabled by stronger local or global geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Driven Rate Improvements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear proximal-point convergence induced by a local subdifferential error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, closed, and convex with minimizer set \(X^*\ne\varnothing\), and suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial f(x))\) throughout a region containing the proximal-point iterates. For fixed \(\lambda>0\), define \(x_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x_k)\). Then \[\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},X^*)\le\rho\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*),\qquad \rho=\left(1+\frac{\lambda^2}{\kappa^2}\right)^{-1/2}<1.\] Hence \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\le\rho^k\operatorname{dist}(x_0,X^*)\), and attaining distance at most \(\varepsilon\) requires at most \(\left\lceil\log(\operatorname{dist}(x_0,X^*)/\varepsilon)/\log(1/\rho)\right\rceil\) proximal evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subdifferential error bound converts proximal-point convergence into a geometric rate with logarithmic accuracy complexity.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and has \(X^*\ne\varnothing\).
The error bound with modulus \(\kappa\) holds along all iterates.
The proximal parameter \(\lambda>0\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterates satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,X^*)\le\rho^k\operatorname{dist}(x_0,X^*)\) with \(\rho=(1+\lambda^2/\kappa^2)^{-1/2}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: contraction follows from proximal-point firm nonexpansiveness and the stated error bound
authoritative theorem locator needed for the exact contraction factor

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem-style complexity bound fits the rate-improvement leaf, and its hypotheses identify convexity, a fixed proximal parameter, and an error bound along the iterates. The exact contraction factor and resulting evaluation bound are nontrivial and require an authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Effective-Dimension Structure Family
children.top_down_role: Navigation for effective-dimension reductions that evade ambient worst cases.

children.title: Low-Rank Structure
children.top_down_role: Instance families whose relevant operators or solutions have restricted rank.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix optimization instances admitting a solution of bounded rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have nonempty minimizer set \(X^*=\operatorname*{argmin}F\). The instance has solution-level rank \(r\) structure when \[\min_{X\in X^*}\operatorname{rank}(X)\le r<\min\{m,n\}.\] An algorithm exploits this structure only if its representation or oracle operations have costs controlled by \(r\), for example through factors \(X=UV^{\mathsf T}\) with \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times r}\) and \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\). The existence of a low-rank minimizer alone does not imply a reduced complexity bound without such rank-adaptive access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Low-rank structure means that some optimal matrix has rank at most r; complexity improves only with rank-adaptive representation or access.
assumptions_latex: The matrix objective \(F\) attains its minimum.
The rank threshold satisfies \(r<\min\{m,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(X^*_{r}\in\operatorname*{argmin}F\) such that \(\operatorname{rank}(X^*_{r})\le r\).

notation.meaning: rank-r factors of a represented matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard solution-level low-rank structural condition
source needed to confirm whether the taxonomy intends solution rank, iterate rank, or oracle rank

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition precisely defines solution-level low rank and appropriately warns that existence alone does not imply reduced complexity. A source is needed because the leaf could instead intend low rank of data, operators, iterates, or accessible representations, and the taxonomy context does not resolve that choice.

children.title: Sparse Structure
children.top_down_role: Instance families governed by a restricted support pattern.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-coordinate sparsity that reduces a nominally finite-dimensional optimization problem to known active coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and let \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) have cardinality \(s\). The function has coordinate-sparse structure on \(S\) if there exists \(g:\mathbb{R}^s\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \(f(x)=g(x_S)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\). Equivalently, \(f(x)=f(y)\) whenever \(x_S=y_S\). If \(f\) is differentiable, then \(\operatorname{supp}(\nabla f(x))\subseteq S\) for every \(x\). When \(S\) is known, optimization and first-order oracle queries can be restricted to \(\mathbb{R}^s\), so the relevant dimension is \(s\), not \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is coordinate-sparse when it depends only on a fixed set of s coordinates; if that set is known, first-order optimization reduces to s dimensions.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper.
\(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}\) is fixed and known to the method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=g(x_S)\), and the problem admits an \(s\)-dimensional formulation with \(s=|S|\).

notation.meaning: Subvector of x indexed by S.
Indices of the nonzero coordinates of v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically coherent and fits the Sparse Structure leaf, but no citation supports the fixed-coordinate factorization, gradient-support consequence, or oracle-dimension reduction. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Active-Subspace Structure
children.top_down_role: Instance families whose optimization dynamics occupy a reduced subspace.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Subspace Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear-subspace dependence for objectives whose variation is confined to fewer than the ambient number of directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) satisfy \(U^{\mathsf T}U=I_r\), and write \(P_U=UU^{\mathsf T}\). A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) has active-subspace structure with active space \(\operatorname{range}(U)\) if there exists \(g:\mathbb{R}^r\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \(f(x)=g(U^{\mathsf T}x)\) for all \(x\). Thus \(f(x+v)=f(x)\) for every \(v\in\ker(U^{\mathsf T})\). If \(f\) is differentiable, then \(\nabla f(x)=U\nabla g(U^{\mathsf T}x)\in\operatorname{range}(U)\), so all first-order information lies in an \(r\)-dimensional subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective has an active subspace when it varies only along an r-dimensional linear space and is constant along its orthogonal complement.
assumptions_latex: \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) has orthonormal columns.
\(f\) factors through the map \(x\mapsto U^{\mathsf T}x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=g(U^{\mathsf T}x)\) and, when differentiable, \(\nabla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}(U)\).

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis matrix for the active subspace.
Orthogonal projector onto the active subspace.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact factorization and gradient-range statement are internally consistent and fit the Active-Subspace Structure leaf. No source is supplied for this definition or its first-order-information consequence, so authoritative evidence with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Effective-Dimension Escape
children.top_down_role: Complexity improvements tied to intrinsic dimension rather than ambient dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Dimension Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact oracle reduction showing when ambient-dimensional lower bounds cease to govern a structured instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f(x)=g(U^{\mathsf T}x)\), where \(U\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) has orthonormal columns and \(g:\mathbb{R}^r\to\mathbb{R}\) belongs to a first-order class. A query to \(g\) at \(z\) is simulated by querying \(f\) at \(Uz\), since \(f(Uz)=g(z)\) and \(U^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(Uz)=\nabla g(z)\). Hence any method attaining accuracy \(g(z_T)-\inf g\leq\varepsilon\) in \(T(r,\varepsilon,\theta)\) oracle calls yields \(x_T=Uz_T\) with \(f(x_T)-\inf f\leq\varepsilon\) in the same number of calls. A lower bound driven solely by \(d>r\) therefore does not transfer to this structured class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact factorization through an r-dimensional subspace transfers any r-dimensional first-order guarantee to the ambient problem, invalidating lower bounds that require d independent directions.
assumptions_latex: \(U^{\mathsf T}U=I_r\) and \(f=g\circ U^{\mathsf T}\).
The oracle returns exact function values and gradients.
Accuracy is measured by objective suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_f(\varepsilon)\leq T(r,\varepsilon,\theta)\), independently of the ambient dimension \(d\).

notation.meaning: Number of first-order oracle calls needed for epsilon suboptimality.
Remaining regularity parameters of the reduced problem class.

children.title: Spectral Preconditionability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for instance structure stronger than a worst-case condition-number description.

children.title: Clustered Spectra
children.top_down_role: Instance classes organized by eigenvalue clustering beyond spectral extremes.

knowledge_statements.title: Clustered Spectra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A spectral structure condition stronger than specifying only the extreme eigenvalues or condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) be symmetric positive definite. Its spectrum is \((q,\delta)\)-clustered around positive centers \(c_1<\cdots<c_q\) if \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^q[c_j-\delta,c_j+\delta]\), each interval lies in \((0,\infty)\), and the intervals are pairwise disjoint. The special case \(\delta=0\) means that \(A\) has at most \(q\) distinct eigenvalues. This condition records spectral information absent from \(\kappa(A)=\lambda_{\max}(A)/\lambda_{\min}(A)\): matrices with identical extreme eigenvalues and condition number may have different numbers, widths, and separations of spectral clusters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite matrix has clustered spectrum when all eigenvalues lie in a small number of separated narrow intervals, information not captured by its condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is real, symmetric, and positive definite.
\(c_j-\delta>0\) and the cluster intervals are pairwise disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{spec}(A)\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^q[c_j-\delta,c_j+\delta]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed condition is a coherent explicit convention and fits the Clustered Spectra leaf, but the common-width, disjoint-interval definition is not uniquely standard. A specific authoritative source is needed to establish the intended convention and its relevance beyond the condition number.

children.title: Preconditionable Geometry
children.top_down_role: Instance structure permitting an effective improvement in conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditionable Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric change under which smooth strongly convex quadratic geometry has a substantially smaller effective condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a quadratic objective \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x\) with \(A\succ0\), let \(P\succ0\) be an admissible preconditioner. The geometry is \(P\)-preconditionable with constants \(0<m_P\leq L_P\) if \(m_PI\preceq P^{-1/2}AP^{-1/2}\preceq L_PI\). Under the coordinate change \(x=P^{-1/2}y\), the transformed Hessian is \(P^{-1/2}AP^{-1/2}\), and its condition number is \(\kappa_P=L_P/m_P\). Preconditionability is meaningful only relative to an admissibility model requiring applications of \(P^{-1}\) or \(P^{-1/2}\) to be available at controlled cost; otherwise an exact inverse could trivialize the condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic is preconditionable when an efficiently applicable metric transformation produces a transformed Hessian with a much smaller condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(A\succ0\) and \(P\succ0\).
Applying the chosen preconditioner has controlled computational cost.

notation.meaning: Condition number in the preconditioned metric.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordinate transformation and transformed condition number are correct for the stated quadratic setting, and the condition role fits the leaf. The notion of an admissible preconditioner and its controlled-cost application is essential but not formally specified or cited; a source and a concrete admissibility/cost model are required.

children.title: Condition-Number Description Gaps
children.top_down_role: Cases where a worst-case condition number conceals exploitable spectral organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Number Description Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete quadratic family showing that extreme-eigenvalue condition numbers omit algorithmically relevant spectral distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\mu<L\). Let \(A_2\) be positive definite with spectrum \(\{\mu,L\}\), and let \(A_q\) have \(q\geq3\) distinct eigenvalues including \(\mu\) and \(L\). Both satisfy \(\kappa(A_2)=\kappa(A_q)=L/\mu\). For linear-span first-order methods on quadratics, an error polynomial \(p_t\) of degree at most \(t\), with \(p_t(0)=1\), acts on the spectrum. A degree-two polynomial can vanish on \(\operatorname{spec}(A_2)\), whereas exact annihilation on all eigenvalues of \(A_q\) requires degree at least \(q\). Thus equal condition numbers do not determine exact-step Krylov complexity or capture spectral clustering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two quadratics can share the same condition number while requiring different polynomial degrees for exact solution because their numbers of distinct eigenvalues differ.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\mu<L\) and \(q\geq3\).
The method obeys the standard linear-span oracle model in exact arithmetic.
The initial error has a nonzero component in every eigenspace considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(A_2)=\kappa(A_q)\) but the respective exact annihilation degrees are at most \(2\) and at least \(q\).

notation.meaning: Degree-at-most-t polynomial mapping the initial quadratic error to the current error.
Positive-definite matrix having q distinct eigenvalues.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example appropriately illustrates a condition-number description gap, and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. The polynomial representation and exact-annihilation degree claims depend on the precise linear-span/Krylov oracle model and exact arithmetic; no source is provided for those nontrivial claims.

children.title: Distribution-Specific Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Navigation for problem distributions narrower than a worst-case oracle class.

children.title: Distribution-Specific Instance Classes
children.top_down_role: Problem families restricted by a specified distribution over instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Specific Instance Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-law refinement of an optimization class for distribution-dependent oracle analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal{I},\mathcal{F})\) be a measurable space of optimization instances, where an instance \(I\) specifies an objective, feasible region, starting point, and oracle. A distribution-specific instance class is a pair \((\mathcal{I},\mathbb{P})\), where \(\mathbb{P}\) is a probability measure on \((\mathcal{I},\mathcal{F})\). For a possibly randomized method \(M\), performance is evaluated under the joint law of \(I\sim\mathbb{P}\) and the internal randomness of \(M\). The support of \(\mathbb{P}\), rather than all of \(\mathcal{I}\), determines which instances can contribute to distribution-specific risk or expected complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distribution-specific class equips a measurable optimization instance space with a probability law and evaluates algorithms jointly over sampled instances and algorithmic randomness.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal{I},\mathcal{F})\) is a measurable instance space.
Algorithmic losses and stopping times are measurable under the joint law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal{I},\mathbb{P})\) defines the distribution-specific population used for average-case evaluation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent and matches the Distribution-Specific Instance Classes leaf, including the joint treatment of instance and method randomness. It lacks an optimization-specific source with a precise locator for this measurable-instance formulation and support-based interpretation.

children.title: Average-Case Complexity
children.top_down_role: Rates evaluated over a problem distribution rather than a worst-case class.

knowledge_statements.title: Average-Case Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-error first-order oracle complexity under a fixed distribution of problem instances; other average-case conventions are outside this record.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\sim\mathbb{P}\) be an optimization instance, let \(M\) be a possibly randomized first-order method, and let \(x_t(I,M)\) be its iterate after \(t\) oracle calls. Under the expected-error convention, define the average-case oracle complexity at accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) by \[N_{\mathrm{avg}}(\varepsilon;M,\mathbb{P})=\inf\left\{t\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{E}_{I,M}\left[f_I(x_t(I,M))-f_I^*\right]\leq\varepsilon\right\},\] with the infimum of the empty set interpreted as \(+\infty\). For an admissible method family \(\mathcal{M}\), define \[N_{\mathrm{avg}}^*(\varepsilon;\mathbb{P})=\inf_{M\in\mathcal{M}}N_{\mathrm{avg}}(\varepsilon;M,\mathbb{P}).\] These quantities depend on \(\mathbb{P}\) and, without further uniform or tail assumptions, do not provide an instancewise guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the expected-error convention, average-case complexity is the least number of oracle calls needed to make expected suboptimality at most epsilon under the specified instance distribution and the method's internal randomness; optimizing over an admissible method family gives the corresponding optimal average-case complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is distributed according to \(\mathbb{P}\).
\(M\) is a possibly randomized first-order method and \(x_t(I,M)\) is defined after \(t\) oracle calls.
\(f_I^*=\inf_x f_I(x)\) is finite almost surely.
\(f_I(x_t(I,M))-f_I^*\) is jointly measurable and integrable.
One oracle call is the resource unit, and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{avg}}^*(\varepsilon;\mathbb{P})=\inf_{M\in\mathcal{M}}\inf\{t\in\mathbb{N}:\mathbb{E}_{I,M}[f_I(x_t(I,M))-f_I^*]\leq\varepsilon\}\), under the stated expected-error convention.

notation.meaning: Expected-error average-case oracle complexity for a fixed method and instance distribution.
Optimal objective value for instance I.
Expectation jointly over the sampled instance and the internal randomness of the method.

children.title: Worst-Case Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on comparing distributional guarantees with worst-case oracle lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixture construction separating distributional complexity from worst-case complexity on the same support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an instance distribution assign probability \(1-\delta\) to an easy instance \(I_0\) and probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\) to a hard instance \(I_1\). If a method requires \(N_0(\varepsilon)\) and \(N_1(\varepsilon)\) oracle calls, respectively, then its expected stopping complexity is \[(1-\delta)N_0(\varepsilon)+\delta N_1(\varepsilon),\] while its worst-case complexity over \(\operatorname{supp}(\mathbb{P})\) is \(\max\{N_0(\varepsilon),N_1(\varepsilon)\}\). Taking \(\delta\) arbitrarily small makes the average contribution of \(I_1\) negligible without reducing its worst-case cost. Therefore an average-case upper bound transfers to a worst-case bound only with additional uniform or tail-control assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rare hard instance can contribute negligibly to expected complexity while determining worst-case complexity, so average-case guarantees do not transfer without uniform or tail control.
assumptions_latex: \(N_i(\varepsilon)\) is the stopping cost on instance \(I_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[N]=(1-\delta)N_0+\delta N_1\) does not uniformly bound \(\sup_{I\in\operatorname{supp}(\mathbb{P})}N_I=\max\{N_0,N_1\}\).

notation.meaning: Probability of sampling the hard instance.
Oracle calls needed for epsilon accuracy on instance i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-point mixture correctly separates expected stopping cost from the maximum cost on the support, and failure_boundary is appropriate for the leaf. No citation is supplied for the average-to-worst-case transfer limitation or its required uniform/tail-control qualifications.
